a.title: A Day for Animals
text: October 4 is World Animal Day. It is a day to think about animals and how we treat them.
Animals share our world. Some live in our homes, like cats and dogs. Others live in forests, oceans, and the sky.
On this day, people learn how to care for animals. They talk about pets, farm animals, and wild animals in danger.
Many animals need our help. Some lose their homes when forests are cut down. Some need a kind family to adopt them.
You can help too. Be gentle with pets. Give them food, water, and love. Never leave an animal alone in the cold.
When we are kind to animals, the whole world becomes a better home for everyone.

opts: Saint Francis and his great love of animals
Why so many forests are being cut down
Caring about animals and how we treat them

q.why: 全文講善待動物。

opts: to take an animal home and care for it

q.why: adopt = 領養。

q.why: 線索：“Give them food, water, and love.”

q.why: 文中建議領養代替購買，也提醒不要遺棄。

tz: 10 月 4 日是世界動物日。這是一個想一想動物、以及我們如何對待牠們的日子。
動物和我們共享這個世界。有些住在我們家裡，像貓和狗；其他的住在森林、海洋和天空中。
在這一天，人們學習如何照顧動物。他們討論寵物、農場動物，以及面臨危險的野生動物。
很多動物需要我們的幫助。有些動物在森林被砍伐時失去了家；有些需要一個善良的家庭來領養牠們。
你也可以幫忙。溫柔地對待寵物，給牠們食物、水和愛。永遠不要把動物獨自留在寒冷中。
當我們善待動物，整個世界就會成為一個對大家都更好的家。

b.title: Sharing the Planet
text: Every year on 4 October, people mark World Animal Day, a global event that asks a simple question: how well do we treat the creatures we share the planet with?
The date honours Saint Francis of Assisi, a man remembered for his love of animals. Today it is used to raise awareness of animal welfare all over the world.

The concerns are wide. Pets are sometimes abandoned when families no longer want them. Farm animals are often kept in poor conditions. And in the wild, many species are losing their homes as forests are cleared and the climate warms.

There is also good news. Animal shelters find new homes for millions of pets each year, and laws in many countries now protect animals from cruelty. Some once-endangered species have slowly recovered.
Small choices matter. Adopting a pet instead of buying one, supporting local shelters, and simply treating animals with respect all make a difference.
The message of the day is gentle but important: animals cannot speak for themselves, so it is up to people to speak, and act, for them.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The day raises awareness of animal welfare and our duty to animals.
The date was chosen to honour Saint Francis of Assisi's love of animals.
Animal shelters now find new homes for millions of pets each year.
Many wild species are losing their homes as forests are cleared.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；其他只是細節。

q.q: Whom does the date honour?
opts: The founder of the first animal shelter
Saint Francis of Assisi
Mother Teresa
The United Nations
q.why: 原文：“The date honours Saint Francis of Assisi, a man remembered for his love of animals.”

q.q: What is described as a threat to wild species?
opts: Being abandoned by families who no longer want them
Being kept in poor conditions on crowded farms
Losing their homes as forests are cleared
Being moved into animal shelters far from home
q.why: 文中；遺棄與飼養條件指的是寵物與農場動物。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “abandoned” is closest in meaning to ___.
opts: adopted by a new, loving family
kept in poor, crowded conditions
protected by the law from cruelty

q.why: abandon = 遺棄。

q.q: Why does the writer say it is “up to people to speak…for them”?
opts: People should talk to their pets more often at home
Only trained experts can really understand animals
Laws in every country already protect every animal
Animals cannot speak for themselves, so we must act
q.why: 線索：“The message of the day is gentle but important: animals cannot speak for themselves, so it is up to people to speak, and act, for them.”

q.q: A classmate says: “Things are hopeless for animals.” Which evidence from the text best challenges this?
opts: Shelters rehome millions of pets, and some species recovered
Farm animals are often kept in poor and crowded conditions
Pets are sometimes abandoned when families no longer want them
Forests are being cleared and the climate keeps getting warmer
q.why: 文中「好消息」段落反駁了「沒希望」的說法。

tr.en: Today it is used to raise awareness of animal welfare all over the world.
tr.zh: 如今，這一天被用來提高全世界對動物福利的意識。

tr.en: Pets are sometimes abandoned when families no longer want them.
tr.zh: 當家庭不再想要寵物時，寵物有時候會被遺棄。

tr.en: Animal shelters find new homes for millions of pets each year, and laws in many countries now protect animals from cruelty.
tr.zh: 動物收容所每年為數百萬隻寵物找到新家，而許多國家的法律現在也保護動物免於受虐。

tz: 每年 10 月 4 日，人們會紀念世界動物日；這個全球性的活動提出一個簡單的問題：我們對待和我們共享地球的生物，到底好不好？
這個日期是為了紀念阿西西的聖方濟各，一位以熱愛動物而被人記住的人。今天，這一天被用來提升全世界對動物福利的重視。
需要關心的問題很廣。寵物有時會在家庭不想要牠們時被遺棄；農場動物常常被飼養在惡劣的環境中；而在野外，許多物種正隨著森林被砍伐、氣候暖化而失去棲地。
也有好消息。動物收容所每年為數百萬隻寵物找到新家，許多國家現在也有法律保護動物免於虐待。一些曾經瀕臨絕種的物種，已經慢慢恢復了。
小小的選擇也很重要。用領養代替購買寵物、支持在地的收容所，以及單純地尊重動物，都能帶來改變。
這一天的訊息溫和卻重要：動物無法為自己發聲，所以要靠人類為牠們發聲，也為牠們行動。

ph.exzh: 這張海報提醒大家要節約用水。

ph.ex: He no longer plays video games every night.
ph.exzh: 他不再每晚打電動了。

ph.ex: Adopt a pet instead of buying one.
ph.exzh: 用領養代替購買寵物。

ph.ex: Even small changes can make a difference.
ph.exzh: 即使是小小的改變也能帶來不同。

ph.ex: It is up to you to choose.
ph.exzh: 要由你自己來選。

c.title: The Creatures We Live Among
text: Each 4 October, World Animal Day invites a reckoning of sorts: an annual pause to ask what humans owe the millions of other species with which they share a crowded planet.

The day traces its spirit to Saint Francis of Assisi, the medieval friar who spoke of animals as brothers and sisters. Yet its modern purpose is less devotional than practical — to focus attention on animal welfare, from the family pet to the vanishing tiger.

The moral landscape is complicated. Few people wish animals harm, and yet human choices — what we eat, what we buy, how we build — shape the fate of countless creatures we will never see. Habitat loss, driven by farming and a warming climate, remains the greatest threat to wild species.

Progress, where it exists, tends to be quiet. Stronger animal-protection laws, the steady work of shelters and sanctuaries, and shifting attitudes toward adoption have all improved millions of individual lives, even as the larger picture stays fragile.

Perhaps that is the day's real lesson: that kindness to animals is not sentimentality but a measure of a society's character, and that a species clever enough to reshape the Earth bears some responsibility for the others living on it.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Progress on animal welfare has been quiet, but it has been real.
Kindness to animals reflects a society's character and responsibility.
Human choices shape the fate of many animals we will never see.
Animal shelters and new laws have now largely solved animal welfare problems.
q.why: 其他選項是文中論點的一部分。

q.q: In paragraph 1, “a reckoning of sorts” suggests the day is ___.
opts: a serious moment of reflection about what we owe animals
a cheerful celebration with parties, gifts and pet shows
a day to count how many animal species still exist
a day to find and punish people who hurt animals
q.why: reckoning = 清算、反省。

q.q: What does “human choices…shape the fate of countless creatures we will never see” imply?
opts: Only people who actually meet wild animals can affect them
Animals we never see are not really affected by what happens in cities
Everyday choices — food, shopping, building — affect many animals
Pets deserve more attention than animals living in the wild
q.why: 線索：“Few people wish animals harm, and yet human choices — what we eat, what we buy, how we build — shape the fate of countless creatures we will never see.”

q.q: How does the writer regard kindness to animals?
opts: As a pleasant but ultimately unimportant habit
As a matter best left to animal welfare experts
As a goal most societies have already achieved
As a serious measure of a society's character
q.why: 語氣。

q.q: What is the role of paragraph 4 (“Progress…tends to be quiet”)?
opts: To argue that the problem has now largely been solved
To list the new animal-protection laws in full detail
To criticise animal shelters for working too slowly
To note real but modest progress in a fragile picture
q.why: 結構。

q.q: Which personal choice best reflects the writer's idea that unseen animals are affected by everyday decisions?
opts: Checking whether products you buy come from cleared forests
Feeding a stray cat that you happen to see one afternoon
Visiting a zoo to see endangered animals for yourself
Posting a photo of your pet online on World Animal Day
q.why: 日常消費會間接影響看不到的動物。

tz: 每年 10 月 4 日，世界動物日都邀請我們做一次某種意義上的清算：每年停下來一次，問問人類虧欠了那些和我們共享這個擁擠星球的數百萬個物種什麼。
這一天的精神可以追溯到阿西西的聖方濟各，那位把動物稱為兄弟姊妹的中世紀修士。然而，它在現代的目的與其說是宗教性的，不如說是實際的——把注意力集中在動物福利上，從家裡的寵物到正在消失的老虎。
道德的圖景是複雜的。很少有人希望動物受到傷害，但人類的選擇——我們吃什麼、買什麼、怎麼建設——決定了無數我們永遠不會看見的生物的命運。由農業和氣候暖化所造成的棲地喪失，仍然是野生物種面臨的最大威脅。
進步即使存在，也往往是安靜的。更嚴格的動物保護法、收容所和保護區持續不斷的努力，以及人們對領養態度的轉變，已經改善了數百萬個個別的生命，儘管整體的情況仍然脆弱。
也許這才是這一天真正的啟示：善待動物不是多愁善感，而是衡量一個社會品格的標準；而一個聰明到足以改造地球的物種，對生活在地球上的其他物種負有某種責任。

ph.ex: The test was less about speed than about care.

ph.ex: Adults bear responsibility for children's safety.
ph.exzh: 大人對孩子的安全負有責任。

topic: A Nobel Prize for Controlling the Brain with Light
zh: 用光控制大腦：2026 諾貝爾醫學獎
tag: Nobel Medicine · 諾貝爾醫學獎

a.title: Turning Brain Cells On with Light
text: On October 5, 2026, three scientists won the Nobel Prize in Medicine. Their names are Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel.
They found a way to control brain cells with light. This idea is called optogenetics.
The brain has billions of tiny cells. These cells send signals that make us move, think, and feel.
The scientists took a special protein from algae — tiny green plants that live in water. This protein reacts to light.
They put the protein inside brain cells. Now, when light shines on a cell, the cell turns on. When the light stops, the cell turns off.
This tool helps scientists understand the brain. One day, it may even help blind people see again.

q.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: Tiny green plants called algae that live in water
A prize for controlling brain cells with light
How the human brain has billions of cells
How light has made many blind people see again
q.why: 全文講用光控制腦細胞的獲獎研究。

q.q: How many scientists won the prize?
opts: Two
Four
Three
One
q.why: 文中：三位科學家。

q.q: Where did the special protein come from?
opts: The human brain itself
Fish that glow in the sea
A machine in a laboratory
Algae (tiny green plants)
q.why: 原文：“The scientists took a special protein from algae — tiny green plants that live in water.”

q.q: In the text, “control” means ___.
opts: to make something do what you want
to watch something very carefully
to repair something that is broken
to measure how big something is
q.why: control = 控制。

q.q: Why is this tool useful?
opts: It has already cured all brain diseases in many hospitals
It makes tiny green algae grow much faster in water
It helps us understand the brain and may help blind people
It can replace doctors when they are too busy to help
q.why: 線索：“One day, it may even help blind people see again.”

q.q: A scientist wants to know which brain cells make a mouse feel hungry. How could this tool help?
opts: Switch chosen brain cells on with light and see if it eats
Feed the mouse some algae and see if it feels less hungry
Shine a bright light into the mouse's eyes and nowhere else
Count all of the brain cells inside the mouse's brain
q.why: 開關特定神經元、觀察行為——正是光遺傳學的用途。

gt.en: They found a way to control brain cells with light.
gt.zh: 他們找到了用光來控制腦細胞的方法。

gt.en: The brain has billions of tiny cells.
gt.zh: 大腦有數十億個微小的細胞。

gt.en: The scientists took a special protein from algae — tiny green plants that live in water.
gt.zh: 科學家從藻類——生活在水中的微小綠色植物——取出一種特別的蛋白質。

gt.en: They put the protein inside brain cells.
gt.zh: 他們把這種蛋白質放進腦細胞裡。

tz: 2026 年 10 月 5 日，三位科學家獲得了諾貝爾醫學獎。他們的名字是卡爾・戴瑟羅斯、彼得・赫格曼和格奧爾格・納格爾。
他們找到了一種用光來控制腦細胞的方法。這個概念叫做光遺傳學。
大腦裡有數十億個微小的細胞。這些細胞會傳送訊號，讓我們能夠移動、思考和感受。
科學家從藻類——住在水裡的微小綠色植物——身上取出一種特別的蛋白質。這種蛋白質會對光產生反應。
他們把這種蛋白質放進腦細胞裡。現在，當光照到細胞時，細胞就會啟動；光一停，細胞就會關閉。
這個工具幫助科學家了解大腦。有一天，它甚至可能幫助盲人重新看見。

ph.ex: Scientists found a way to clean the river.
ph.exzh: 科學家找到了清理河川的方法。

ph.ex: Some plants react to touch.
ph.exzh: 有些植物會對觸碰產生反應。

ph.ex: The lights turn on when it gets dark.
ph.exzh: 天一黑燈就會亮。

ph.ex: Please turn off your phone in class.
ph.exzh: 上課時請把手機關機。

b.title: Optogenetics: Switching Neurons On and Off
text: On 5 October 2026, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel for a powerful technique known as optogenetics.

The brain is made of billions of nerve cells, or neurons, that communicate using tiny electrical signals. For a long time, scientists could watch these signals, but they could not switch a single neuron on or off whenever they wanted.
The breakthrough began with green algae. Hegemann and Nagel discovered that these simple organisms carry light-sensitive proteins called channelrhodopsins, which open when light hits them.
Deisseroth then had a bold idea: place these proteins inside neurons. Shine a blue light, and the neuron fires; take the light away, and it falls silent — all within milliseconds.
This gave researchers a precise 'switch' for the brain. By turning chosen neurons on and off, they can study how brain circuits control movement, memory, and mood.
Optogenetics is also moving toward medicine. In one remarkable case reported in Nature Medicine, light-sensitive proteins helped restore partial vision to a man who had been blind for decades.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Hegemann and Nagel discovered light-sensitive proteins in green algae.
Blue light makes treated neurons fire, while yellow light silences them.
Optogenetics switches neurons on and off with light and won a Nobel Prize.
Optogenetics has already restored vision in most blind patients today.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；第四項過度誇大。

q.q: What did Hegemann and Nagel discover?
opts: A way to grow brand-new neurons in the lab
Light-sensitive proteins in green algae
A new kind of scanner that photographs the brain
A cure for blindness that works in most patients
q.why: 原文：“Hegemann and Nagel discovered that these simple organisms carry light-sensitive proteins called channelrhodopsins, which open when light hits them.”

q.q: What happens when blue light hits a treated neuron?
opts: It switches off at once
It is slowly destroyed
It changes colour to blue
It fires — it turns on
q.why: 原文：“Shine a blue light, and the neuron fires; take the light away, and it falls silent — all within milliseconds.”

q.q: In paragraph 5, a “switch” for the brain means ___.
opts: a way to turn neurons on and off
a wire connected directly to the brain
a kind of brain surgery done with light
a medicine that calms the brain down
q.why: switch = 開關。

q.q: Why is optogenetics important for medicine?
opts: It is already used in almost every hospital today
It will soon replace all medicines for the brain
It has already restored full vision to most blind patients
It could lead to treatments, such as restoring vision
q.why: 線索：“In one remarkable case reported in Nature Medicine, light-sensitive proteins helped restore partial vision to a man who had been blind for decades.”

q.q: A headline says: “Light therapy now cures all brain diseases!” Based on the text, how should you judge it?
opts: Accurate — the text says it has cured most brain diseases
Exaggerated — it could lead to treatments, not cure everything
Accurate, because winning a Nobel Prize proves that it works
Exaggerated — the text says it has no medical use at all
q.why: 文中只說可能帶來治療，標題過度誇大。

tr.en: The brain is made of billions of nerve cells, or neurons, that communicate using tiny electrical signals.
tr.zh: 大腦由數十億個神經細胞（也就是神經元）組成，它們用微小的電訊號彼此溝通。

tr.en: Hegemann and Nagel discovered that these simple organisms carry light-sensitive proteins called channelrhodopsins, which open when light hits them.
tr.zh: 黑格曼和納格爾發現，這些簡單的生物帶有一種叫做通道視紫質的感光蛋白質，光一照到它們就會打開。

tr.en: By turning chosen neurons on and off, they can study how brain circuits control movement, memory, and mood.
tr.zh: 藉由開啟和關閉特定的神經元，他們可以研究大腦迴路如何控制動作、記憶和情緒。

tz: 2026 年 10 月 5 日，諾貝爾生理學或醫學獎頒給了卡爾・戴瑟羅斯、彼得・赫格曼和格奧爾格・納格爾，表彰一項叫做「光遺傳學」的強大技術。
大腦由數十億個神經細胞（神經元）組成，它們用微小的電訊號彼此溝通。很長一段時間，科學家可以觀察這些訊號，卻無法隨心所欲地打開或關閉單一個神經元。
這項突破從綠藻開始。赫格曼和納格爾發現，這些簡單的生物帶有一種叫做「通道視紫質」的感光蛋白質，光一照到就會打開。
戴瑟羅斯接著想到一個大膽的點子：把這些蛋白質放進神經元裡。照上藍光，神經元就會發出訊號；把光移開，它就安靜下來——這一切都在幾毫秒內發生。
這讓研究人員擁有了一個控制大腦的精準「開關」。透過打開和關閉選定的神經元，他們可以研究大腦迴路如何控制動作、記憶和情緒。
光遺傳學也正在走向醫療。在《自然醫學》期刊報導的一個驚人案例中，感光蛋白質幫助一位失明了幾十年的男子恢復了部分視力。

ph.ex: I haven't seen my cousin for a long time.
ph.exzh: 我很久沒看到我表哥了。

ph.ex: You can switch the lamp on or off with your voice.
ph.exzh: 你可以用聲音開關這盞燈。
ph.m: switch a single neuron on or off

ph.ex: If you take the light away, the plant stops growing.
ph.exzh: 如果拿走光線，植物就會停止生長。

ph.ex: The crowd fell silent when the music began.
ph.exzh: 音樂開始時，人群安靜了下來。

ph.ex: The project is moving toward its goal.
ph.exzh: 這個計畫正朝目標邁進。

c.title: A Light Switch for the Mind
text: When the Nobel Assembly announced the 2026 Prize in Physiology or Medicine on 5 October, it honoured a discovery that has quietly transformed neuroscience: optogenetics, the art of controlling individual neurons with nothing more than a beam of light.

The award was shared equally by Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University, and Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel of Germany. Their work answered a question that had frustrated researchers for generations — how to study the living brain not by observing it, but by commanding it.

The key came from an unlikely source: pond-dwelling green algae. Hegemann and Nagel showed that these microbes steer toward light using proteins called channelrhodopsins, molecular gates that spring open the instant light strikes them.

Deisseroth's insight was to borrow these gates and install them in mammalian neurons. A pulse of blue light could now make a chosen neuron fire, while darkness silenced it — with a speed and precision that earlier methods could never match.

The consequences were profound. Because behaviour, emotion and memory all arise from the firing of particular circuits, scientists could finally test cause and effect directly, switching circuits on and off to see exactly what each one does.

The technique is now reaching the clinic. In a landmark trial published in Nature Medicine, optogenetic therapy restored a measure of sight to a patient blinded by an inherited eye disease — a hint of future treatments for blindness, paralysis and disorders of the brain.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: How light-sensitive proteins were first discovered in single-celled algae
Why the living brain could not be studied at all before the 2000s
How optogenetics is already widely used to treat brain disorders
How optogenetics lets scientists command neurons with light, earning a Nobel
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: According to the text, what was the scientists' key insight?
opts: To grow living neurons inside algae in the laboratory
To use electric shocks instead of light to control cells
To install algae's light-sensitive gates in mammal neurons
To study only dead brain tissue under bright light
q.why: 原文：“Deisseroth's insight was to borrow these gates and install them in mammalian neurons.”

q.q: What makes optogenetics better than earlier methods?
opts: It needs no equipment or genes of any kind
Its speed and precision in switching neurons
It is far cheaper than all other methods
It can be used safely on any patient today
q.why: 原文：“A pulse of blue light could now make a chosen neuron fire, while darkness silenced it — with a speed and precision that earlier methods could never match.”

q.q: In paragraph 1, “transformed” most nearly means ___.
opts: changed completely
slowed down a lot
copied exactly
explained clearly
q.why: transform = 徹底改變。

q.q: What can we infer about the future of optogenetics?
opts: It is already used to treat most brain disorders in clinics
It will only ever be useful for studying algae in ponds
It will probably be banned because of safety worries
It may lead to treatments for blindness and brain disorders
q.why: 文中用 may。

q.q: This breakthrough began with curiosity about pond algae. What does this suggest about funding science?
opts: Only research with clear medical goals deserves any funding
Studying pond algae is a waste of money for medical science
Basic research with no obvious use can lead to breakthroughs
Scientists should avoid following their curiosity in research
q.why: 出於好奇的基礎研究也可能帶來重大突破。

tz: 諾貝爾大會在 10 月 5 日宣布 2026 年生理學或醫學獎時，表彰的是一項默默改變了神經科學的發現：光遺傳學——只用一道光束就能控制單一神經元的技術。
這個獎由史丹佛大學的卡爾・戴瑟羅斯，以及德國的彼得・赫格曼和格奧爾格・納格爾平分。他們的研究回答了一個困擾研究人員好幾個世代的問題：如何研究活生生的大腦——不是靠觀察它，而是靠指揮它。
關鍵來自一個意想不到的地方：住在池塘裡的綠藻。赫格曼和納格爾證明，這些微生物會利用一種叫做「通道視紫質」的蛋白質朝光源移動；這些分子閘門在光照到的那一瞬間就會彈開。
戴瑟羅斯的洞見是借用這些閘門，把它們安裝到哺乳動物的神經元裡。現在，一道藍光脈衝就能讓選定的神經元發出訊號，而黑暗則讓它安靜下來——速度和精準度是過去任何方法都比不上的。
這帶來了深遠的影響。由於行為、情緒和記憶都來自特定迴路的活動，科學家終於可以直接檢驗因果關係：打開和關閉迴路，看看每一個迴路到底做了什麼。
這項技術現在正進入臨床。在一項發表於《自然醫學》的里程碑試驗中，光遺傳療法讓一位因遺傳性眼疾而失明的病人恢復了一定程度的視力——這預示了未來治療失明、癱瘓和腦部疾病的可能性。

ph.ex: It was nothing more than a small mistake.
ph.exzh: 那只不過是一個小錯誤。

ph.ex: This shop has been in the family for generations.
ph.exzh: 這家店在這個家族裡傳了好幾代。

ph.ex: The box sprang open when I touched it.
ph.exzh: 我一碰盒子就彈開了。

ph.ex: The dog barked the instant the door opened.
ph.exzh: 門一開狗就叫了。

ph.ex: Many problems arise from poor sleep.
ph.exzh: 很多問題是因為睡不好而產生的。

ph.ex: The medicine gave her a measure of relief.
ph.exzh: 這種藥讓她舒緩了一些。

discuss: Optogenetics can switch brain cells on and off. What exciting uses can you imagine — and what worries might it raise?
This huge breakthrough started with curiosity about pond algae. Why do important discoveries so often begin with 'useless' questions about nature?
If doctors could one day switch neurons on and off to treat illness, where should we draw the line?

topic: World Teachers' Day
zh: 世界教師日
src: VOA · UNESCO · The New York Times

a.title: Thank You, Teachers
text: October 5 is World Teachers' Day. It is a day to say thank you to teachers everywhere.
Teachers help us learn to read, write, count, and think. They also teach us how to be kind and work with others.
A good teacher does more than give lessons. They listen, they care, and they help students believe in themselves.
Being a teacher is not easy. They work long hours, plan lessons, and worry about every student.
In many countries, there are not enough teachers. The world needs millions more so that every child can go to school.
On this day, we say two small but powerful words to our teachers: thank you.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Why the world does not have enough teachers
How teachers can use AI to plan better lessons each day
Saying thank you to teachers and why they matter
Why AI and computers cannot teach children
q.why: 全文講感謝老師與老師的重要。

q.q: When is World Teachers' Day?
opts: September 28
October 15
September 5
October 5
q.why: 原文：“October 5 is World Teachers' Day.”

q.q: What does the text say about the number of teachers?
opts: There are too many teachers
The world needs millions more
Every country has enough teachers
Teachers are being replaced by machines
q.why: 原文：“The world needs millions more so that every child can go to school.”

q.q: “Believe in” a student means to ___.
opts: have confidence in the student
give the student a difficult test
punish the student for mistakes
ignore the student in class
q.why: believe in = 相信。

q.q: What two “powerful words” does the text end with?
opts: “Good luck”
“Well done”
“Keep going”
“Thank you”
q.why: 線索：“On this day, we say two small but powerful words to our teachers: thank you.”

q.q: Which is the best way to celebrate World Teachers' Day, based on the text?
opts: Writing a card that tells a teacher how they helped you
Asking the teacher to give the class less homework
Asking the teacher to take the whole day off to rest at home
Skipping class so the teacher can have a rest
q.why: 文章強調說聲謝謝、讓老師知道他們的影響。

gt.en: Teachers help us learn to read, write, count, and think.
gt.zh: 老師幫助我們學會閱讀、寫字、算數和思考。

gt.en: A good teacher does more than give lessons.
gt.zh: 一位好老師做的不只是上課而已。

gt.en: They work long hours, plan lessons, and worry about every student.
gt.zh: 他們工作很長的時間、備課，還為每一個學生操心。

gt.en: In many countries, there are not enough teachers.
gt.zh: 在許多國家，老師的人數不夠。

tz: 10 月 5 日是世界教師節。這是一個向世界各地的老師說謝謝的日子。
老師幫助我們學會讀、寫、算和思考，也教我們如何善待別人、與人合作。
一位好老師做的不只是上課。他們會傾聽、會關心，也會幫助學生相信自己。
當老師並不容易。他們工作很長的時間、準備課程，還會擔心每一個學生。
在許多國家，老師的人數不夠。世界還需要好幾百萬名老師，才能讓每個孩子都能上學。
在這一天，我們對老師說兩個小小卻很有力量的字：謝謝。

ph.ex: Let's say thank you to the cleaners.
ph.exzh: 我們向清潔人員說聲謝謝吧。

ph.ex: Good teams know how to work with others.
ph.exzh: 好的團隊知道如何與他人合作。

ph.ex: A home is more than a house.
ph.exzh: 家不只是一棟房子。

ph.ex: My coach always believed in me.
ph.exzh: 我的教練一直都相信我。

b.title: The People Who Shape Us
text: Each year on 5 October, UNESCO leads the world in celebrating World Teachers' Day, a moment to honour the people who quietly shape every other profession.
Teachers do far more than deliver facts. They spark curiosity, build confidence, and are often the first adults outside the family to believe in a child's future.

Yet the job is under strain. Many teachers work long unpaid hours, face crowded classrooms, and earn less than others with similar training. In some places, respect for the profession has slowly faded.
The world also faces a shortage. The United Nations estimates that tens of millions of new teachers are needed so that every child can receive a decent education, especially in poorer regions.
Technology is changing the classroom too. Useful tools, and even AI, can support teaching, but few believe they can replace the patience, warmth, and judgement of a real teacher.
The day's message is simple: a society that wants a better future must value, support, and fairly pay the people it trusts to build it.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: UNESCO leads World Teachers' Day, held every year on 5 October.
The day honours teachers, whose vital work is under growing strain.
Teachers face long unpaid hours, stagnant pay and crowded classrooms.
Technology and AI can support teaching but cannot replace it.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: Who leads World Teachers' Day?
opts: UNICEF
The World Bank
UNESCO
Each country's government
q.why: 原文：“Each year on 5 October, UNESCO leads the world in celebrating World Teachers' Day, a moment to honour the people who quietly shape every other profession.”

q.q: Which is a problem teachers face, according to the text?
opts: Too much free time between their lessons
Too few lessons to plan for each week
Students who learn much too fast for them
Long unpaid hours and crowded classrooms
q.why: 原文：“Many teachers work long unpaid hours, face crowded classrooms, and earn less than others with similar training.”

q.q: In paragraph 4, a “shortage” means ___.
opts: not enough of something
too much of something
a short staff meeting
a small, crowded classroom
q.why: shortage = 短缺。

q.q: What is the writer's view of technology and AI in teaching?
opts: They should replace most teachers in the future
They are completely useless in today's schools
They can help, but cannot replace a real teacher
They make teachers lazy and less careful
q.why: 線索：“Useful tools, and even AI, can support teaching, but few believe they can replace the patience, warmth, and judgement of a real teacher.”

q.q: A city plans to solve its teacher shortage by replacing teachers with AI tutors. Based on the text, what is the strongest concern?
opts: AI cannot replace a teacher's patience, warmth and judgement
AI tutors would cost the city far too much money to buy
Most students would prefer to learn from books instead
AI tutors work well, so the city should replace teachers quickly
q.why: 作者認為 AI 無法取代老師的耐心、溫暖與判斷。

tr.en: They spark curiosity, build confidence, and are often the first adults outside the family to believe in a child's future.
tr.zh: 他們激發好奇心、建立自信，而且常常是家人以外第一個相信孩子未來的大人。

tr.en: In some places, respect for the profession has slowly faded.
tr.zh: 在某些地方，人們對這個職業的尊重已經漸漸淡去。

tr.en: Useful tools, and even AI, can support teaching, but few believe they can replace the patience, warmth, and judgement of a real teacher.
tr.zh: 好用的工具、甚至人工智慧都能輔助教學，但很少人相信它們能取代真正老師的耐心、溫暖和判斷力。

tz: 每年 10 月 5 日，聯合國教科文組織帶領全世界慶祝世界教師節，這是一個向那些默默塑造了其他所有職業的人致敬的時刻。
老師做的遠遠不只是傳授知識。他們點燃好奇心、建立自信，而且常常是家人之外，第一個相信孩子未來的大人。
然而，這份工作正承受壓力。許多老師長時間無薪加班、面對擁擠的教室，薪水也比受過類似訓練的人少。在某些地方，人們對這個職業的尊重已經慢慢淡去。
世界也面臨師資短缺。聯合國估計，需要數千萬名新老師，才能讓每個孩子都接受像樣的教育，尤其是在比較貧窮的地區。
科技也在改變教室。好用的工具、甚至人工智慧，都能輔助教學，但很少人相信它們能取代一位真正老師的耐心、溫暖和判斷力。
這一天的訊息很簡單：一個想要更好未來的社會，必須重視、支持並公平地支付那些它託付去打造未來的人。

ph.ex: She does far more than her job asks.
ph.exzh: 她做的遠遠超過工作要求。

ph.ex: The old bridge is under strain from heavy trucks.
ph.exzh: 老橋承受著重型卡車的壓力。

ph.ex: The colours of the poster have faded.
ph.exzh: 海報的顏色已經褪了。

ph.ex: Speak clearly so that everyone can hear you.
ph.exzh: 說清楚一點，讓大家都聽得到。

ph.ex: Few believe that robots can replace friends.
ph.exzh: 很少人相信機器人能取代朋友。

c.title: In Praise of the Teacher
text: On 5 October the world observes World Teachers' Day, an occasion easy to sentimentalise and just as easy to overlook. Behind the greeting cards lies a serious claim: that no profession does more to determine a nation's future, and few are asked to do so much with so little.

The work resists measurement. A teacher's influence — a question that sparks a career, a word of belief on a hard day — often surfaces years later, in lives the teacher never sees. What can be measured tells a harder story: rising workloads, stagnant pay, and, in many places, a slow erosion of public respect.

The result is a global shortage. UNESCO warns that the world needs tens of millions more teachers to meet its education goals, a gap widest precisely where schooling is most needed. Recruiting them is one thing; keeping them, when so many leave within a few years, is another.

Into this arrives technology, promising to lighten the load. Well-designed tools can indeed help, but the enthusiasm for automation can obscure a stubborn truth: learning is relational. A screen can deliver information; it cannot notice the quiet child at the back of the room.
That, in the end, is what the day defends — not a job title, but a human relationship on which almost everything else depends.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Teaching is a demanding human relationship that deserves real support.
Above all, teachers need better technology to cope with their work.
Teaching is an easy, well-paid job that society already respects.
Teachers' Day is mainly about sending cards and saying thank you.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “stagnant pay” means pay that ___.
opts: rises very quickly
does not rise
is always paid late
is very high already
q.why: stagnant = 停滯的。

q.q: What does “learning is relational” mean?
opts: Learning is really only about memorising facts
Relatives at home must teach children instead
Learning works best when students study alone at home with apps
Learning depends on human relationships, not just facts
q.why: 線索：“That, in the end, is what the day defends — not a job title, but a human relationship on which almost everything else depends.”

q.q: How would you describe the writer's attitude toward teachers?
opts: Critical and dismissive of teachers' complaints
Neutral and uninterested in teachers' problems
Admiring and protective, while facing hard realities
Admiring teachers, while hoping AI will take over their work
q.why: 敬佩、維護，也正視困境。

q.q: What is the purpose of paragraph 4 (about technology)?
opts: To argue that AI should run classrooms in the near future
To list useful apps that teachers can use in their lessons
To admit technology helps but cannot replace the human bond
To criticise teachers who refuse to use any technology
q.why: 第四段。

q.q: Which policy would best show society 'values' teachers, according to the writer?
opts: Fair pay, smaller classes and respect for the profession
More greeting cards and flowers on World Teachers' Day
Replacing teachers with recorded video lessons online
Longer school days so teachers can finish their work
q.why: 作者指出薪資停滯、班級擁擠等問題，真正的支持要改善這些。

tz: 10 月 5 日，全世界紀念世界教師節；這個日子很容易被弄得多愁善感，也同樣容易被忽略。在賀卡的背後，是一個嚴肅的主張：沒有哪一個職業比教師更能決定一個國家的未來，也很少有職業被要求用這麼少的資源做這麼多的事。
這份工作難以被衡量。一位老師的影響——一個開啟一段職業生涯的問題、在辛苦的一天裡一句相信你的話——常常要好幾年後，才在老師從未看見的人生中浮現。而能被衡量的部分，說的是一個更艱難的故事：工作量增加、薪水停滯，而且在許多地方，公眾的尊重正慢慢流失。
結果是全球性的短缺。聯合國教科文組織警告，世界還需要數千萬名老師才能達成教育目標，而缺口最大的，正是最需要學校教育的地方。招募他們是一回事；當這麼多人在幾年內就離開時，留住他們又是另一回事。
科技在這時登場，承諾要減輕負擔。設計良好的工具確實能有幫助，但對自動化的熱情，可能會掩蓋一個頑固的事實：學習是建立在關係上的。螢幕可以傳遞資訊，卻注意不到坐在教室後面那個安靜的孩子。
說到底，這一天所捍衛的，不是一個職稱，而是一段人與人之間的關係——幾乎所有其他事情都倚賴著它。

ph.ex: Small acts of kindness are easy to overlook.
ph.exzh: 小小的善舉很容易被忽略。

ph.ex: They did so much with so little.
ph.exzh: 他們用這麼少的資源做了這麼多事。

ph.ex: Happiness resists measurement.
ph.exzh: 快樂很難衡量。

ph.ex: Years later, she still remembered his words.
ph.exzh: 多年後，她仍記得他說的話。

ph.p: it is one thing … ; it is another
ph.ex: Starting is one thing; finishing is another.
ph.exzh: 開始是一回事，完成又是另一回事。

ph.ex: In the end, it's about people, not machines.
ph.exzh: 說到底，重要的是人，不是機器。

discuss: Think of a teacher who influenced you. What did they do that mattered?
Teachers are often underpaid. How should society show that it values them?
Can technology or AI ever replace a human teacher? What can it not do?

topic: Catching Ghost Particles Under the Ice
zh: 在冰層下捕捉幽靈粒子：2026 諾貝爾物理獎
tag: Nobel Physics · 諾貝爾物理獎

a.title: A Giant Telescope Made of Ice
text: On October 6, 2026, a scientist named Francis Halzen won the Nobel Prize in Physics.
He helped build IceCube, a huge detector deep in the ice of Antarctica, near the South Pole.
IceCube hunts for tiny particles called neutrinos. They are so small that they fly right through you — and through the whole Earth!
Trillions of neutrinos pass through your body every second, but you never feel them.
Once in a while, a neutrino hits the ice and makes a tiny blue flash of light. Thousands of sensors in the ice can see it.
Some neutrinos come from faraway, powerful events in space. By catching them, scientists can study the universe in a brand-new way.

q.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: A huge ice detector that catches tiny particles from space
Why Antarctica is the coldest place on the planet
How scientists catch light from distant stars with telescopes
Daily life for scientists working at the South Pole
q.why: 全文講冰立方與獲獎。

q.q: Where is IceCube?
opts: On a high mountain in Chile
Under the sea near Japan
Deep in the ice of Antarctica
In space, close to the Moon
q.why: 原文：“He helped build IceCube, a huge detector deep in the ice of Antarctica, near the South Pole.”

q.q: What are neutrinos?
opts: Tiny bits of light that cannot pass through thick ice at all
Tiny particles that fly through almost everything
Tiny stars that are very far away from Earth
Particles that the thick ice stops completely
q.why: 原文：“IceCube hunts for tiny particles called neutrinos.”

q.q: In the text, “flash” means ___.
opts: a loud, sudden sound
a long, dark shadow
a strong, cold wind
a quick burst of light
q.why: flash = 閃光。

q.q: Why is catching neutrinos useful?
opts: It helps keep the Antarctic ice clean and clear
It can be used to make electricity for cities
It lets scientists study the universe in a new way
It helps people live and work in Antarctica
q.why: 線索：“By catching them, scientists can study the universe in a brand-new way.”

q.q: Why do you think scientists built IceCube in a quiet, dark, icy place instead of a big city?
opts: Because building in big cities is too expensive
Because neutrinos only exist in Antarctica
Because the scientists enjoy cold weather
So the tiny blue flashes are easier to see
q.why: 乾淨、黑暗的冰層較容易捕捉微弱藍光。

gt.en: He helped build IceCube, a huge detector deep in the ice of Antarctica, near the South Pole.
gt.zh: 他協助建造了冰立方，一個位在南極附近、深埋在南極冰層裡的巨大偵測器。

gt.en: IceCube hunts for tiny particles called neutrinos.
gt.zh: 冰立方在尋找一種叫做微中子的微小粒子。

gt.en: Once in a while, a neutrino hits the ice and makes a tiny blue flash of light.
gt.zh: 偶爾會有一個微中子撞上冰，發出一道微小的藍色閃光。

gt.en: By catching them, scientists can study the universe in a brand-new way.
gt.zh: 藉由捕捉它們，科學家可以用全新的方式研究宇宙。

tz: 2026 年 10 月 6 日，一位名叫法蘭西斯・哈爾森的科學家獲得了諾貝爾物理學獎。
他協助建造了冰立方（IceCube），一個深埋在南極洲冰層裡、靠近南極點的巨大偵測器。
冰立方在尋找一種叫做微中子的微小粒子。它們小到可以直接穿過你的身體——甚至穿過整個地球！
每一秒都有好幾兆個微中子穿過你的身體，但你完全感覺不到。
偶爾，一個微中子會撞到冰，發出一道微小的藍色閃光。冰裡的數千個感測器可以看到它。
有些微中子來自太空中遙遠而強大的事件。藉由捕捉它們，科學家能用一種全新的方式研究宇宙。

ph.ex: Students helped build the school garden.
ph.exzh: 學生們協助建造了學校花園。

ph.ex: We hunted for shells on the beach.
ph.exzh: 我們在海灘上找貝殼。

ph.ex: The ball flew through the window.
ph.exzh: 球飛過了窗戶。

ph.ex: Once in a while, we eat out.
ph.exzh: 我們偶爾會出去吃飯。

b.title: IceCube: Hunting Ghost Particles at the South Pole
text: On 6 October 2026, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Francis Halzen for his leading role in the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos from space.

Neutrinos are among the strangest particles in nature. They have almost no mass, carry no electric charge, and hardly ever bump into anything. Trillions stream through your body every second without leaving a trace.
That makes them incredibly hard to catch. To do it, scientists turned a cubic kilometre of clear Antarctic ice into a detector, burying over 5,000 light sensors deep beneath the South Pole.
Now and then, a neutrino crashes into the ice and creates a faint blue glow. The sensors record this light and reveal where the particle came from.
In 2013, IceCube found the first neutrinos born far beyond our solar system, in some of the most violent events in the universe.
Because neutrinos travel in straight lines and pass through almost everything, they carry clues that ordinary light cannot. Halzen's work opened a new field: neutrino astronomy.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Neutrinos have almost no mass, carry no charge and rarely interact.
IceCube found its first high-energy cosmic neutrinos back in 2013.
IceCube detects neutrinos by drilling sensors deep into the ice of Antarctica.
IceCube turns Antarctic ice into a neutrino detector — Nobel-winning work.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: Why are neutrinos hard to catch?
opts: They move far too slowly to be measured
They hide deep underground in the ice
They have almost no mass and rarely interact
They are too big for most detectors to hold
q.why: 原文：“They have almost no mass, carry no electric charge, and hardly ever bump into anything.”

q.q: How does IceCube detect a neutrino?
opts: By weighing the ice before and after a neutrino passes
By recording the faint blue light from a neutrino hit
By listening for sounds deep inside the Antarctic ice
By taking photos of the night sky above the South Pole
q.why: 原文：“Now and then, a neutrino crashes into the ice and creates a faint blue glow.”

q.q: In paragraph 2, “trace” means ___.
opts: a sign or mark left behind
a straight line across the ice
a large amount of something
a dangerous kind of particle
q.why: trace = 痕跡。

q.q: Why do neutrinos carry clues that light cannot?
opts: They are much brighter than ordinary light from stars
They travel straight and pass through almost everything
They are made of a special kind of light themselves
They only come from the Sun, so they are easy to trace
q.why: 線索：“Because neutrinos travel in straight lines and pass through almost everything, they carry clues that ordinary light cannot.”

q.q: A news report says IceCube catches billions of neutrinos every second. Based on the text, why is this unlikely?
opts: IceCube is switched off for most of the year to save power
Most scientists now think neutrinos may not really exist
The thick ice blocks every neutrino before it reaches sensors
Neutrinos rarely interact, so it catches one only now and then
q.why: 微中子極少交互作用，只是偶爾被捕捉到。

tr.en: They have almost no mass, carry no electric charge, and hardly ever bump into anything.
tr.zh: 它們幾乎沒有質量、不帶電荷，而且幾乎從不撞上任何東西。

tr.en: Now and then, a neutrino crashes into the ice and creates a faint blue glow.
tr.zh: 偶爾會有一個微中子撞進冰裡，產生微弱的藍光。

tr.en: In 2013, IceCube found the first neutrinos born far beyond our solar system, in some of the most violent events in the universe.
tr.zh: 2013 年，冰立方找到了第一批誕生在太陽系之外遙遠地方的微中子，它們來自宇宙中一些最劇烈的事件。

tz: 2026 年 10 月 6 日，諾貝爾物理學獎頒給了法蘭西斯・哈爾森，表彰他在冰立方微中子天文台的領導角色，以及發現來自太空的高能微中子。
微中子是自然界最奇特的粒子之一。它們幾乎沒有質量、不帶電，也幾乎從不撞上任何東西。每一秒都有好幾兆個微中子流過你的身體，卻不留下任何痕跡。
這讓它們極難被捕捉。為了做到這件事，科學家把一立方公里清澈的南極冰層變成一個偵測器，在南極點底下深處埋設了五千多個光感測器。
偶爾，會有一個微中子撞進冰裡，產生一道微弱的藍光。感測器記錄這道光，並顯示這個粒子是從哪裡來的。
2013 年，冰立方找到了第一批誕生於太陽系之外的微中子，它們來自宇宙中一些最劇烈的事件。
因為微中子沿直線前進，又能穿過幾乎所有東西，它們帶著一般光線無法帶來的線索。哈爾森的研究開創了一個新領域：微中子天文學。

ph.ex: She is among the best players in Asia.
ph.exzh: 她是亞洲最好的選手之一。

ph.ex: I bumped into my teacher at the mall.
ph.exzh: 我在購物中心碰到我的老師。

ph.ex: Now and then, I visit my old school.
ph.exzh: 我偶爾會回母校看看。

ph.ex: Some stars are far beyond our galaxy.
ph.exzh: 有些星星遠在我們的銀河系之外。

ph.ex: Her research opened a new field of science.
ph.exzh: 她的研究開創了一個新的科學領域。

c.title: Reading the Universe with Neutrinos
text: When the Royal Swedish Academy named Francis Halzen the 2026 Nobel laureate in Physics on 6 October, it recognised a discovery that gave astronomers an entirely new sense: the ability to 'see' the cosmos through neutrinos.
Neutrinos are nature's great escape artists. Nearly massless and electrically neutral, they interact so weakly that most slip through the entire Earth as though it were empty space.

Capturing them demanded an instrument of extraordinary scale. Under Halzen's leadership, the IceCube Observatory transformed a cubic kilometre of pristine Antarctic ice into a detector, threaded with thousands of sensors more than a kilometre below the surface.

On the rare occasion that a neutrino strikes an atom in the ice, it releases a ghostly blue flash. From the pattern of light, scientists can reconstruct the particle's energy and trace its path back across the sky.
In 2013, IceCube detected the first high-energy neutrinos of cosmic origin, later linking some to distant galaxies with supermassive black holes at their hearts.

Unlike light, neutrinos stream unblocked from the universe's most hidden and violent corners. Halzen's achievement founded neutrino astronomy, opening a fresh window onto events no ordinary telescope could ever observe.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: How IceCube opens the universe to study through neutrinos, winning a Nobel
How IceCube's sensors were lowered into holes drilled in Antarctic ice
Why neutrinos are dangerous to the scientists who try to study them
How neutrinos are made inside the Sun and why the ice can stop them from escaping
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: What did IceCube achieve in 2013?
opts: It was first built and switched on at the South Pole
It detected the first high-energy cosmic neutrinos
It detected the first neutrinos coming from the Sun
It took the first photograph of a distant black hole
q.why: 原文：“In 2013, IceCube detected the first high-energy neutrinos of cosmic origin, later linking some to distant galaxies with supermassive black holes at their hearts.”

q.q: Why build the detector inside Antarctic ice?
opts: Very cold ice makes the passing neutrinos grow much bigger
Antarctica is much closer to outer space than other places
Ice is the cheapest material for building a large detector
Pristine ice lets sensors spot the faint flash of a rare hit
q.why: 原文：“Under Halzen's leadership, the IceCube Observatory transformed a cubic kilometre of pristine Antarctic ice into a detector, threaded with thousands of sensors more …”

q.q: In paragraph 1, “laureate” means ___.
opts: a scientist's assistant
a research station
a prize winner
a type of particle
q.why: laureate = 得獎者。

q.q: Why is neutrino astronomy called a fresh 'window'?
opts: It uses much larger glass lenses than old telescopes
It reveals violent, hidden events light cannot show
It can only work when looking through real windows
It will soon replace every other kind of astronomy
q.why: 線索：“Unlike light, neutrinos stream unblocked from the universe's most hidden and violent corners.”

q.q: Which idea from the text best explains why scientists combine neutrinos with light-based telescopes?
opts: Light-based telescopes are no longer useful to astronomers
Neutrinos and light show exactly the same events in space
Each reveals what the other cannot, giving a fuller picture
Combining the two makes building detectors much cheaper
q.why: 微中子揭示光看不到的事件，兩者互補。

tz: 瑞典皇家科學院在 10 月 6 日宣布法蘭西斯・哈爾森為 2026 年諾貝爾物理學獎得主時，表彰的是一項讓天文學家擁有全新「感官」的發現：透過微中子「看見」宇宙的能力。
微中子是大自然的脫逃大師。它們幾乎沒有質量、不帶電，交互作用微弱到大部分都能穿過整個地球，好像地球是一片空無一物的空間。
要捕捉它們，需要一台規模驚人的儀器。在哈爾森的領導下，冰立方天文台把一立方公里純淨的南極冰層變成了一個偵測器，在地表下一公里多的深處布滿了數千個感測器。
在極少數的情況下，當一個微中子撞上冰裡的一個原子，它會釋放出一道幽靈般的藍色閃光。從光的分布模式，科學家可以重建這個粒子的能量，並沿著天空追溯它的路徑。
2013 年，冰立方偵測到第一批來自宇宙的高能微中子，後來還把其中一些連結到中心有超大質量黑洞的遙遠星系。
和光不同，微中子能不受阻擋地從宇宙最隱密、最劇烈的角落流出來。哈爾森的成就創立了微中子天文學，為那些任何普通望遠鏡都無法觀測的事件，打開了一扇新的窗。

ph.ex: He walked in as though nothing had happened.
ph.exzh: 他走進來，彷彿什麼事都沒發生。

ph.ex: On the rare occasion that it snows, everyone goes outside.
ph.exzh: 偶爾下雪的時候，大家都會跑到外面。

ph.ex: We traced the river back to its source.
ph.exzh: 我們沿著河往回追溯到源頭。

ph.ex: Scientists link poor sleep to bad moods.
ph.exzh: 科學家把睡不好和心情差連結在一起。

ph.ex: The old cities had markets at their hearts.
ph.exzh: 這些古城的中心都有市集。

ph.ex: Books open a window onto other worlds.
ph.exzh: 書本為我們打開一扇看見其他世界的窗。

discuss: Trillions of neutrinos pass right through you every second. Does knowing that change how you see the world?
IceCube was hugely expensive and sits in Antarctic ice. Is 'pure curiosity' science like this worth the cost? Why or why not?
Light, sound, and now neutrinos each tell us something about the universe. What new 'sense' might science invent next?

topic: Molecules with a Left Hand and a Right Hand
zh: 分子的左手與右手：2026 諾貝爾化學獎
tag: Nobel Chemistry · 諾貝爾化學獎

a.title: Molecules That Come in Two Hands
text: On October 7, 2026, two scientists won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Their names are Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai.
Hold up your two hands. They look the same, but they are mirror images — a left and a right. You cannot put a left glove on your right hand.
Many tiny molecules are like this too. They come in a 'left' form and a 'right' form.
This really matters for medicine. Often only one hand helps your body. The other hand may do nothing — or even cause harm.
Kagan and Soai found clever ways to make mostly the hand we want. Soai even built a reaction that copies itself, turning a tiny difference into a big one.
Thanks to their work, chemists can make safer medicines, one careful hand at a time.

q.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: Why our left and right hands are mirror images of each other
Left and right forms of molecules, and making the one we want
How new medicines are carefully tested on people in hospitals
How scientists can see tiny molecules with special machines
q.why: 全文講手性分子與獲獎研究。

q.q: Why are a left and right hand like these molecules?
opts: They are mirror images that don't match up
They are exactly the same in every way
They are different sizes and shapes
They always move in opposite directions
q.why: 原文：“They look the same, but they are mirror images — a left and a right.”

q.q: Why does handedness matter for medicine?
opts: Both forms of a medicine always work the same way
Left-handed people need a different kind of medicine
Often only one form helps; the other may harm
The handedness changes how the medicine tastes
q.why: 原文：“The other hand may do nothing — or even cause harm.”

q.q: In the text, “harm” means ___.
opts: help or support
change or mix
test or check
damage or hurt
q.why: harm = 傷害。

q.q: Why is their work important?
opts: It makes molecules bigger and easier to see
It helps chemists build safer medicines
It explains why some people are left-handed
It makes all medicine cheaper for everyone
q.why: 線索：“Thanks to their work, chemists can make safer medicines, one careful hand at a time.”

q.q: Try to put your left glove on your right hand. Which idea from the text does this show?
opts: Mirror images look alike but do not fit the same way
Gloves, like medicines, are made of tiny molecules
Everybody's left and right hands are the same size
Gloves can be used as a kind of medicine for hands
q.why: 左右手套是鏡像但不能互換——就像手性分子。

gt.en: They look the same, but they are mirror images — a left and a right.
gt.zh: 它們看起來一樣，但其實是鏡像——一左一右。

gt.en: Many tiny molecules are like this too.
gt.zh: 許多微小的分子也是這樣。

gt.en: This really matters for medicine.
gt.zh: 這對醫藥來說真的非常重要。

gt.en: Soai even built a reaction that copies itself, turning a tiny difference into a big one.
gt.zh: 碩井甚至設計出一種會自我複製的反應，把微小的差異變成很大的差異。

tz: 2026 年 10 月 7 日，兩位科學家獲得了諾貝爾化學獎。他們的名字是亨利・卡岡和是相憲三（Kenso Soai）。
舉起你的兩隻手。它們看起來一樣，但其實是鏡像——一左一右。你沒辦法把左手的手套戴在右手上。
很多微小的分子也是這樣。它們有「左手」型和「右手」型。
這對醫藥來說非常重要。常常只有其中一種「手」對身體有幫助，另一種可能沒有作用——甚至會造成傷害。
卡岡和是相想出了聰明的方法，讓化學反應大部分產生我們想要的那種「手」。是相甚至設計出一種會複製自己的反應，把一個微小的差異變成很大的差異。
多虧了他們的研究，化學家能夠一次一隻「手」地，小心做出更安全的藥物。

ph.ex: Hold up your hand if you know the answer.
ph.exzh: 知道答案的話就舉手。

ph.ex: Shoes come in a left and a right.
ph.exzh: 鞋子分一左一右。

ph.ex: Too much sun can cause harm to your skin.
ph.exzh: 曬太多太陽可能傷害你的皮膚。

ph.ex: Climb the stairs one step at a time.
ph.exzh: 一次爬一階樓梯。
ph.m: one careful hand at a time

b.title: Left-Handed and Right-Handed Molecules
text: On 7 October 2026, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Henri Kagan of France and Kenso Soai of Japan for work on 'asymmetric synthesis' — building molecules with a chosen handedness.
Just as your left and right hands are mirror images that cannot overlap, many molecules exist in two mirror-image forms, which chemists call 'left' and 'right'.
Inside living bodies, the two forms can behave completely differently. One form of a drug may heal, while its mirror twin does nothing — or causes side effects.
For a long time, ordinary reactions made both forms in equal amounts, and separating them afterwards was slow and costly.
Kagan discovered that a small amount of a one-handed 'helper', called a catalyst, could steer a reaction to produce far more of a single form — a surprising amplifying effect.

Soai went further, creating a reaction that makes a product which then helps make more of itself. A tiny imbalance at the start grows into an almost perfectly one-handed result — a powerful tool for cleaner, safer medicines.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Kagan and Soai found ways to make one chosen 'hand' of a molecule.
The two mirror forms of a drug can behave completely differently.
Soai built a special reaction whose product helps make more of itself.
Separating the mirror forms of a molecule used to be slow and costly.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: In the body, the two mirror forms of a drug can ___.
opts: always behave the same
never enter the body
behave completely differently
cancel each other out completely
q.why: 原文：“Inside living bodies, the two forms can behave completely differently.”

q.q: What did Soai's special reaction do?
opts: It made both mirror forms in equal amounts
Its product helped make more of itself
It separated the two forms by hand
It destroyed the harmful mirror form
q.why: 原文：“Soai went further, creating a reaction that makes a product which then helps make more of itself.”

q.q: In paragraph 5, “amplifying” means ___.
opts: making smaller or weaker
separating into two parts
copying something exactly
making larger or stronger
q.why: amplify = 放大。

q.q: Why was making one single form hard before?
opts: Chemists did not yet know that molecules have different shapes
Making the right-handed form of a drug was against the law
Machines were not yet able to measure molecules accurately
Reactions made both forms equally, and separating them was costly
q.why: 線索：“For a long time, ordinary reactions made both forms in equal amounts, and separating them afterwards was slow and costly.”

q.q: A medicine company can make a drug as a 50–50 mix of both forms or as only the helpful form. Based on the text, why might the second choice be better?
opts: The single form always tastes much better to patients
The single form is always cheaper for companies to make
The other form may do nothing or cause side effects
The single form works twice as fast in every case
q.why: 另一種型態可能無效或造成副作用。

tr.en: One form of a drug may heal, while its mirror twin does nothing — or causes side effects.
tr.zh: 一種藥物的某一種型態可能能治病，而它的鏡像雙胞胎卻沒有作用——甚至會造成副作用。

tr.en: For a long time, ordinary reactions made both forms in equal amounts, and separating them afterwards was slow and costly.
tr.zh: 很長一段時間，一般的化學反應會做出等量的兩種型態，而事後把它們分開既慢又昂貴。

tr.en: A tiny imbalance at the start grows into an almost perfectly one-handed result — a powerful tool for cleaner, safer medicines.
tr.zh: 一開始的微小不平衡，會擴大成幾乎完全單一手性的結果——這是製造更純淨、更安全藥物的強大工具。

tz: 2026 年 10 月 7 日，諾貝爾化學獎頒給了法國的亨利・卡岡和日本的是相憲三，表彰他們在「不對稱合成」——製造具有指定「手性」的分子——方面的研究。
就像你的左手和右手是無法重疊的鏡像一樣，許多分子也以兩種互為鏡像的形式存在，化學家把它們叫做「左手」和「右手」。
在生物體內，這兩種形式的作用可能完全不同。一種形式的藥物可能治病，而它的鏡像雙胞胎卻沒有作用——或是會引起副作用。
很長一段時間，一般的化學反應都會產生等量的兩種形式，之後要把它們分開，既慢又昂貴。
卡岡發現，少量的單手性「幫手」——也就是催化劑——就能引導反應產生多得多的單一形式，這是一種令人驚訝的放大效應。
是相更進一步，創造出一種反應：它的產物會反過來幫忙製造更多的自己。一開始微小的不平衡，會成長為幾乎完全單一手性的結果——這是製造更純淨、更安全藥物的有力工具。

ph.ex: The first prize went to a girl from Hualien.
ph.exzh: 首獎頒給了一位來自花蓮的女孩。

ph.ex: Just as plants need water, children need love.
ph.exzh: 正如植物需要水，孩子需要愛。

ph.ex: Mix the sugar and flour in equal amounts.
ph.exzh: 把糖和麵粉等量混合。

ph.ex: We sold far more cakes than last year.
ph.exzh: 我們賣出的蛋糕比去年多得多。

ph.ex: He went further and wrote a whole book.
ph.exzh: 他更進一步，寫了一整本書。

c.title: The Chemistry of Handedness
text: When the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry on 7 October, it honoured Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for taming one of chemistry's most elegant puzzles: handedness.
Countless molecules are 'chiral' — they exist as two mirror images, like a pair of hands, that can never be laid perfectly on top of each other. The two versions are known as enantiomers.

In biology, the distinction is anything but trivial. The receptors in our cells are themselves handed, so one enantiomer of a drug may cure a patient while its mirror image is useless, or even dangerous.
Ordinary reactions, however, tend to produce the two forms in equal measure. The challenge was to tip the balance — to make one hand far more often than the other.

Kagan showed that this could be done with startling efficiency: a catalyst only slightly biased toward one hand could yield a product overwhelmingly of that hand, a counter-intuitive 'non-linear' effect.

Soai then revealed something close to chemical magic — a self-replicating, or autocatalytic, reaction in which the product speeds up its own formation, amplifying a faint initial imbalance into near-perfect purity. Together, their insights underpin the clean, precise synthesis of modern medicines.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: Why the two mirror forms of the same drug behave so differently in the body
How chemists first invented catalysts to speed up chemical reactions
Why biology largely ignores the shape of the molecules it encounters
How Kagan and Soai learned to control molecular handedness, winning a Nobel
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: Why is handedness 'anything but trivial' in biology?
opts: Our receptors are handed, so one form may cure and its mirror harm
All molecules in the human body happen to be of the same hand
Cells cannot tell the difference between the two mirror forms
Handedness affects only the colour of a molecule, not its action
q.why: 原文：“The receptors in our cells are themselves handed, so one enantiomer of a drug may cure a patient while its mirror image is useless, or even dangerous.”

q.q: What was Kagan's surprising 'non-linear' effect?
opts: A catalyst had to be completely one-handed before it would work
Reactions always produced equal amounts of both mirror forms
A slightly biased catalyst gave an overwhelmingly one-handed product
A fully one-handed catalyst always gave a perfectly one-handed product
q.why: 原文：“Kagan showed that this could be done with startling efficiency: a catalyst only slightly biased toward one hand could yield a product overwhelmingly of that hand, a …”

q.q: In paragraph 6, “autocatalytic” describes a reaction that ___.
opts: needs no starting materials
speeds up its own formation
produces both hands equally
stops by itself after a while
q.why: autocatalytic = 自我催化。

q.q: Why does this chemistry matter beyond the laboratory?
opts: It replaces the need for biology in medical research
It allows mirrors to be made far more accurately
It underpins the precise making of modern medicines
It is used mainly in cooking and food production
q.why: 線索：“Together, their insights underpin the clean, precise synthesis of modern medicines.”

q.q: Which everyday situation is most like Kagan's 'small bias, big result' effect?
opts: A slightly tilted table sends every marble to one side
Two teams finishing a match with the same points
Mixing equal amounts of two paint colours together
A coin that lands on heads and tails about equally over time
q.why: 微小偏向放大成壓倒性結果。

tz: 瑞典皇家科學院在 10 月 7 日宣布 2026 年諾貝爾化學獎時，表彰亨利・卡岡和是相憲三馴服了化學中最優雅的謎題之一：手性。
無數分子都是「手性」的——它們以兩個鏡像的形式存在，就像一雙手一樣，永遠無法完美地疊在一起。這兩種版本被稱為「鏡像異構物」。
在生物學裡，這個區別絕非微不足道。我們細胞裡的受體本身就有手性，所以一種藥物的某個鏡像異構物可能治好病人，而它的鏡像卻毫無用處，甚至很危險。
然而，一般的反應往往會等量地產生兩種形式。挑戰在於打破這個平衡——讓其中一隻「手」出現得遠比另一隻多。
卡岡證明這可以用驚人的效率做到：一個只稍微偏向某一隻手的催化劑，能產生壓倒性地屬於那隻手的產物——這是一種違反直覺的「非線性」效應。
是相接著揭示了一種近乎化學魔法的東西——一種自我複製、或稱「自催化」的反應，產物會加速自己的生成，把起初一點點微弱的不平衡，放大成近乎完美的純度。他們的洞見合在一起，奠定了現代藥物純淨、精準合成的基礎。

ph.ex: The trip was anything but boring.
ph.exzh: 這趟旅行一點也不無聊。

ph.ex: Cats tend to sleep during the day.
ph.exzh: 貓往往在白天睡覺。

ph.ex: The film is funny and sad in equal measure.
ph.exzh: 這部電影好笑和悲傷的程度一樣多。

ph.zh: 打破平衡、成為決定因素
ph.ex: Her last goal tipped the balance.
ph.exzh: 她最後一球打破了平衡。

ph.ex: I take the bus far more often than the train.
ph.exzh: 我搭公車比搭火車頻繁得多。

ph.ex: Practice speeds up your typing.
ph.exzh: 練習會讓你打字變快。

discuss: Your two hands are mirror images, yet not the same. Where else in nature or daily life do you notice 'handedness'?
One form of a molecule can heal while its mirror harms. Why is being precise so important in science and medicine?
Soai's reaction grows a tiny difference into a big one. Can you think of small starts in life that grow into big results?

topic: A Poet Who Bridges Ancient and Modern
zh: 連結古今的詩人：2026 諾貝爾文學獎
tag: Nobel Literature · 諾貝爾文學獎

a.title: A Poet Who Loves Old Stories
text: On October 8, 2026, the writer Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in Literature. She is a poet from Canada.
Carson loves the stories and poems of ancient Greece, written thousands of years ago.
She takes these very old tales and tells them again in fresh, surprising, modern ways.
In one famous book, she retells a Greek myth about a small red monster — but as a tender story about growing up and falling in love.
Carson also teaches ancient Greek, and she has translated old poems so that people today can enjoy them.
The prize judges praised her bold and playful writing, which builds new shapes for poetry out of very old stories.

q.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: A poet who retells old Greek stories in new ways
Ancient Greek stories written thousands of years ago
How to translate old poems from Greek into English
Why poets in Canada teach ancient Greek at school
q.why: 全文介紹卡森與獲獎。

q.q: Where is Anne Carson from?
opts: Greece
Canada
The United States
England
q.why: 文中。

q.q: What does Carson do with ancient tales?
opts: She keeps them exactly as they were
She writes new endings for them in Greek only
She turns them into films
She tells them again in fresh, modern ways
q.why: 原文：“She takes these very old tales and tells them again in fresh, surprising, modern ways.”

q.q: In the text, “ancient” means ___.
opts: very famous
very short
very old
very difficult
q.why: ancient = 古代的。

q.q: Why did the judges praise her?
opts: She writes the longest books of any living poet
She writes only in ancient Greek, not in English
She is the first writer from Canada to win anything
She makes new kinds of poetry out of very old stories
q.why: 線索：“The prize judges praised her bold and playful writing, which builds new shapes for poetry out of very old stories.”

q.q: Which project is MOST like what Anne Carson does?
opts: Retelling an old Taiwanese legend as a modern comic
Translating an old Greek poem carefully into modern Chinese
Writing a science report about ancient Greece
Reading a newspaper article about a new prize
q.why: 把古老故事用現代形式重新說，正是卡森的做法。

gt.en: She is a poet from Canada.
gt.zh: 她是一位來自加拿大的詩人。

gt.en: Carson loves the stories and poems of ancient Greece, written thousands of years ago.
gt.zh: 卡森熱愛幾千年前寫成的古希臘故事和詩。

gt.en: Carson also teaches ancient Greek, and she has translated old poems so that people today can enjoy them.
gt.zh: 卡森也教古希臘文，她還翻譯古老的詩，讓今天的人也能欣賞。

tz: 2026 年 10 月 8 日，作家安妮・卡森獲得了諾貝爾文學獎。她是一位來自加拿大的詩人。
卡森熱愛古希臘的故事和詩歌，那些是幾千年前寫成的。
她把這些非常古老的故事，用新鮮、令人驚喜又現代的方式重新說一遍。
在一本有名的書裡，她改寫了一個關於紅色小怪物的希臘神話——卻把它變成一個關於成長和戀愛的溫柔故事。
卡森也教古希臘文，她還翻譯了古老的詩，讓今天的人也能欣賞。
評審稱讚她大膽又充滿玩心的寫作，用非常古老的故事，為詩歌打造出新的形式。

ph.ex: Grandpa tells the old story again every New Year.
ph.exzh: 爺爺每年過年都會重講那個老故事。

ph.ex: She fell in love with Paris on her first visit.
ph.exzh: 她第一次去巴黎就愛上了那裡。

ph.ex: Speak slowly so that everyone understands.
ph.exzh: 說慢一點，讓大家都聽得懂。

ph.ex: She made a bag out of old jeans.
ph.exzh: 她用舊牛仔褲做了一個包包。

b.title: Anne Carson: New Shapes from Old Stories
text: On 8 October 2026, the Canadian poet Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in Literature for work that brings the ancient world into playful, modern form.
Carson is both a poet and a scholar of ancient Greek. For her, writers who lived thousands of years ago — like the poet Sappho — are living voices, not dusty books.
Her most loved work, 'Autobiography of Red', takes a strange Greek myth about a winged red monster and turns it into a moving story about a shy boy growing up.
She refuses to stay inside one form. Her books mix poetry, essay, and story; one even unfolds like a long paper accordion.
She has also translated ancient poems, carefully keeping their gaps and silences so that readers feel how much time has passed.
The Nobel judges praised her 'bold and inventive' writing, which, in playful dialogue with the classics, has created new forms for today's literature.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Autobiography of Red retells a Greek myth about a winged red monster.
Carson's books refuse to stay in one form, mixing poetry, essay and story.
Carson won the Nobel for turning ancient Greek writing into bold modern forms.
Carson won the Nobel because she taught ancient Greek for most of her life.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: What is 'Autobiography of Red' about?
opts: A Greek myth about a red monster, retold as a boy growing up
A Greek myth about a hero who defeats a red monster in battle
The poet's own childhood growing up in Toronto, Canada
A war between the Greek gods, told in the original Greek
q.why: 原文：“Her most loved work, 'Autobiography of Red', takes a strange Greek myth about a winged red monster and turns it into a moving story about a shy boy growing up.”

q.q: How does Carson treat writers from thousands of years ago?
opts: As great masters whose words must never change
As forgotten figures
As rivals
As living voices
q.why: 原文：“For her, writers who lived thousands of years ago — like the poet Sappho — are living voices, not dusty books.”

q.q: In paragraph 4, 'refuses to stay inside one form' means she ___.
opts: writes only poems, never essays
mixes different kinds of writing
refuses to publish her new work
writes only in ancient Greek
q.why: 混合多種文體。

q.q: Why keep the 'gaps and silences' in old poems?
opts: Because she could not translate those parts
To make the old poems shorter and easier
So readers feel how much time has passed
Because modern readers prefer short poems
q.why: 線索：“She has also translated ancient poems, carefully keeping their gaps and silences so that readers feel how much time has passed.”

q.q: A friend says: “Old Greek stories have nothing to say to teenagers today.” What would the text suggest?
opts: Agree — stories that old are too far from our lives
Agree — only modern stories matter to young people
Disagree — because ancient Greek is easy to learn
Carson shows ancient stories can speak to modern lives
q.why: 《紅的自傳》把神話寫成少年的成長故事。

tr.en: Carson is both a poet and a scholar of ancient Greek.
tr.zh: 卡森既是詩人，也是研究古希臘文的學者。

tr.en: Her books mix poetry, essay, and story; one even unfolds like a long paper accordion.
tr.zh: 她的書混合了詩、散文和故事；其中一本甚至像一長條紙做的手風琴一樣展開。

tr.en: She has also translated ancient poems, carefully keeping their gaps and silences so that readers feel how much time has passed.
tr.zh: 她也翻譯古詩，小心地保留其中的缺漏與空白，讓讀者感受到時間已經過了多久。

tz: 2026 年 10 月 8 日，加拿大詩人安妮・卡森獲得諾貝爾文學獎，因為她的作品以充滿玩心的現代形式，把古代世界帶到我們面前。
卡森既是詩人，也是研究古希臘文的學者。對她來說，幾千年前的作家——像是詩人莎芙——是活生生的聲音，而不是積滿灰塵的書。
她最受喜愛的作品《紅的自傳》，把一則關於長著翅膀的紅色怪物的奇特希臘神話，變成一個關於害羞男孩成長的動人故事。
她不肯只待在一種形式裡。她的書混合了詩、散文和故事；其中一本甚至像一長條紙風琴一樣展開。
她也翻譯古老的詩，小心地保留原詩中的缺口和空白，讓讀者感受到時間已經過了多久。
諾貝爾評審稱讚她「大膽而富有創意」的寫作，在與古典作品充滿玩心的對話中，為今天的文學創造出新的形式。

ph.ex: The teacher brings music into every lesson.
ph.exzh: 老師在每堂課都融入音樂。

ph.ex: She turned her notes into a song.
ph.exzh: 她把筆記改編成一首歌。

ph.ex: The cat refuses to take a bath.
ph.exzh: 那隻貓拒絕洗澡。

ph.ex: The map unfolds like a fan.
ph.exzh: 這張地圖像扇子一樣展開。

ph.ex: Her art is in dialogue with old Chinese paintings.
ph.exzh: 她的藝術和中國古畫在對話。

c.title: In Playful Dialogue with the Ancients
text: When the Swedish Academy named Anne Carson the 2026 Nobel laureate in Literature on 8 October, it celebrated a writer who has spent her life in conversation with the distant past.
A Canadian poet, essayist, and professor of classics, Carson treats the ancient Greeks not as relics to be studied, but as companions to argue and play with.
Her signature work, 'Autobiography of Red', reimagines an obscure myth — the red, winged monster Geryon — as a luminous coming-of-age story written as a novel in verse.
Across her career she has dissolved the borders between genres, weaving together poetry, scholarship, and memoir; her elegy 'Nox' arrives as a single folded page in a box, part book, part object.
As a translator, she renders the surviving fragments of Sappho with their losses intact, letting the blank spaces speak as loudly as the words.

The Academy honoured her 'bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature' — proof that the oldest voices can still sound startlingly new.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: Why ancient Greek writers are still studied in universities today
How Carson renews ancient literature in modern forms, earning the Nobel
How Carson translates ancient poems word for word, keeping every detail
Why poetry is disappearing in an age of short online writing
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: What is 'Nox' described as?
opts: A long novel about modern life in Greece
A short book of new poems about ancient Greece
A collection of essays about old poets
A folded page in a box, part book, part object
q.why: 原文：“Across her career she has dissolved the borders between genres, weaving together poetry, scholarship, and memoir; her elegy 'Nox' arrives as a single folded page in …”

q.q: How does Carson treat the ancient Greeks, according to the text?
opts: As companions to argue and play with
As great masters to be copied exactly
As objects to be studied only
As people to be forgotten
q.why: 原文：“A Canadian poet, essayist, and professor of classics, Carson treats the ancient Greeks not as relics to be studied, but as companions to argue and play with.”

q.q: In paragraph 3, “obscure” means ___.
opts: very famous
very long
little-known
very new
q.why: obscure = 鮮為人知的。

q.q: What does her win suggest about old stories?
opts: The oldest voices can still sound startlingly new
Only old stories are truly worth reading today
Modern writing has little real value of its own
Old stories must be kept exactly as they were
q.why: 線索：“The Academy honoured her 'bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature' — …”

q.q: Which approach to teaching classic literature best matches Carson's attitude?
opts: Making students memorise texts without discussion
Avoiding old texts completely in modern classrooms
Inviting students to question and respond creatively
Reading only short summaries of the classic works
q.why: 卡森把古人當作可以爭論、遊戲的同伴。

tz: 瑞典學院在 10 月 8 日宣布安妮・卡森為 2026 年諾貝爾文學獎得主時，所表彰的是一位一生都在和遙遠過去對話的作家。
卡森是加拿大詩人、散文家，也是古典學教授；她不把古希臘人當成要研究的遺物，而是當成可以爭論、可以一起玩的同伴。
她的代表作《紅的自傳》，把一則冷門的神話——長著翅膀的紅色怪物革律翁——重新想像成一個以詩體小說寫成、光彩奪目的成長故事。
在她的整個創作生涯中，她消融了文類之間的界線，把詩、學術研究和回憶錄交織在一起；她的輓歌《夜》（Nox）是裝在盒子裡的一張摺疊長紙，一半是書，一半是物件。
作為譯者，她翻譯莎芙流傳下來的殘篇時，保留了其中的缺失，讓空白處和文字說得一樣響亮。
瑞典學院表彰她「大膽而富有創意的作品，在與古典傳統充滿玩心的對話中，為當代文學創造了新的形式」——證明最古老的聲音，依然能聽起來新鮮得令人吃驚。

ph.ex: He spent his life helping others.
ph.exzh: 他一生都在幫助別人。

ph.ex: Treat mistakes not as failures but as lessons.
ph.exzh: 把錯誤當成教訓，而不是失敗。
ph.m: not as relics to be studied, but as companions

ph.ex: I like to argue with my friends about books.
ph.exzh: 我喜歡和朋友爭論書的內容。

ph.ex: The film weaves together three stories.
ph.exzh: 這部電影交織了三個故事。

ph.ex: The old vase arrived intact.
ph.exzh: 那個舊花瓶完好無缺地送到了。

ph.ex: Her silence spoke as loudly as words.
ph.exzh: 她的沉默和言語一樣有力。

discuss: Carson makes ancient stories feel new. Is there an old story, song, or legend you would love to retell in a modern way?
She mixes poetry, essay, and story in one book. Why might breaking the 'rules' of a form lead to something powerful?
Why do you think people still read writers who lived thousands of years ago?

topic: A Lifelong Fight for Human Rights
zh: 為人權奮鬥一生：2026 諾貝爾和平獎
tag: Nobel Peace · 諾貝爾和平獎

a.title: A Judge Who Fights for Fairness
text: On October 9, 2026, Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize. She is a judge and lawyer from South Africa.
Pillay grew up poor, at a time when her country treated people unfairly because of the colour of their skin.
She worked very hard, became a lawyer, and fought for people who had no voice.
Later, she became a judge in important world courts that try terrible crimes, such as war crimes.
She also led the part of the United Nations that protects human rights around the world.
The prize honours her long fight for peace and for fair laws that protect everyone, everywhere.

q.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: How the United Nations was first started
A judge who led the United Nations for many years
A judge who fought all her life for fairness
What daily life is like in South Africa
q.why: 全文介紹皮萊。

q.q: Where is Navi Pillay from?
opts: South Africa
Rwanda
South Korea
Norway
q.why: 原文：“She is a judge and lawyer from South Africa.”

q.q: What did Pillay do at the United Nations?
opts: She led the whole of the United Nations
She led the part that protects human rights
She worked there as a language translator
She was in charge of the UN's money
q.why: 原文：“She also led the part of the United Nations that protects human rights around the world.”

q.q: In the text, “unfair” means ___.
opts: very difficult to do
very old and tired
not very important
not equal or just
q.why: unfair = 不公平的。

q.q: Why did she win the Peace Prize?
opts: For ending apartheid in South Africa all by herself
For stopping a war between two countries in Africa
For her long fight for fair laws that protect everyone
For building new schools for poor children in Africa
q.why: 線索：“The prize honours her long fight for peace and for fair laws that protect everyone, everywhere.”

q.q: In class, some students are treated unfairly because they are new. What would Pillay's example encourage you to do?
opts: Ignore it, because it is not really your problem
Speak up and ask for fair rules that protect everyone
Join in with the others so that you fit in
Wait quietly for a teacher or someone else to help
q.why: 她一生為沒有聲音的人爭取公平。

gt.en: She is a judge and lawyer from South Africa.
gt.zh: 她是一位來自南非的法官和律師。

gt.en: She worked very hard, became a lawyer, and fought for people who had no voice.
gt.zh: 她非常努力，成為律師，並為沒有發聲機會的人奮鬥。

gt.en: Later, she became a judge in important world courts that try terrible crimes, such as war crimes.
gt.zh: 後來，她成為重要國際法庭的法官，審理像戰爭罪這樣可怕的罪行。

gt.en: She also led the part of the United Nations that protects human rights around the world.
gt.zh: 她也領導過聯合國中負責保護全世界人權的部門。

tz: 2026 年 10 月 9 日，納維・皮萊獲得了諾貝爾和平獎。她是一位來自南非的法官和律師。
皮萊在貧窮中長大；在那個時代，她的國家因為人的膚色而不公平地對待他們。
她非常努力，成為一名律師，為那些沒有聲音的人奮鬥。
後來，她成為重要國際法庭的法官，這些法庭負責審判戰爭罪等可怕的罪行。
她也領導過聯合國負責保護全世界人權的部門。
這個獎表彰她長期為和平奮鬥，也為保護每一個地方、每一個人的公平法律奮鬥。

ph.ex: He grew up in a small village.
ph.exzh: 他在一個小村莊長大。

ph.ex: If you work hard, you will improve.
ph.exzh: 只要努力，你就會進步。

ph.ex: They fought for the right to vote.
ph.exzh: 他們為投票權而奮鬥。

ph.ex: Children around the world love stories.
ph.exzh: 全世界的孩子都愛聽故事。

b.title: Navi Pillay: Justice Without Borders
text: On 9 October 2026, Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay of South Africa won the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
Pillay was born into a poor family and grew up under apartheid, a cruel system that gave people different rights based on their race.
Against the odds, she studied law and became the first woman to open her own law practice in her province, defending people who were treated unjustly.
Her work later took her to the world stage. She served as a judge on international courts that hold leaders responsible for war crimes and genocide.
From 2008 to 2014, she led the United Nations office for human rights, speaking up for the vulnerable in every corner of the globe.
Her life shows that peace is built not only by stopping wars, but by building fair laws that protect the dignity of every person.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Pillay won the Peace Prize for a lifetime promoting human rights and law.
Pillay was the first woman to open her own law practice in her province.
Pillay grew up under apartheid, a cruel system based on race, in South Africa.
Pillay led the UN human rights office for six years, from 2008 to 2014.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: What was apartheid?
opts: A special court that tried people for war crimes
A political party that ruled South Africa for years
A law that protected the human rights of everyone
A cruel system giving people rights based on race
q.why: 原文：“Pillay was born into a poor family and grew up under apartheid, a cruel system that gave people different rights based on their race.”

q.q: What was Pillay the first woman to do in her province?
opts: Become a judge in the high court
Go to university to study law
Open her own law practice
Lead a political party in elections
q.why: 原文：“Against the odds, she studied law and became the first woman to open her own law practice in her province, defending people who were treated unjustly.”

q.q: In paragraph 5, “vulnerable” means ___.
opts: very powerful and hard to stop
easily hurt and needing protection
well protected and safe from harm
very brave in a time of danger
q.why: vulnerable = 弱勢、易受傷害的。

q.q: What does her life show about peace?
opts: Peace only means stopping wars between different countries
Peace comes mainly from building large and strong armies
Peace is impossible unless strong leaders are in charge
Peace also means fair laws that protect everyone's dignity
q.why: 線索：“Her life shows that peace is built not only by stopping wars, but by building fair laws that protect the dignity of every person.”

q.q: Someone says: “A judge can't win a Peace Prize; only people who stop wars can.” Which point from the text best answers this?
opts: Judges are more important to peace than soldiers or leaders
Fair laws that protect dignity are a foundation of peace
Pillay personally stopped many wars during her time at the UN
The Peace Prize has always been given only to lawyers
q.why: 和平也包括建立保障尊嚴的公平法律。

tr.en: Pillay was born into a poor family and grew up under apartheid, a cruel system that gave people different rights based on their race.
tr.zh: 皮萊出生在貧窮的家庭，在種族隔離制度下長大——那是一個依照種族給人不同權利的殘酷制度。

tz: 2026 年 10 月 9 日，南非的納瓦內瑟姆・「納維」・皮萊因為致力推動和平與國際法，獲得了諾貝爾和平獎。
皮萊出生在一個貧窮的家庭，在種族隔離制度下長大——那是一種依照種族給予人們不同權利的殘酷制度。
她克服重重困難讀了法律，成為她所在省份第一位自己開設律師事務所的女性，為受到不公平對待的人辯護。
她的工作後來把她帶上了世界舞台。她擔任國際法庭的法官，這些法庭追究領導人在戰爭罪和種族滅絕罪上的責任。
2008 到 2014 年，她領導聯合國人權辦公室，為全球每一個角落的弱勢者發聲。
她的一生顯示，和平不只是靠停止戰爭建立的，也要靠建立保護每一個人尊嚴的公平法律。

c.title: Building Peace Through Law
text: When the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the 2026 Peace Prize to Navi Pillay on 9 October, it recognised a lifetime spent insisting that justice belongs to everyone, not only the powerful.

Born in 1941 into a working-class family in South Africa, Pillay came of age under apartheid, a system that stripped most of the population of basic rights. Education became her way out — and her weapon.
She became the first non-white woman to open a law practice in her province, often defending opponents of the regime when few others dared.

Her reach grew global. As a judge, and later president, of the international tribunal for Rwanda, she helped establish that rape could be prosecuted as a crime of genocide — a landmark for international justice.
From 2008 to 2014 she served as the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, a fearless voice for the persecuted regardless of politics or borders.
Her career embodies a quiet but radical idea: that lasting peace rests on the rule of law, and that protecting the rights of the weakest protects us all.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: How the Rwanda tribunal was set up to try those behind the genocide
Why education, above all else, is the only true path to lasting peace
How apartheid finally ended in South Africa through peaceful protest
How Pillay built peace through law and human rights, earning the Nobel
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: What landmark did Pillay help establish at the Rwanda tribunal?
opts: That war leaders could never be put on trial
That rape could be prosecuted as genocide
That only countries, not people, commit crimes
That such courts must close once a war ends
q.why: 原文：“As a judge, and later president, of the international tribunal for Rwanda, she helped establish that rape could be prosecuted as a crime of genocide — a landmark …”

q.q: What role did she hold from 2008 to 2014?
opts: UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
President of the Rwanda tribunal in Arusha
Chief Justice of the South African courts
Secretary-General of the United Nations
q.why: 原文：“From 2008 to 2014 she served as the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, a fearless voice for the persecuted regardless of politics or borders.”

q.q: In paragraph 2, education is called her 'way out — and her weapon.' This means education ___.
opts: was dangerous for girls who grew up under apartheid
made her leave South Africa for a life abroad
helped her escape poverty and fight injustice
was used by the government as a weapon in war
q.why: 文中。

q.q: What 'radical idea' does her career embody?
opts: Peace comes mainly from strong leaders who keep order
The powerful deserve more protection than the weak
Lasting peace rests on law and on protecting the weakest
Laws matter far less than armies in keeping peace
q.why: 線索：“Her career embodies a quiet but radical idea: that lasting peace rests on the rule of law, and that protecting the rights of the weakest protects us all.”

q.q: Why might holding leaders responsible for war crimes help prevent future wars?
opts: It makes the leaders of countries more popular at home

Leaders who could face justice may avoid terrible acts
q.why: 追究責任能嚇阻未來的暴行。

tz: 挪威諾貝爾委員會在 10 月 9 日把 2026 年和平獎頒給納維・皮萊時，表彰的是她一生都在堅持：正義屬於每一個人，而不只屬於有權勢的人。
皮萊 1941 年出生於南非一個勞工階級的家庭，在種族隔離制度下長大，這個制度剝奪了大多數人口的基本權利。教育成了她的出路——也成了她的武器。
她成為她所在省份第一位開設律師事務所的非白人女性，常常在很少有人敢站出來的時候，為反對政權的人辯護。
她的影響力擴及全球。她擔任盧安達問題國際刑事法庭的法官、後來成為庭長，協助確立了強暴可以被當作種族滅絕罪起訴——這是國際司法的一個里程碑。
2008 到 2014 年，她擔任聯合國人權事務高級專員，不分政治或國界，無畏地為受迫害的人發聲。
她的職業生涯體現了一個安靜卻激進的想法：持久的和平建立在法治之上，而保護最弱勢者的權利，就是保護我們所有人。

ph.exzh: 法律保護兒童的權利。
