She believed that protecting the weakest protects everyone. Do you agree? Why or why not?

topic: Pompeii: The City Frozen in Time
zh: 龐貝：凝固在時間裡的城市

a.title: The City the Volcano Buried
text: Pompeii was a busy Roman city in Italy, almost two thousand years ago. People lived, worked, and shopped there every day.
Near the city stood a mountain called Mount Vesuvius. The people did not know it was a dangerous volcano.
In the year 79, the volcano erupted. It threw ash and rock high into the sky for two days.
The whole city was buried under deep ash. Sadly, many people could not escape in time.
For hundreds of years, Pompeii lay hidden and forgotten. Then, much later, people dug it up again.
Today we can walk through its streets and houses. Pompeii shows us exactly how Romans lived long ago.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Why Mount Vesuvius is such a dangerous volcano
How hot ash from a volcano covers a whole city
What daily life is like in modern Italy today
A Roman city buried by a volcano and found again
q.why: 全文講龐貝。

q.q: What was Mount Vesuvius?
opts: A dangerous volcano
A mountain with a Roman temple
A green hill with farms only
A Roman city
q.why: 原文：“The people did not know it was a dangerous volcano.”

q.q: What happened to the city in the year 79?
opts: It was flooded by the sea
It was buried under ash
Everyone escaped before the ash came
It was destroyed by an earthquake only
q.why: 原文：“The whole city was buried under deep ash.”

q.q: In the text, “erupt” means a volcano ___.
opts: slowly grows taller over many years
goes quiet and sleeps for a long time
suddenly throws out ash, rock, and fire
is covered with snow in the winter
q.why: erupt = 噴發。

q.q: Why is Pompeii special today?
opts: It is now the largest and busiest city in Italy
It shows us exactly how Romans lived long ago
It has the newest and most modern museums
It is still a busy Roman city with many shops
q.why: 線索：“Pompeii shows us exactly how Romans lived long ago.”

q.q: If a city today were suddenly covered and found 2,000 years later, which object would best show how we live?
opts: A famous painting hanging in a big museum
A tall statue of a president in a park
An ordinary school lunch box with food in it
A gold medal won at the Olympic Games
q.why: 龐貝的價值在於日常生活的細節。

gt.en: Pompeii was a busy Roman city in Italy, almost two thousand years ago.
gt.zh: 龐貝是將近兩千年前義大利一座熱鬧的羅馬城市。

gt.en: The people did not know it was a dangerous volcano.
gt.zh: 人們不知道那是一座危險的火山。

gt.en: In the year 79, the volcano erupted.
gt.zh: 西元 79 年，火山爆發了。

gt.en: The whole city was buried under deep ash.
gt.zh: 整座城市被埋在厚厚的火山灰下。

tz: 龐貝是將近兩千年前義大利一座熱鬧的羅馬城市。人們每天在那裡生活、工作和購物。
城市附近有一座叫做維蘇威火山的山。人們不知道它是一座危險的火山。
西元 79 年，火山爆發了。它連續兩天把火山灰和石頭噴向高空。
整座城市被埋在厚厚的火山灰底下。很可惜，許多人來不及逃走。
好幾百年來，龐貝一直被掩埋、被遺忘。後來，過了很久，人們才把它挖了出來。
今天，我們可以走在它的街道上、走進它的房子。龐貝讓我們清楚地看到古羅馬人以前是怎麼生活的。

ph.ex: Almost two thousand years ago, this was a busy port.
ph.exzh: 將近兩千年前，這裡是一個熱鬧的港口。

ph.ex: The car was buried under snow.
ph.exzh: 車子被埋在雪底下。

ph.ex: We got to the station just in time.
ph.exzh: 我們及時趕到了車站。

ph.ex: The dog dug up an old bone.
ph.exzh: 小狗挖出了一根舊骨頭。

b.title: A Day That Stopped Forever
text: Nearly two thousand years ago, Pompeii was a lively Roman town near the bay of Naples, in Italy — home to shops, baths, theatres, and around twelve thousand people.
Looming above it was Mount Vesuvius. Few people realised that the green mountain was in fact a sleeping volcano.
In AD 79, Vesuvius exploded with terrible force. For two days it rained ash and burning rock, until the town — and many who had stayed behind — lay buried under metres of volcanic debris.
Terrible as it was, the ash also preserved the city. Buildings, wall paintings, loaves of bread, and even the shapes of people were sealed and protected underground for centuries.
Rediscovered and slowly excavated from the 1700s onward, Pompeii became a window into the ancient world. Archaeologists could read shop signs, study homes, and learn what Romans ate and wore.
Vesuvius is still active today, and scientists watch it closely. Pompeii remains a haunting reminder of nature's power — and a priceless record of a single ancient day.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Pompeii was a lively town of about twelve thousand people near Naples.
A volcano destroyed Pompeii, but its ash preserved a record of Roman life.
A volcano destroyed Pompeii so completely that nothing of Roman life survived.
Pompeii was rediscovered and slowly excavated from the 1700s onward.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: About how many people lived in Pompeii?
opts: About 1,200
About 120,000
About 12,000
About 2,000
q.why: 文中。

q.q: How did the ash help, despite the disaster?
opts: It sealed and preserved buildings and objects
It made the soil rich, so the city was rebuilt
It put out the fires that started in the town
It warned people that they needed to leave
q.why: 原文：“Buildings, wall paintings, loaves of bread, and even the shapes of people were sealed and protected underground for centuries.”

q.q: In paragraph 5, “excavated” means ___.
opts: completely rebuilt in modern style
covered again to protect it
sold piece by piece to museums
carefully dug out of the ground
q.why: excavate = 挖掘。

q.q: Why is Pompeii called “a window into the ancient world”?
opts: Its houses had many glass windows that still survive
It can be seen clearly from far away across the bay
It was once the capital city of the Roman Empire
Its preserved streets and objects show how Romans lived
q.why: 文中。

q.q: Why might the ash that killed people also be called a 'gift' to historians?
opts: It made the city rich because tourists came to see the ash
It created new kinds of Roman art from the burnt buildings
It preserved everyday life as it was, which rarely survives
It stopped Mount Vesuvius from ever erupting again
q.why: 火山灰把日常生活原封保存下來。

tr.en: Few people realised that the green mountain was in fact a sleeping volcano.
tr.zh: 很少人意識到，那座綠色的山其實是一座沉睡的火山。

tr.en: Terrible as it was, the ash also preserved the city.
tr.zh: 雖然這場災難很可怕，火山灰卻也把這座城市保存了下來。

tr.en: Rediscovered and slowly excavated from the 1700s onward, Pompeii became a window into the ancient world.
tr.zh: 從十八世紀起重新被發現並慢慢挖掘出來，龐貝成了一扇通往古代世界的窗。

tz: 將近兩千年前，龐貝是義大利那不勒斯灣附近一座熱鬧的羅馬小城——有商店、浴場、劇院，住著大約一萬兩千人。
高高聳立在城市上方的是維蘇威火山。很少有人知道，這座綠色的山其實是一座沉睡的火山。
西元 79 年，維蘇威火山以可怕的力量爆發。連續兩天，火山灰和燃燒的岩石如雨般落下，直到整座小城——以及許多留下來的人——被埋在好幾公尺深的火山碎屑底下。
雖然可怕，火山灰也保存了這座城市。建築、壁畫、麵包，甚至人的形狀，都被封存在地底，受到保護好幾個世紀。
從 1700 年代開始被重新發現並慢慢挖掘後，龐貝成了一扇通往古代世界的窗。考古學家可以閱讀商店招牌、研究住宅，並了解羅馬人吃什麼、穿什麼。
維蘇威火山至今仍然活躍，科學家密切監測著它。龐貝依然是一個令人難忘的提醒，提醒我們大自然的力量——也是古代某一天的無價紀錄。

ph.ex: The forest is home to many birds.
ph.exzh: 這片森林是許多鳥類的家。

ph.ex: Two students stayed behind to clean the room.
ph.exzh: 兩名學生留下來打掃教室。

ph.ex: The castle has stood here for centuries.
ph.exzh: 這座城堡已經在這裡好幾個世紀了。

ph.ex: From that day onward, she practised every morning.
ph.exzh: 從那天開始，她每天早上都練習。

ph.ex: Watch the weather closely before you go hiking.
ph.exzh: 去爬山前要密切注意天氣。

c.title: The Gift of Catastrophe
text: Among the ironies of history, few are sharper than Pompeii: a catastrophe that destroyed a city and, in the same stroke, saved it. When Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, it ended thousands of lives; it also sealed an entire Roman town beneath a blanket of ash, pausing it, mid-gesture, for nearly two millennia.

What makes Pompeii extraordinary is not grandeur but ordinariness. Rome left behind temples and monuments by design; Pompeii left behind the unguarded everyday — graffiti scratched on walls, election posters, a dog chained in a doorway, a meal abandoned on a table. The eruption froze not emperors but ordinary people, caught in an ordinary morning.

The ash proved a cruel kind of preservative. By packing tightly around bodies that later decayed, it left hollow moulds; when archaeologists poured plaster into these voids, the victims' final postures emerged — figures crouching, shielding children, holding one another.
Such discoveries raise uneasy questions about how we study the dead. Pompeii is at once a scientific treasure and a mass grave, and the line between learning and intrusion is not always clear.
Still, the town endures as our most vivid link to antiquity — proof that the smallest details of a vanished life can outlast the empires that once seemed so much more permanent.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's central idea?
opts: In destroying Pompeii, the disaster preserved a uniquely ordinary record.
Pompeii shows that volcanic disasters destroy everything they touch.
Pompeii is important mainly for its grand temples and public buildings.
Pompeii should be left untouched, since studying it disturbs the dead.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In paragraph 2, the writer says Pompeii's value is “not grandeur but ordinariness,” meaning its worth lies in ___.
opts: its huge palaces and grand public buildings
the ordinary, everyday details of real lives
the famous leaders who once lived there
the great wealth found in its richest homes
q.why: 文中。

q.q: How were the famous body shapes of victims created?
opts: They are Roman statues that were found buried in the ash
They are modern wax models made for visiting tourists
Plaster was poured into hollows the bodies left in the ash
They were painted on the walls of houses by survivors
q.why: 線索：“By packing tightly around bodies that later decayed, it left hollow moulds; when archaeologists poured plaster into these voids, the victims' final postures emerged …”

q.q: What tension does paragraph 4 raise?
opts: Most tourists would rather visit Rome than Pompeii
The excavation of the site is moving far too slowly
Mount Vesuvius is likely to erupt again very soon
It is both a scientific treasure and a mass grave
q.why: 第四段。

q.q: The whole essay is framed around ___.
opts: a comparison between Pompeii and Rome
a list of the objects found in the ash
an irony: destruction that also preserved
a timeline of the main excavations
q.why: 反諷架構。

q.q: A museum wants to display the plaster casts of Pompeii's victims. Which approach best respects the tension the writer describes?
opts: Display them as scary attractions in a dark, haunted room
Show them with notes reminding visitors they were real people
Display them as art, without saying who these people were at all
Sell small copies of them in the gift shop as souvenirs
q.why: 既是科學寶藏也是墓地，展示應尊重逝者。

tz: 在歷史的諷刺之中，很少有比龐貝更尖銳的：一場摧毀了一座城市、卻同時拯救了它的災難。西元 79 年維蘇威火山爆發時，奪走了數千條生命；它也把一整座羅馬小城封存在一層火山灰底下，讓它停在動作的一半，停了將近兩千年。
龐貝的非凡之處不在於宏偉，而在於平凡。羅馬是有意地留下神殿和紀念碑；龐貝留下的，卻是毫無防備的日常——刻在牆上的塗鴉、選舉海報、一隻被拴在門口的狗、一頓被丟在桌上的飯。這場火山爆發凍結的不是皇帝，而是普通人，被困在一個普通的早晨裡。
火山灰成了一種殘酷的防腐劑。它緊緊包住那些後來腐爛的屍體，留下了中空的模子；當考古學家把石膏灌進這些空洞，受害者最後的姿勢就浮現出來——有人蹲著、有人護著孩子、有人緊緊抱在一起。
這樣的發現引出一些令人不安的問題：我們該如何研究死者？龐貝同時是一座科學寶庫和一個集體墳墓，而學習與打擾之間的界線並不總是清楚的。
儘管如此，這座小城仍然是我們與古代之間最生動的連結——證明一段消失的生活中最微小的細節，能比那些曾經看起來永恆得多的帝國活得更久。

ph.ex: The new road saved time and, in the same stroke, cut pollution.
ph.exzh: 這條新路省了時間，同時也減少了污染。

ph.ex: The storm left behind broken trees.
ph.exzh: 暴風雨過後留下了斷裂的樹木。

ph.ex: Silence can be a cruel kind of answer.
ph.exzh: 沉默有時是一種殘酷的回答。

ph.ex: The video raises questions about safety.
ph.exzh: 這段影片引發了關於安全的問題。

ph.ex: She is at once a teacher and a student.
ph.exzh: 她同時是老師也是學生。

ph.ex: Good books outlast their writers.
ph.exzh: 好書比作者的生命更長久。

discuss: Why do you think people today are so fascinated by Pompeii?
Pompeii is both a scientific treasure and a mass grave. Should human remains be shown to the public? Why or why not?
If a city today were suddenly frozen in time, what everyday objects would best tell the future about us?

topic: Kyoto: Japan's Ancient Capital
zh: 京都：日本的千年古都
src: The New York Times · National Geographic · Taipei Times

a.title: Welcome to Kyoto
text: Kyoto is a beautiful old city in Japan. For more than a thousand years, it was the country's capital.
Kyoto is famous for its temples and shrines. Some are made of wood and are very, very old.
One famous place is Fushimi Inari, where thousands of bright orange gates stand in a long line up a hill.
In spring, pink cherry blossoms cover the city. In autumn, the leaves turn red and gold. Many people visit just to see them.
In the old streets of Gion, you might see a geisha in a beautiful kimono walking quietly by.
Kyoto mixes the old and the new. It is a wonderful place to learn about Japanese history and culture.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: The thousands of orange gates at Fushimi Inari
A beautiful old Japanese city and what to see there
Cherry blossoms that bloom across Japan in spring
Geisha and the old tea houses of the Gion district
q.why: 全文介紹京都。

q.q: What was Kyoto for more than a thousand years?
opts: A small fishing village
A famous port
Japan's capital
A mountain temple
q.why: 原文：“For more than a thousand years, it was the country's capital.”

q.q: What is famous about Fushimi Inari?
opts: Thousands of orange gates up a hill
A golden temple standing by a lake
A long, quiet path through bamboo
A tall wooden tower near the station
q.why: 原文：“One famous place is Fushimi Inari, where thousands of bright orange gates stand in a long line up a hill.”

q.q: In the text, a “shrine” is ___.
opts: a small house for drinking tea
a busy market selling food
a quiet garden with a pond
a holy place where people pray
q.why: shrine = 神社。

q.q: Why do many people visit Kyoto in spring and autumn?
opts: Because hotels are much cheaper at those times
To see cherry blossoms and red autumn leaves
Because many temples close during the summer
Because there are fewer tourists in those seasons
q.why: 線索：“In autumn, the leaves turn red and gold.”

q.q: You want to see Kyoto's famous seasonal colours but avoid the biggest crowds. Based on the text, what is the challenge?
opts: Kyoto does not really have different seasons
The temples are closed to visitors in spring
The most beautiful seasons are also the busiest
There are never any crowds in Kyoto
q.why: 最美的季節也是人最多的時候。

gt.en: For more than a thousand years, it was the country's capital.
gt.zh: 一千多年來，它都是這個國家的首都。

gt.en: Kyoto is famous for its temples and shrines.
gt.zh: 京都以它的寺廟和神社聞名。

gt.en: In spring, pink cherry blossoms cover the city.
gt.zh: 春天時，粉紅色的櫻花覆蓋整座城市。

gt.en: In the old streets of Gion, you might see a geisha in a beautiful kimono walking quietly by.
gt.zh: 在祇園的老街上，你可能會看到一位穿著美麗和服的藝妓靜靜地走過。

tz: 京都是日本一座美麗的古城。一千多年來，它都是日本的首都。
京都以寺廟和神社聞名。有些是木造的，而且非常非常古老。
有一個有名的地方叫伏見稻荷，成千上萬座鮮橘色的鳥居排成長長一列，一路延伸上山。
春天，粉紅色的櫻花覆蓋整座城市；秋天，樹葉變成紅色和金色。很多人專程來看這些景色。
在祇園的老街上，你可能會看到一位穿著美麗和服的藝妓靜靜地走過。
京都融合了古老和現代，是學習日本歷史和文化的好地方。

ph.ex: Tainan is famous for its food.
ph.exzh: 台南以美食聞名。

ph.ex: The table is made of wood.
ph.exzh: 這張桌子是木頭做的。

ph.ex: People waited in a long line for bubble tea.
ph.exzh: 人們排成長長一列等珍珠奶茶。

ph.ex: A cat walked by our window.
ph.exzh: 一隻貓從我們窗前走過。

b.title: A City of a Thousand Years
text: For over a thousand years, until 1868, Kyoto was the capital of Japan. Though Tokyo holds that title now, Kyoto remains the nation's cultural heart.

The city is home to around two thousand temples and shrines. At Kiyomizu-dera, a wooden hall stands on tall pillars over a hillside; at Fushimi Inari, thousands of vermilion gates form glowing tunnels up the mountain.
Kyoto changes beautifully with the seasons. Spring brings clouds of cherry blossom; autumn sets the maples of Arashiyama ablaze in red and orange. These two seasons draw by far the largest crowds.
The old district of Gion is famous for its wooden tea houses and its geisha, women trained for years in traditional dance, music, and the art of conversation.
Visitors can still enjoy a simple cup of matcha tea, a quiet temple garden, or a meal of local tofu and vegetables.
Above all, Kyoto asks to be taken slowly. It rewards those who wander its back streets and pause to notice small, carefully made beauty.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Kyoto was the capital of Japan for over a thousand years, until 1868.
Kyoto, Japan's old capital, is a cultural city best enjoyed slowly.
The Gion district is famous for its wooden tea houses and geisha.
Spring and autumn draw the largest crowds of visitors to the city.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: Until what year was Kyoto the capital of Japan?
q.why: 原文：“For over a thousand years, until 1868, Kyoto was the capital of Japan.”

q.q: What is the Gion district known for?
opts: Thousands of orange shrine gates
Large, modern shopping malls
Wooden tea houses and geisha
Parks full of cherry blossoms
q.why: 原文：“The old district of Gion is famous for its wooden tea houses and its geisha, women trained for years in traditional dance, music, and the art of conversation.”

q.q: In paragraph 4, a “district” is ___.
opts: an area or part of a city
a famous old building
a kind of Shinto shrine
a yearly festival
q.why: district = 區。

q.q: What does “Kyoto asks to be taken slowly” suggest?
opts: Kyoto is best enjoyed by slowing down and noticing details
Walking quickly is not allowed in the old parts of the city
The trains in Kyoto are slower than those in other cities
Kyoto is a rather boring place for most young visitors
q.why: 線索：“Above all, Kyoto asks to be taken slowly.”

q.q: Which travel plan best fits the writer's advice for Kyoto?
opts: Visit as many famous sites as possible in a single day
Visit fewer places and wander the quiet back streets
Stay mostly in your hotel and watch the city from there
Spend most of your time in the big shopping areas
q.why: 作者建議放慢腳步、在小巷中漫步。

tr.en: For over a thousand years, until 1868, Kyoto was the capital of Japan.
tr.zh: 一千多年來，直到 1868 年，京都都是日本的首都。

tr.en: These two seasons draw by far the largest crowds.
tr.zh: 這兩個季節吸引的人潮是最多的。

tr.en: It rewards those who wander its back streets and pause to notice small, carefully made beauty.
tr.zh: 它會回報那些在小巷裡漫步、停下來欣賞細膩之美的人。

tz: 一千多年來，直到 1868 年，京都都是日本的首都。雖然現在首都是東京，京都仍然是這個國家的文化中心。
這座城市有大約兩千座寺廟和神社。在清水寺，一座木造殿堂立在高高的柱子上，凌空於山坡之上；在伏見稻荷，數千座朱紅色的鳥居一路往山上排成發光的隧道。
京都隨著四季變化得非常美麗。春天帶來一片片雲朵般的櫻花；秋天讓嵐山的楓葉燃燒成紅色和橘色。這兩個季節吸引的人潮最多。
古老的祇園區以木造茶屋和藝妓聞名；藝妓是經過多年傳統舞蹈、音樂和談話藝術訓練的女性。
遊客仍然可以享受一杯簡單的抹茶、一座安靜的寺院庭園，或是一頓在地豆腐和蔬菜的料理。
最重要的是，京都要人慢慢體會。它會回報那些在小巷裡漫步、停下來留意那些精心製作的小小美好的人。

ph.ex: Our city is home to three museums.
ph.exzh: 我們的城市有三座博物館。

ph.ex: The night market draws big crowds on weekends.
ph.exzh: 夜市週末吸引大批人潮。
ph.m: draw by far the largest crowds

ph.ex: Hualien is famous for its mountains and sea.
ph.exzh: 花蓮以山海聞名。

ph.ex: Take the hike slowly and enjoy the view.
ph.exzh: 慢慢爬，好好欣賞風景。

ph.ex: Above all, be kind to yourself.
ph.exzh: 最重要的是，要善待自己。

c.title: The Art of Going Slowly
text: To arrive in Kyoto expecting a museum is to misread it. Japan's capital for more than a millennium, the city wears its history not as a relic under glass but as a living habit — in the rhythm of its seasons, the manners of its streets, and a quiet insistence on doing things with care.

Its set-piece treasures are rightly famous: the vermilion corridors of Fushimi Inari, the hillside stage of Kiyomizu-dera, the towering bamboo groves of Arashiyama. Yet the first-time visitor, hurrying between them with a guidebook, often misses what makes Kyoto itself — the unhurried attention it pays to small things.

That attention shows everywhere: in a bowl of tea whisked just so, in a raked gravel garden meant to be contemplated rather than entered, in the training of a geisha measured not in weeks but in years.
Modern Kyoto, of course, also has traffic, convenience stores, and crowds that strain its most delicate corners, raising hard questions about how a living city can carry so priceless a past.
Perhaps that is Kyoto's deepest lesson for the traveller — and a useful one anywhere: that beauty is often found not by seeing more, but by slowing down enough to notice what was already there.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Kyoto's real beauty lies mainly in its famous temples and shrines.
Kyoto is a museum that should be preserved completely unchanged.
Mass tourism has ruined Kyoto beyond any hope of recovery.
Kyoto is a living city whose beauty is found by paying attention.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In paragraph 1, a “relic under glass” is used to describe what Kyoto is NOT — meaning Kyoto's history is ___.
opts: locked away and untouchable
forgotten by most people
alive and part of daily life
fake, built for tourists
q.why: 文中。

q.q: What do hurried first-time visitors tend to miss?
opts: The unhurried attention Kyoto pays to small things
The famous temples listed in every guidebook
The famous orange gates that cover the hill at Fushimi
The cherry blossoms that bloom each spring
q.why: 線索：“Yet the first-time visitor, hurrying between them with a guidebook, often misses what makes Kyoto itself — the unhurried attention it pays to small things.”

q.q: What does paragraph 4 add to the essay?
opts: It argues that tourists should stay away
It admits modern strains on a fragile city
It praises the city's modern buildings
It lists the prices of the best hotels
q.why: 第四段。

q.q: How does the writer mainly develop the piece?
opts: By listing the main sights in the order you see them
By comparing Kyoto's old streets with modern Tokyo
By contrasting rushing with slowing down to notice
By telling only the long history of the old capital
q.why: 結構。

q.q: Which habit from the writer's advice could you use in your own neighbourhood?
opts: Visiting only the famous places in your neighbourhood
Walking slowly and noticing details you usually miss
Taking lots of photos without really looking at things
Going everywhere by car so you can see more places
q.why: 放慢腳步、留意細節，在哪裡都適用。

tz: 抱著參觀博物館的期待來到京都，就誤解了它。這座做了一千多年日本首都的城市，並不是把它的歷史當作放在玻璃櫃裡的遺物，而是當成一種活著的習慣——在它的四季節奏裡、在它街道的禮儀裡，以及在一種「凡事都要用心去做」的安靜堅持裡。
它那些招牌景點名不虛傳：伏見稻荷朱紅色的長廊、清水寺依山而建的舞台、嵐山高聳的竹林。然而，第一次來的遊客拿著旅遊書在景點之間匆忙奔走，往往錯過了京都之所以是京都的東西——它對小事那份從容不迫的用心。
這份用心處處可見：一碗剛剛好打出泡沫的茶、一座用來凝視而不是走進去的枯山水庭園，還有藝妓的養成——不是以週來計算，而是以年來計算。
當然，現代的京都也有車潮、便利商店，還有讓它最脆弱的角落不堪負荷的人群，這引出一些困難的問題：一座活著的城市，要如何承載如此珍貴的過去？
也許這就是京都給旅人最深的一課——而且在哪裡都很有用：美往往不是靠看更多而找到的，而是要放慢腳步，慢到足以注意到那些原本就在那裡的東西。

ph.ex: Don't misread his silence as anger.
ph.exzh: 不要把他的沉默誤解成生氣。

ph.ex: She sees mistakes not as failures but as lessons.
ph.exzh: 她不把錯誤當失敗，而是當成教訓。
ph.m: not as a relic under glass but as

ph.ex: The beef noodles here are rightly famous.
ph.exzh: 這裡的牛肉麵名不虛傳。

ph.ex: The tea was made just so.
ph.exzh: 這杯茶泡得恰到好處。

ph.ex: Of course, big cities also have problems.
ph.exzh: 當然，大城市也有問題。

ph.ex: Slow down and look around you.
ph.exzh: 放慢腳步，看看你的周圍。

discuss: Would you rather travel to see as much as possible, or slow down and experience a few places deeply? Why?
Kyoto struggles with too many tourists. How can a city protect its culture and still welcome visitors?
Think of a place in Taiwan that mixes old and new. How would you introduce it to a foreign friend in English?

topic: How to Keep a Whole Economy Steady
zh: 如何穩住整個經濟：2026 諾貝爾經濟獎
tag: Nobel Economics · 諾貝爾經濟獎

a.title: Keeping Prices and Jobs Steady
text: On October 12, 2026, two economists won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences. Their names are Robert Hall and Michael Woodford.
An economy is all the buying, selling, saving, and working in a country.
Sometimes prices rise too fast, so money buys less. Sometimes many people lose their jobs. Both are big problems.
Countries have special banks, called central banks, that try to keep prices and jobs steady.
Hall and Woodford studied how the small choices of ordinary people and shops add up to the whole economy.
Their ideas help central banks choose good actions — like changing interest rates — to calm prices and help people keep working.

q.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: How central banks change their interest rates every single month
Why prices in shops sometimes rise too fast to follow
Two economists who showed how to make everyone richer
Two economists who studied keeping prices and jobs steady
q.why: 全文介紹兩位經濟學家的研究；其他是細節。

q.q: What do central banks try to do?
opts: Keep prices and jobs steady
Make prices rise as fast as possible
Lend money to every family
Decide how much people earn
q.why: 文中：try to keep prices and jobs steady。

q.q: What did Hall and Woodford study?
opts: How central banks can safely print a lot more money
How people's small choices add up to the whole economy
How to stop prices from ever changing in any shop
How big banks make profits from lending to people
q.why: 文中說明他們研究的內容。

q.q: In the text, “steady” means ___.
opts: rising very quickly each year
very low and getting lower
not changing too much; stable
hard to predict or understand
q.why: steady = 穩定的。

q.q: Why are their ideas useful?
opts: They help central banks choose actions, like changing rates
They let central banks control every single price in shops
They make sure that everyone in the country becomes rich
They stop people from saving too much money in banks
q.why: 文中：幫助央行做出好決策。

q.q: Your snack shop's prices go up every week, so your pocket money buys less. Which problem from the text is this?
opts: Too many people losing their jobs at once
Banks closing down across the country
People saving far too much of their money
Prices rising too fast, so money buys less
q.why: 文中：Sometimes prices rise too fast, so money buys less。

gt.en: An economy is all the buying, selling, saving, and working in a country.
gt.zh: 經濟就是一個國家裡所有的買、賣、儲蓄和工作。

gt.en: Sometimes prices rise too fast, so money buys less.
gt.zh: 有時候物價漲得太快，錢就買得到比較少的東西。

gt.en: Countries have special banks, called central banks, that try to keep prices and jobs steady.
gt.zh: 各國都有特別的銀行，叫做中央銀行，它們努力讓物價和就業保持穩定。

tz: 2026 年 10 月 12 日，兩位經濟學家獲得了諾貝爾經濟學獎。他們的名字是羅伯特・霍爾和麥可・伍德福德。
經濟就是一個國家裡所有的買、賣、存錢和工作。
有時候物價漲得太快，錢能買到的東西就變少了。有時候很多人失去工作。這兩種都是大問題。
國家有特別的銀行，叫做中央銀行，它們試著讓物價和就業保持穩定。
霍爾和伍德福德研究了一般人和商店的小小選擇，是如何加起來變成整個經濟的。
他們的想法幫助中央銀行選擇好的做法——像是調整利率——來穩定物價、幫助人們保住工作。

ph.ex: Small choices add up to big changes.
ph.exzh: 小小的選擇累積起來就是大改變。

ph.ex: His father lost his job last year.
ph.exzh: 他爸爸去年失業了。

ph.ex: Try to drink more water every day.
ph.exzh: 試著每天多喝點水。

ph.ex: The machines keep working all night.
ph.exzh: 這些機器整夜不停運轉。

b.title: The Science of a Stable Economy
text: On 12 October 2026, Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on the 'microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation'.
That long phrase hides a simple question: how do the everyday choices of millions of people and businesses add up to the ups and downs of a whole country's economy?
When prices rise too quickly, savings lose value; when demand falls, factories close and workers lose their jobs. Governments want to avoid both.
Hall and Woodford built careful models showing how people's spending, saving, and especially their expectations about the future shape the bigger picture.
Their work gave central banks a firmer basis for using tools like interest rates to steer the economy between overheating and slowing down.
Because of ideas like theirs, the banks that guard our money can act with more confidence when they try to keep prices stable and jobs plentiful.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Central banks use interest rates to stop prices from rising too fast.
When demand falls, factories may close and many workers lose jobs.
Hall and Woodford showed how everyday choices shape a whole economy.
People's expectations about the future help shape the economy.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；其他是細節。

q.q: What two problems do governments want to avoid?
opts: Prices falling too slowly, and too many new jobs
Prices rising too fast, and many people losing jobs
Too much saving, and too little spending in shops
Banks lending too much, and shops closing early
q.why: 原文：“When prices rise too quickly, savings lose value; when demand falls, factories close and workers lose their jobs.”

q.q: Besides spending and saving, what especially shapes the big picture?
opts: The number of banks in each country
The price of gold on world markets
How much the government advertises
People's expectations about the future
q.why: 文中：especially their expectations about the future。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “steer” means ___.
opts: to guide or direct
to slow down completely
to borrow money
to predict
q.why: steer = 引導。

q.q: Why does their work give central banks 'more confidence'?
opts: It lets central banks control people's daily choices
It guarantees that prices will never rise again
It gives a firmer basis for tools like interest rates
It makes central banks far richer than before
q.why: 線索：“Their work gave central banks a firmer basis for using tools like interest rates to steer the economy between overheating and slowing down.”

q.q: If people expect prices to rise next year, they may buy more now. Which idea from the text does this example show?
opts: Central banks always control how much people spend
Saving money is always more important than spending
Prices never really depend on people's own choices
Expectations about the future shape the bigger picture
q.why: 預期心理影響當下的消費——正是他們研究的重點。

tr.en: When prices rise too quickly, savings lose value; when demand falls, factories close and workers lose their jobs.
tr.zh: 物價上漲太快時，存款就會貶值；需求下降時，工廠關門，工人失業。

tr.en: Hall and Woodford built careful models showing how people's spending, saving, and especially their expectations about the future shape the bigger picture.
tr.zh: 霍爾和伍德福德建立了嚴謹的模型，說明人們的消費、儲蓄，特別是他們對未來的預期，如何影響整體的經濟。

tr.en: Their work gave central banks a firmer basis for using tools like interest rates to steer the economy between overheating and slowing down.
tr.zh: 他們的研究讓中央銀行在運用利率等工具、讓經濟在過熱與放緩之間保持平衡時，有了更穩固的依據。

tz: 2026 年 10 月 12 日，羅伯特・霍爾和麥可・伍德福德因為「總體經濟穩定的個體經濟基礎」方面的研究，獲得了諾貝爾經濟學獎。
這個長長的說法背後藏著一個簡單的問題：數百萬人和企業的日常選擇，是如何加總起來，變成一整個國家經濟的起起落落？
物價上漲太快時，存款就會貶值；需求下降時，工廠就會關門，工人就會失業。政府希望兩者都能避免。
霍爾和伍德福德建立了嚴謹的模型，說明人們的消費、儲蓄，特別是他們對未來的預期，如何塑造整體的局面。
他們的研究讓中央銀行在使用利率等工具、引導經濟避免過熱和放緩時，有了更穩固的依據。
因為有像他們這樣的想法，守護我們金錢的銀行在努力維持物價穩定、就業充足時，能更有信心地採取行動。

ph.ex: Ten minutes a day adds up to an hour a week.
ph.exzh: 每天十分鐘，一週加起來就是一個小時。

ph.ex: Every friendship has its ups and downs.
ph.exzh: 每段友誼都有起起落落。

ph.ex: Phones lose value quickly after you buy them.
ph.exzh: 手機買了之後很快就貶值了。

ph.ex: Don't worry about one test — look at the bigger picture.
ph.exzh: 不要只擔心一次考試，要看整體情況。

ph.ex: After practice, she spoke with more confidence.
ph.exzh: 練習之後，她說話更有自信了。

c.title: From Small Choices to the Whole Economy
text: On 12 October 2026, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford 'for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation'.

Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole — inflation, unemployment, growth — while microeconomics studies the decisions of single households and firms. The laureates helped bind the two together.

Their central insight is that the great swings of a national economy grow out of countless individual choices: how much to spend or save, what prices to set, and above all, what people expect to happen next.
Woodford showed how a central bank's words and credibility shape those expectations, so that guiding what people believe about future inflation can be as powerful as any single change in rates.
Hall illuminated how labour markets and spending respond over the business cycle, clarifying why recessions deepen and how recoveries take hold.

Together, their rigorous models turned central banking from something of an art into something far closer to a science, underpinning how institutions today fight both runaway prices and painful slumps.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: How central banks have fought inflation by raising interest rates
Why macroeconomics matters more than the study of single firms
How Hall and Woodford proved central banks can control every single price
How Hall and Woodford linked individual choices to economy-wide stability
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: How do macroeconomics and microeconomics differ?
opts: Macro studies only banks; micro studies only small shops
Macro studies the whole economy; micro, single firms and homes
Macro studies prices, while micro studies jobs and wages
Macro studies single households; micro studies the whole economy
q.why: 原文：“Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole — inflation, unemployment, growth — while microeconomics studies the decisions of single households and firms.”

q.q: What did Woodford show about a central bank?
opts: It should keep its future plans secret
It can directly control all prices
Its words and credibility shape expectations
Its decisions have little effect on people
q.why: 原文：“Woodford showed how a central bank's words and credibility shape those expectations, so that guiding what people believe about future inflation can be as powerful …”

q.q: In paragraph 6, “slumps” most nearly means ___.
opts: downturns or recessions
sudden rises in prices
failures of large banks
long periods of growth
q.why: slump = 經濟衰退。

q.q: Why is central banking now 'closer to a science'?
opts: Most central bankers today have trained in physics instead
Powerful computers now make all of the important decisions
Recessions no longer happen in any of the major economies
Rigorous models now guide how they fight inflation and slumps
q.why: 線索：“Together, their rigorous models turned central banking from something of an art into something far closer to a science, underpinning how institutions today fight …”

q.q: A central bank clearly announces its plan to keep inflation low, and people trust it. According to Woodford's idea, what is likely to happen?
opts: Expectations stay calm, which helps keep prices steady
Prices rise faster, because the plan worries people
Nothing changes, because words have no real effect
People stop spending entirely and save everything
q.why: 央行的話語與信譽會影響預期。

tz: 2026 年 10 月 12 日，瑞典皇家科學院把紀念諾貝爾的經濟學獎頒給羅伯特・E・霍爾和麥可・伍德福德，表彰他們「為總體經濟穩定奠定的個體經濟基礎」。
總體經濟學研究的是整體經濟——通貨膨脹、失業、成長——而個體經濟學研究的是單一家庭和企業的決策。兩位得主幫助把這兩者綁在一起。
他們的核心洞見是：一個國家經濟的大起大落，來自無數個人的選擇——要花多少、存多少，要訂什麼價格，而最重要的是，人們預期接下來會發生什麼。
伍德福德證明了中央銀行的話語和公信力會如何塑造這些預期，因此引導人們對未來通膨的看法，可能和任何一次調整利率一樣有力。
霍爾則闡明了勞動市場和消費在景氣循環中如何反應，釐清了為什麼經濟衰退會加深，以及復甦如何站穩腳步。
他們嚴謹的模型合在一起，讓中央銀行的工作從某種程度上的藝術，變得更接近一門科學，也成為今天各機構對抗物價失控和痛苦衰退的基礎。

ph.ex: Music binds people together.
ph.exzh: 音樂把人們凝聚在一起。

ph.exzh: 這個想法源自一次課堂討論。

ph.ex: Above all, we need good sleep.
ph.exzh: 最重要的是，我們需要好好睡覺。

ph.ex: A kind word can be as powerful as a gift.
ph.exzh: 一句好話可以和一份禮物一樣有力。

ph.ex: The new habit took hold after a month.
ph.exzh: 一個月後，這個新習慣就養成了。

ph.ex: Cooking is something of an art.
ph.exzh: 烹飪可說是一門藝術。

The laureates say our 'expectations about the future' shape the economy. Can expecting something make it more likely to happen?
If you ran a central bank, would you focus more on stable prices or on more jobs? Why?

topic: Iceland: The Land of Fire and Ice
zh: 冰島：冰與火之地
src: National Geographic · The New York Times · Nature

a.title: Welcome to Iceland
text: Iceland is a small island country in the north Atlantic Ocean. It is famous for fire and ice.
The land has many volcanoes. It also has huge glaciers — slow rivers of thick ice.
Hot water bubbles up from under the ground. People relax in warm pools, even when snow is falling around them.
In winter, you can sometimes see the northern lights — green and pink lights dancing in the night sky.
Iceland has waterfalls, black sand beaches, and tall cliffs full of seabirds called puffins.
The capital city is Reykjavik. From there, visitors drive out to explore one of the most beautiful lands on Earth.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Why Iceland has so many volcanoes
How to see the northern lights in winter
The puffins that live on Iceland's cliffs
Iceland and its amazing nature
q.why: 全文介紹冰島的自然；其他是細節。

q.q: Iceland is famous for ___.
opts: sand and sun
forests and rivers
fire and ice
cities and towers
q.why: 原文：“It is famous for fire and ice.”

q.q: When can you sometimes see the northern lights?
opts: In winter
In summer
At noon
Every night all year
q.why: 原文：“In winter, you can sometimes see the northern lights — green and pink lights dancing in the night sky.”

q.q: In the text, a “glacier” is ___.
opts: a hot spring in the snow
a huge, slow river of ice
a long beach of black sand
a tall cliff above the sea
q.why: glacier = 冰川。

q.q: Why can people relax in warm pools even in the snow?
opts: The bright summer sun heats them all day
Hot water from under the ground heats them
The pools are all inside warm buildings
Big electric heaters warm the pools at night
q.why: 線索：“Hot water bubbles up from under the ground.”

q.q: You are planning a trip to see the northern lights in Iceland. When should you go?
opts: In winter
In midsummer
Only in spring
It does not matter
q.why: 文中：冬天有時能看到極光。

gt.en: Iceland is a small island country in the north Atlantic Ocean.
gt.zh: 冰島是北大西洋上的一個小島國。

gt.en: The land has many volcanoes.
gt.zh: 這片土地上有許多火山。

gt.en: Hot water bubbles up from under the ground.

gt.zh: 冰島有瀑布、黑沙灘，還有布滿海鸚這種海鳥的高聳懸崖。

tz: 冰島是北大西洋上的一個小島國。它以火和冰聞名。
這片土地上有很多火山，也有巨大的冰川——一種由厚厚的冰形成、慢慢流動的河。
熱水從地底冒出來。即使周圍下著雪，人們也能在溫暖的池子裡放鬆。
冬天，你有時候能看到北極光——綠色和粉紅色的光在夜空中跳舞。
冰島有瀑布、黑沙灘，還有住滿一種叫做海鸚的海鳥的高聳懸崖。
首都是雷克雅維克。遊客從那裡開車出發，去探索地球上最美麗的土地之一。

ph.ex: Iceland is famous for fire and ice.
ph.exzh: 冰島以火和冰聞名。

ph.ex: Hot water bubbles up from the ground.
ph.exzh: 熱水從地底冒出來。

ph.ex: He smiles even when he is tired.
ph.exzh: 他即使累了也會微笑。

ph.ex: On Sundays we drive out to the countryside.
ph.exzh: 星期天我們開車到鄉下。

b.title: Where the Earth Is Still Being Made
text: Few countries feel as otherworldly as Iceland, a volcanic island near the Arctic Circle where fire and ice share the same landscape.
The island sits where two of Earth's great plates pull apart, so volcanoes and earthquakes are common. At the same time, vast glaciers cover much of the interior.
This restless geology is also a gift. Heat from underground warms homes and fills open-air pools such as the famous Blue Lagoon, even in freezing weather.
Nature is never far away. The 'Golden Circle' route takes visitors past a thundering waterfall, erupting hot springs, and a rift valley where two continents slowly split.
In the long winter nights, the sky sometimes glows with the aurora — curtains of green and violet light; in summer, by contrast, the sun barely sets at all.
With a tiny population and enormous open spaces, Iceland offers travellers something rare: the chance to feel the raw power of the planet up close.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Iceland is a volcanic island where fire and ice meet in raw nature.
The Blue Lagoon is warmed by geothermal heat from deep underground.
Iceland sits on the line where two of Earth's plates pull apart.
The Golden Circle route passes a great waterfall and hot springs.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: Why are volcanoes and earthquakes common in Iceland?
opts: It lies very close to the North Pole and its ice
Its many glaciers press down hard on the rock
It sits where two of Earth's plates pull apart
It is a small island in a stormy, cold ocean
q.why: 原文：“The island sits where two of Earth's great plates pull apart, so volcanoes and earthquakes are common.”

q.q: What warms the Blue Lagoon and many homes?
opts: Large electric heaters
Heat from underground
The long midnight sun
Warm air from the sea
q.why: 原文：“Heat from underground warms homes and fills open-air pools such as the famous Blue Lagoon, even in freezing weather.”

q.q: In paragraph 5, the “aurora” is ___.
opts: a hot spring that shoots water up
a small volcano under a glacier
a lagoon full of floating ice
coloured lights in the night sky
q.why: aurora = 極光。

q.q: What does the writer say is “rare” about visiting Iceland?
opts: Travel that is cheaper than anywhere else in Europe
Warm, sunny weather for most of the year
The chance to feel the planet's raw power up close
Quiet cities with very few other visitors
q.why: 線索：“With a tiny population and enormous open spaces, Iceland offers travellers something rare: the chance to feel the raw power of the planet up close.”

q.q: Why might Iceland be a good place to study how the Earth's surface moves?
opts: It has more tourists than any other island in the world
Plates pull apart there, so the movement can be seen on land
It has the coldest winters, which freeze the moving ground
Its puffins and other seabirds help scientists track change
q.why: 板塊交界位於陸地上，可直接觀察。

tr.en: Few countries feel as otherworldly as Iceland, a volcanic island near the Arctic Circle where fire and ice share the same landscape.
tr.zh: 很少有國家像冰島一樣讓人覺得不像在地球上——這座靠近北極圈的火山島，火與冰共享同一片風景。

tr.en: The island sits where two of Earth's great plates pull apart, so volcanoes and earthquakes are common.
tr.zh: 這座島位在地球兩大板塊分開的地方，所以火山和地震很常見。

tr.en: The 'Golden Circle' route takes visitors past a thundering waterfall, erupting hot springs, and a rift valley where two continents slowly split.
tr.zh: 「黃金圈」路線帶遊客經過轟隆作響的瀑布、噴發的溫泉，還有兩塊大陸慢慢分開的裂谷。

tz: 很少有國家像冰島一樣，讓人覺得像是另一個世界；這座靠近北極圈的火山島，火與冰共享同一片風景。
這座島位於地球兩大板塊互相拉開的地方，所以火山和地震很常見。同時，廣大的冰川覆蓋了內陸的大部分地區。
這種躁動的地質也是一份禮物。來自地底的熱能溫暖了住家，也注滿了像著名的藍湖這樣的露天溫泉池，即使天寒地凍也一樣。
大自然從來不遠。「黃金圈」路線帶遊客經過一座轟隆作響的瀑布、會噴發的溫泉，以及一座兩塊大陸正慢慢裂開的裂谷。
在漫長的冬夜裡，天空有時會亮起極光——一片片綠色和紫色的光幕；相反地，到了夏天，太陽幾乎整天都不會落下。
人口很少、空曠的空間卻非常廣大，冰島給旅人一樣很難得的東西：近距離感受地球原始力量的機會。

ph.ex: The two kids pulled apart the bread.
ph.exzh: 兩個孩子把麵包撕開。

ph.ex: At the same time, the city is very safe.
ph.exzh: 同時，這座城市也很安全。

ph.ex: In Taiwan, the sea is never far away.
ph.exzh: 在台灣，海從來不遠。

ph.ex: Summer is hot; winter, by contrast, is mild.
ph.exzh: 夏天很熱；相對地，冬天很溫和。

ph.ex: We saw the whales up close.
ph.exzh: 我們近距離看到了鯨魚。

c.title: Living on the Seam of the World
text: To travel in Iceland is to be reminded, constantly, that the ground beneath us is alive. The island straddles the boundary between two tectonic plates, and so it is forever being torn apart and built anew — a country, in effect, under construction.

This gives the landscape its strange grandeur: lava fields still black and bare, geysers that fire boiling water skyward, glaciers grinding whole valleys into shape. It also gives Icelanders a practical bargain with the earth, drawing clean heat and power from the volcanic rock below.

That intimacy with nature shapes the culture. A nation of fewer than four hundred thousand people has produced a fierce literary tradition, a deep love of storytelling, and — famously — a lingering half-seriousness about elves said to live in the rocks.

Tourism, now vital to the economy, brings its own tensions: fragile moss and quiet places can be worn away by too many feet, and Icelanders openly debate how to welcome the world without losing what makes the island special.
Still, few places teach the traveller so plainly that the planet is not a fixed stage but a living, moving thing — and that we are, all of us, only its temporary guests.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Iceland's culture is built mainly on its famous belief in elves.
Iceland's shifting land shapes its culture and humbles its visitors.
Mass tourism has already destroyed much of Iceland's fragile nature.
Iceland's land has largely stopped changing in recent centuries.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In paragraph 1, “straddles the boundary between two tectonic plates” means Iceland ___.
opts: lies far away from any plate boundary
is slowly sinking beneath the ocean
lies right in the middle of one huge plate
sits across the line where two plates meet
q.why: straddle = 跨在兩邊。

q.q: How does the land shape Icelandic culture, according to the text?
opts: It makes people avoid telling stories about nature
It stops farming almost everywhere on the island
It feeds storytelling, literature and folk beliefs
It forces many young people to leave the island
q.why: 線索：“A nation of fewer than four hundred thousand people has produced a fierce literary tradition, a deep love of storytelling, and — famously — a lingering …”

q.q: What tension does paragraph 4 add?
opts: Tourism is vital but wears away fragile places
Tourism should be banned in Iceland immediately
Tourism has no real effect on the land at all
Most tourists would rather visit cities than nature
q.why: 第四段。

q.q: How does the essay progress?
opts: Iceland's early history → its modern-day politics
A simple list of attractions for first-time visitors
Living land → culture → tourism's tension → a lesson
From the capital city out to the empty countryside
q.why: 結構如選項。

q.q: Iceland wants to keep earning from tourism while protecting fragile places. Which policy best balances both?
opts: Limit numbers at fragile sites and mark clear paths
Allow unlimited visitors everywhere, all year round
Close the whole country to tourists for ten years
Build new hotels close to every glacier and waterfall
q.why: 限制脆弱景點人數與設置步道，兼顧觀光與保護。

tz: 在冰島旅行，會不斷被提醒：我們腳下的大地是活的。這座島橫跨兩個構造板塊的交界，因此永遠在被撕開、又被重新建造——實際上，這是一個「施工中」的國家。
這賦予了地景奇特的壯麗：仍然漆黑光禿的熔岩原、把滾燙的水噴向天空的間歇泉、把整座山谷磨出形狀的冰川。它也讓冰島人和大地達成一項實際的交易：從底下的火山岩中汲取乾淨的熱能和電力。
與大自然的這份親密，塑造了這裡的文化。一個人口不到四十萬的國家，孕育出強大的文學傳統、對說故事的深深熱愛，還有——眾所周知的——對據說住在岩石裡的精靈，那份半認真的信仰。
如今對經濟至關重要的觀光業，也帶來它自己的緊張關係：脆弱的苔蘚和寧靜的地方，可能被太多的腳步踩壞；冰島人公開地辯論，該如何歡迎全世界，又不失去讓這座島與眾不同的東西。
儘管如此，很少有地方能如此清楚地讓旅人明白：地球不是一座固定的舞台，而是一個活著、移動著的東西——而我們所有人，都只是它暫時的客人。

ph.ex: The old map was torn apart.
ph.exzh: 那張舊地圖被撕破了。

ph.ex: In effect, the shop is closed on weekends.
ph.exzh: 實際上，這家店週末不營業。

ph.ex: Plants draw water from the soil.
ph.exzh: 植物從土壤中汲取水分。
ph.m: drawing clean heat and power from

ph.exzh: 台階被許多人的腳步磨平了。

ph.ex: Can we grow without losing our culture?
ph.exzh: 我們能成長而不失去自己的文化嗎？

ph.ex: The photo shows so plainly how happy they were.
ph.exzh: 這張照片如此清楚地顯示了他們有多快樂。

Too many tourists can damage fragile places. How should a country balance tourism and protection?
Would you rather travel for a place's nature or its cities? Why?

topic: A Rover Plans Its Own Path on Mars
zh: 火星車自己規劃路線：AI 開上火星

a.title: A Robot Driver on Mars
text: On Mars, a NASA robot car called Perseverance explores a dry, rocky world far from Earth.
Mars is about 140 million miles away. A message from Earth takes many minutes to arrive.
Because of this delay, drivers on Earth cannot steer the rover in real time.
In December 2025, something new happened. For the first time, artificial intelligence — AI — planned the rover's path by itself.
The AI looked at pictures of the ground taken from space. It found rocks, sand, and safe places to drive, then drew a route.
The rover followed the plan and drove hundreds of metres. NASA shared the exciting results in January 2026.

q.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: A rover on Mars drove a route planned by AI
Why messages take many minutes to reach Mars
How engineers draw rover routes by hand
How Perseverance takes pictures of rocks
q.why: 全文講 AI 規劃路線。

q.q: Why can't drivers on Earth steer the rover live?
opts: The rover has no radio to receive orders
Mars has no roads for the rover to follow
Messages take many minutes to reach Mars
The rover moves too fast for people to steer
q.why: 原文：“A message from Earth takes many minutes to arrive.”

q.q: What did the AI look at to plan the route?
opts: Maps drawn by hand by NASA engineers
Videos filmed by cameras on the wheels
Weather reports sent from Earth each day
Pictures of the ground taken from space
q.why: 原文：“The AI looked at pictures of the ground taken from space.”

q.q: In the text, “delay” means ___.
opts: a long, rocky road on Mars
a time when something is late
a broken part of a machine
a very fast radio message
q.why: delay = 延遲。

q.q: Why is this a big deal?
opts: For the first time, a rover drove on Mars
For the first time, AI planned the path itself
The rover drove faster than it ever had before
Humans no longer need to check any plans at all
q.why: 首次由 AI 自行規劃。

q.q: Which other situation could benefit MOST from the same kind of AI planning?
opts: A student doing maths homework at the kitchen table
A small shop counting its money at the end of the day
A teacher marking a pile of tests after school
A robot exploring the deep sea, far from its controllers
q.why: 遠離人類、通訊延遲的探索最需要自主規劃。

gt.en: On Mars, a NASA robot car called Perseverance explores a dry, rocky world far from Earth.
gt.zh: 在火星上，一輛叫做毅力號的 NASA 機器車在離地球很遠、乾燥多岩石的世界裡探險。

gt.en: Because of this delay, drivers on Earth cannot steer the rover in real time.
gt.zh: 因為這個延遲，地球上的駕駛員無法即時操控探測車。

gt.en: It found rocks, sand, and safe places to drive, then drew a route.
gt.zh: 它找出岩石、沙子和可以安全行駛的地方，然後畫出一條路線。

tz: 在火星上，一輛名叫「毅力號」的美國太空總署機器車，正在探索一個離地球很遠、乾燥又多岩石的世界。
火星距離地球大約一億四千萬英里。從地球傳過去的訊息，要好幾分鐘才會到達。
因為這段延遲，地球上的駕駛員沒辦法即時操控探測車。
2025 年 12 月，發生了一件新鮮事。人工智慧——AI——第一次自己規劃了探測車的路線。
AI 看了從太空拍攝的地面照片，找出岩石、沙地和可以安全行駛的地方，然後畫出一條路線。
探測車照著計畫行駛了好幾百公尺。美國太空總署在 2026 年 1 月公布了這個令人興奮的結果。

ph.ex: My school is far from my home.
ph.exzh: 我的學校離家很遠。

ph.ex: You can watch the game in real time online.
ph.exzh: 你可以在網路上即時看比賽。

ph.ex: The door closes by itself.
ph.exzh: 這扇門會自動關上。

ph.ex: Draw a route from your home to school.
ph.exzh: 畫出從你家到學校的路線。

b.title: AI Takes the Wheel on Mars
text: In December 2025, NASA's Perseverance rover did something no spacecraft had done before: it drove along a route planned entirely by artificial intelligence. NASA announced the results in January 2026.
Driving on Mars is tricky. The planet is about 225 million kilometres away, so radio signals take many minutes each way. Steering the rover live from Earth is impossible.
For 28 years, human engineers have carefully sketched each route by hand, marking points where the rover stops to receive new instructions.

This time, a kind of generative AI studied high-resolution photos taken from orbit, together with maps of the slopes. It recognised bedrock, boulders, and ripples of sand, then designed a smooth path.
Before sending the plan to Mars, engineers tested it on a 'digital twin' — a virtual copy of the rover — checking hundreds of thousands of details.
The rover then rolled safely across Jezero Crater. One day, AI could let explorers on other worlds make quick decisions on their own.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: For the first time, generative AI planned a route for Perseverance.
Engineers tested the AI's route on a digital twin of the rover.
Radio signals take many minutes to travel between Earth and Mars.
The AI recognised bedrock, boulders and ripples of sand in images.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: How did engineers check the plan before using it?
opts: They drove a second rover along it on Mars first
They asked astronauts on the Moon to check it
They did not check it before sending it to Mars
They tested it on a virtual copy of the rover
q.why: 原文：“Before sending the plan to Mars, engineers tested it on a 'digital twin' — a virtual copy of the rover — checking hundreds of thousands of details.”

q.q: What did the AI recognise in the images?
opts: Water, ice, and clouds above the crater
Other rovers and landers left on Mars
Bedrock, boulders, and ripples of sand
Small plants growing in the soil
q.why: 原文：“It recognised bedrock, boulders, and ripples of sand, then designed a smooth path.”

q.q: In paragraph 4, “recognised” means ___.
opts: drew a careful picture of
identified; knew what it was
drove slowly around it
moved away from it quickly
q.why: recognise = 辨認。

q.q: Why might AI driving matter for the future?
opts: Radio signals between planets will soon become faster
Robots on other worlds could make quick decisions alone
Engineers on Earth will no longer be needed at all
Mars will be easier to reach as it moves closer
q.why: 線索：“One day, AI could let explorers on other worlds make quick decisions on their own.”

q.q: Why was testing on a 'digital twin' a sensible step?
opts: It let engineers find mistakes before risking the rover
It made the real rover drive much faster on Mars
It removed the need for any other kind of testing
It let the AI drive the real rover without any human checks
q.why: 先在虛擬分身測試，避免真實探測車出事。

tr.en: In December 2025, NASA's Perseverance rover did something no spacecraft had done before: it drove along a route planned entirely by artificial intelligence.
tr.zh: 2025 年 12 月，NASA 的毅力號探測車做了一件從來沒有太空船做過的事：它沿著一條完全由人工智慧規劃的路線行駛。

tr.en: The planet is about 225 million kilometres away, so radio signals take many minutes each way.
tr.zh: 這顆行星大約在兩億兩千五百萬公里外，所以無線電訊號單程就要好幾分鐘。

tr.en: For 28 years, human engineers have carefully sketched each route by hand, marking points where the rover stops to receive new instructions.
tr.zh: 二十八年來，人類工程師都是用手仔細畫出每一條路線，標出探測車要停下來接收新指令的地點。

tz: 2025 年 12 月，美國太空總署的毅力號探測車做了一件從來沒有太空船做過的事：它沿著一條完全由人工智慧規劃的路線行駛。美國太空總署在 2026 年 1 月公布了結果。
在火星上開車很棘手。火星距離地球大約 2.25 億公里，所以無線電訊號單程就要好幾分鐘。從地球即時操控探測車是不可能的。
二十八年來，人類工程師都是用手仔細畫出每一條路線，標出探測車要停下來接收新指令的點。
這一次，一種生成式 AI 研究了從軌道上拍攝的高解析度照片，加上坡度地圖。它辨認出基岩、巨石和沙紋，然後設計出一條平順的路線。
在把計畫送到火星之前，工程師先在一個「數位分身」——探測車的虛擬複製品——上測試，檢查了數十萬個細節。
接著，探測車安全地駛過了耶澤羅隕石坑。將來有一天，AI 可能讓其他星球上的探險者自己快速做出決定。

ph.ex: The trip takes two hours each way.
ph.exzh: 這趟路單程要兩個小時。

ph.ex: These cards were made by hand.
ph.exzh: 這些卡片是手工做的。

ph.ex: The book comes together with a CD.
ph.exzh: 這本書附一張光碟。

ph.ex: Check your email before sending it.
ph.exzh: 寄出前先檢查你的電子郵件。

ph.ex: The children made dinner on their own.
ph.exzh: 孩子們自己做了晚餐。

c.title: When a Rover Plans Its Own Path
text: In January 2026, NASA revealed a quiet milestone in space exploration: the previous December, its Perseverance rover had completed the first drives on another world mapped out not by people, but by artificial intelligence.

The challenge is distance. With Mars roughly 225 million kilometres from Earth, radio commands arrive many minutes late, making real-time control impossible. For nearly three decades, engineers have plotted every route by hand, waypoint by waypoint.
The new approach used a form of generative AI known as vision-language models. The system examined sharp images from a Mars orbiter and detailed maps of the terrain's slopes.
From that data it identified bedrock, boulder fields, and ripples of sand, then stitched together a continuous, safe path — spacing its waypoints far more widely than human planners usually dare.
Nothing was sent blindly. The commands were first rehearsed on a 'digital twin', a virtual replica of the rover, where engineers checked over half a million measurements.
The drives, covering several hundred metres across Jezero Crater, hint at a future in which distant robots — and perhaps astronauts — navigate strange landscapes with far less help from home.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: How Perseverance drove an AI-planned route, and why that matters
How engineers have plotted rover routes by hand for decades
Why the great distance to Mars makes live driving impossible
How the AI drove the rover by itself with no human checking at all
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: For how long have engineers plotted rover routes by hand?
opts: For about ten years
For a whole century
For only the last five years
For nearly three decades
q.why: 文中：28 年。

q.q: How did the AI's waypoints differ from human ones?
opts: Placed exactly where human planners put them
Spaced far more widely than humans usually dare
Spaced much closer together than human ones
Chosen at random across the rocky ground
q.why: 原文：“From that data it identified bedrock, boulder fields, and ripples of sand, then stitched together a continuous, safe path — spacing its waypoints far more widely …”

q.q: In paragraph 5, “rehearsed” most nearly means ___.
opts: cancelled at the last minute
recorded on video
practised beforehand
repeated by accident
q.why: rehearse = 預演。

q.q: What does the drive 'hint at'?
opts: Astronauts soon driving rovers on Mars themselves
AI soon taking control of all of NASA
Distant explorers needing less help from Earth
Proof that Mars holds no real dangers
q.why: 線索：“The drives, covering several hundred metres across Jezero Crater, hint at a future in which distant robots — and perhaps astronauts — navigate strange landscapes …”

q.q: Some people worry about trusting AI with important decisions. Which detail from the text shows NASA handled this carefully?
opts: The AI spaced its waypoints far more widely than humans do
The plan was checked on a digital twin before the drive
The rover is many millions of kilometres from Earth
The AI planned the route using pictures from space
q.why: 先在虛擬分身驗證——審慎使用 AI 的證據。

tz: 2026 年 1 月，美國太空總署公布了太空探索中一個安靜的里程碑：前一年 12 月，它的毅力號探測車完成了在另一個星球上、第一批不是由人、而是由人工智慧規劃的行駛。
挑戰在於距離。火星距離地球大約 2.25 億公里，無線電指令要晚好幾分鐘才會到達，讓即時控制變得不可能。將近三十年來，工程師都是用手一個航點、一個航點地規劃每一條路線。
新的做法使用了一種叫做「視覺語言模型」的生成式 AI。這個系統檢視了火星軌道衛星拍攝的清晰影像，以及詳細的地形坡度圖。
它從這些資料中辨認出基岩、巨石區和沙紋，然後拼接出一條連續、安全的路線——航點之間的間隔，比人類規劃者通常敢設的要寬得多。
沒有任何東西是盲目送出的。這些指令先在一個「數位分身」——探測車的虛擬複製品——上預演，工程師在那裡檢查了超過五十萬個測量值。
這幾趟行駛橫越耶澤羅隕石坑好幾百公尺，預示了一個未來：遙遠的機器人——也許還有太空人——在陌生的地形中導航時，需要來自家鄉的幫助會少得多。

ph.ex: We mapped out our trip around Taiwan.
ph.exzh: 我們規劃了環島旅行的路線。

ph.ex: She stitched together clips from her trip.
ph.exzh: 她把旅行的影片片段拼接起來。

ph.ex: Few students dare to ask questions in class.
ph.exzh: 很少學生敢在課堂上提問。

ph.zh: 沒有任何東西是盲目送出的
ph.ex: Nothing was posted blindly — every photo was checked.
ph.exzh: 沒有任何東西是隨便發布的——每張照片都檢查過了。

ph.ex: Her smile hinted at good news.
ph.exzh: 她的微笑暗示有好消息。

ph.ex: We can live well with far less plastic.
ph.exzh: 我們少用很多塑膠也能過得很好。

discuss: Would you trust an AI to plan your path if no one could fix its mistakes for twenty minutes? Why or why not?
Humans planned Mars routes for 28 years. What is gained — and what might be lost — when AI takes over the job?
Where else could machines that 'plan for themselves' help people here on Earth?

topic: The Fall of the Berlin Wall
zh: 柏林圍牆倒塌
src: The New York Times · The Economist · BBC

a.title: The Night the Wall Came Down
text: For 28 years, a long concrete wall cut the city of Berlin in two. On one side was East Germany; on the other, West Germany.
The wall was built in 1961. Families and friends were suddenly split apart. Many could not visit each other for years.
The two sides lived very differently. The West was free and rich; the East was ruled by a strict government with much less freedom.
People in the East wanted change. In 1989, huge but peaceful crowds marched in the streets.
On November 9, 1989, the government finally opened the gates. Crowds climbed the wall, hugged, and cried with joy.
People broke the wall apart with hammers. That night changed Germany — and the world — forever.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: A wall that divided Berlin and the night it fell
Why the wall was built across Berlin in 1961
How life in East and West Germany was different
Why huge crowds marched in the streets in 1989
q.why: 全文講柏林圍牆與倒塌。

q.q: When was the Berlin Wall built?
q.why: 文中。1989 是倒塌。

q.q: What happened on November 9, 1989?
opts: Soldiers knocked the whole wall down at once
The wall was made taller and stronger
The gates opened and crowds climbed the wall
The two Germanys became one country that night
q.why: 原文：“On November 9, 1989, the government finally opened the gates.”

q.q: In the text, “split apart” means ___.
opts: joined closely together
separated from one another
built higher and higher
painted in bright colours
q.why: split apart = 分開。

q.q: Why did the crowds hug and cry with joy?
opts: They were finally free to reach loved ones
They had just won a long and terrible war
The wall was being rebuilt even stronger
They were afraid of the guards on the wall
q.why: 線索：“Many could not visit each other for years.”

q.q: Imagine your family lived on one side of the wall and your grandparents on the other. What would November 9, 1989 most likely mean to you?
opts: You would have to move away
Nothing would change
You would need a new passport to visit
You could finally visit them again
q.why: 圍牆開放讓分隔的家人重逢。

gt.en: For 28 years, a long concrete wall cut the city of Berlin in two.
gt.zh: 二十八年來，一道長長的水泥牆把柏林這座城市切成兩半。

gt.en: The wall was built in 1961.
gt.zh: 這道牆建於 1961 年。

gt.en: The West was free and rich; the East was ruled by a strict government with much less freedom.
gt.zh: 西邊自由又富裕；東邊則由嚴格的政府統治，自由少得多。

gt.en: In 1989, huge but peaceful crowds marched in the streets.
gt.zh: 1989 年，龐大但和平的群眾在街上遊行。

tz: 二十八年來，一道長長的水泥牆把柏林這座城市切成兩半。一邊是東德，另一邊是西德。
這道牆在 1961 年蓋起來。家人和朋友突然被拆散了，很多人好幾年都不能去探望彼此。
兩邊的生活非常不一樣。西邊自由又富有；東邊則由一個嚴格的政府統治，自由少得多。
東邊的人民想要改變。1989 年，大批群眾和平地走上街頭遊行。
1989 年 11 月 9 日，政府終於打開了大門。群眾爬上圍牆、互相擁抱，喜極而泣。
人們用鐵鎚把牆敲碎。那一晚永遠改變了德國——也改變了世界。

ph.ex: The river cuts the town in two.
ph.exzh: 這條河把小鎮切成兩半。
ph.m: cut the city of Berlin in two

ph.ex: The friends were split apart when one moved away.
ph.exzh: 其中一人搬走後，朋友們就被拆散了。

ph.ex: The kids broke the cookie apart to share it.
ph.exzh: 孩子們把餅乾掰開來分著吃。

ph.ex: That trip changed my life forever.
ph.exzh: 那趟旅行永遠改變了我的人生。

b.title: A Wall, and the People Who Ended It
text: For nearly three decades, the Berlin Wall was the world's most famous symbol of division. Built in 1961, it sealed off communist East Germany from the free, democratic West, cutting straight through the heart of Berlin.
The wall was more than concrete. Guards, fences, and watchtowers stopped East Germans from fleeing west, and some who tried were killed. Families were separated for a generation.
By 1989, pressure was building across Eastern Europe. Reforms in the Soviet Union and brave, peaceful protests in East German cities made the old rulers look weak.
Then, on the evening of November 9, 1989, a confused government announcement suggested the border was open. Thousands rushed to the crossings, and the overwhelmed guards simply raised the barriers.
What followed was pure celebration. Strangers embraced, people danced on top of the wall, and crowds began to chip it away with hammers and chisels.
Less than a year later, East and West Germany were reunited. The fall of the wall came to stand for the peaceful end of the Cold War in Europe.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The wall divided Germany for decades, and its peaceful fall ended an era.
The wall separated Berlin for decades, and its fall was carefully planned by leaders.
The wall separated communist East Germany from the democratic West.
Peaceful protests in East German cities steadily weakened the rulers.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: What did the wall separate?
opts: Germany from its neighbour France to the west
Northern Berlin from the southern half of the city
Communist East Germany from the democratic West
Two rival football clubs' areas of the city
q.why: 原文：“Built in 1961, it sealed off communist East Germany from the free, democratic West, cutting straight through the heart of Berlin.”

q.q: Why did the guards raise the barriers on November 9?
opts: The leaders had carefully planned to open it that night
The Soviet Union ordered them to open the border
The wall had been badly damaged by the protests
A confused announcement, and crowds overwhelmed them
q.why: 原文：“Then, on the evening of November 9, 1989, a confused government announcement suggested the border was open.”

q.q: In paragraph 2, “fleeing” means ___.
opts: visiting family members
running away or escaping
protesting in the streets
guarding the border wall
q.why: flee = 逃離。

q.q: What did the fall of the wall come to symbolize?
opts: The beginning of the Cold War in Europe
The peaceful end of the Cold War in Europe
A victory for the West in a world war
The plan to build a new and stronger wall
q.why: 線索：“The fall of the wall came to stand for the peaceful end of the Cold War in Europe.”

q.q: Which detail from the text best shows that the wall's fall was peaceful?
opts: The wall had stood for 28 years before it finally fell
Many people had tried to flee to the West over the years
The guards simply raised the barriers instead of shooting
The announcement that evening was confused and unclear
q.why: 守衛沒有開槍、只是升起柵欄。

tr.en: For nearly three decades, the Berlin Wall was the world's most famous symbol of division.
tr.zh: 將近三十年來，柏林圍牆是全世界最有名的分裂象徵。

tr.en: Reforms in the Soviet Union and brave, peaceful protests in East German cities made the old rulers look weak.
tr.zh: 蘇聯的改革，加上東德各城市勇敢而和平的抗議，讓舊的統治者顯得軟弱。

tr.en: Thousands rushed to the crossings, and the overwhelmed guards simply raised the barriers.
tr.zh: 成千上萬的人衝向檢查哨，不知所措的守衛乾脆把柵欄升了起來。

tz: 將近三十年來，柏林圍牆是世界上最有名的分裂象徵。它在 1961 年建成，把共產主義的東德和自由民主的西方隔開，直接從柏林的中心切過去。
這道牆不只是水泥。守衛、圍籬和瞭望塔阻止東德人逃往西方，有些試圖逃跑的人因此喪命。許多家庭被拆散了一整個世代。
到了 1989 年，整個東歐的壓力越來越大。蘇聯的改革，以及東德各城市勇敢而和平的抗議，讓舊的統治者顯得軟弱。
接著，在 1989 年 11 月 9 日晚上，一則混亂的政府宣布暗示邊界已經開放。數千人湧向檢查站，不知所措的守衛乾脆把柵欄升了起來。
接下來是一場純粹的慶祝。陌生人互相擁抱，人們在圍牆頂上跳舞，群眾開始用鐵鎚和鑿子把牆一塊塊敲下來。
不到一年後，東德和西德重新統一。柏林圍牆的倒塌，成了歐洲冷戰和平結束的象徵。

ph.ex: The new road cuts through the forest.
ph.exzh: 新路從森林中穿過。

ph.ex: A school is more than a building.
ph.exzh: 學校不只是一棟建築。

ph.ex: Pressure builds as the exam gets closer.
ph.exzh: 考試越來越近，壓力越來越大。

ph.ex: Fans rushed to the stage.
ph.exzh: 粉絲們衝向舞台。

ph.ex: They chipped away the old paint.
ph.exzh: 他們把舊油漆一點一點刮掉。

ph.ex: The bridge came to stand for the city.
ph.exzh: 這座橋後來成為這座城市的象徵。

c.title: The Night History Turned
text: Some walls are built to keep enemies out; the Berlin Wall was built to keep a population in. For twenty-eight years it stood as the Cold War made concrete — a 155-kilometre scar dividing not only a city but two visions of how human beings should live.

Its fall, on the night of 9 November 1989, was almost an accident. A muddled press conference, a misread note, a spokesman's uncertain words — and suddenly East Germans were walking, unhindered, toward checkpoints that had meant death to cross. The guards, awaiting orders that never came, stepped aside.

What makes the night remarkable is less the politics than the restraint. A heavily armed border, decades of resentment, vast crowds — and yet almost no violence. The revolution was carried out with hammers against stone, not against people.
The consequences were immense: Germany reunified within a year, the Soviet bloc dissolved, and the long standoff that had shadowed the twentieth century quietly ended.

Yet the wall also leaves a warning. It was raised in a single night and took a generation to fall — a reminder of how quickly freedom can be enclosed, and how much courage, and patience, it can take to open it again.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's central point?
opts: The wall fell because leaders carefully planned to open it.
The wall was, above all, a remarkable feat of engineering.
The fall ended an era — and warns how easily freedom is lost.
Little of real importance changed in Europe after 1989.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “restraint” refers to ___.
opts: a strong wall built along the border
holding back from violence despite anger
a political party that ruled the East
a type of weapon carried by the guards
q.why: restraint = 克制。

q.q: Why does the writer call the fall “almost an accident”?
opts: An earthquake that night damaged a long part of the wall
Soldiers attacked the wall by mistake during a protest
The leaders simply forgot to put guards on the border
Confusion and hesitant guards, not a decision, opened it
q.why: 文中。

q.q: What warning does the final paragraph give?
opts: Freedom is quickly enclosed but slowly restored
Walls like this one always fall by themselves
Public protests are usually far too dangerous
Freedom, once won, never needs protecting
q.why: 最後一段。

q.q: How does the essay move from beginning to end?
opts: Germany's war history → modern European politics
Purpose and fall → consequences → a wider lesson
A list of famous escape stories across the wall
The events told only from the West's point of view
q.why: 結構如選項。

q.q: According to the writer, which lesson from 1989 matters MOST for societies today?
opts: Walls are the best way for countries to keep peace
Accidents in history always lead to good results
Only governments, not people, can change history
Freedom can be lost quickly, so it must be guarded
q.why: 結尾：自由失去容易、恢復困難。

tz: 有些牆是為了把敵人擋在外面而建的；柏林圍牆卻是為了把人民關在裡面而建的。二十八年來，它就是被澆築成水泥的冷戰——一道 155 公里長的傷疤，分隔的不只是一座城市，還有兩種關於人應該如何生活的願景。
它在 1989 年 11 月 9 日晚上的倒塌，幾乎是一場意外。一場混亂的記者會、一張被讀錯的紙條、一位發言人含糊的話語——突然間，東德人毫無阻攔地走向那些曾經意味著「越過就會死」的檢查站。等著永遠不會來的命令的守衛們，退到了一旁。
那一晚之所以了不起，與其說是因為政治，不如說是因為克制。重兵把守的邊界、幾十年的怨恨、龐大的人群——卻幾乎沒有暴力。這場革命是用鐵鎚對著石頭進行的，而不是對著人。
後果是巨大的：德國在一年內統一，蘇聯集團瓦解，籠罩二十世紀的漫長對峙悄悄地結束了。
然而，這道牆也留下了一個警告。它在一夜之間築起，卻花了一個世代才倒下——提醒我們，自由可以多快被圍困，而要再次打開它，又需要多少勇氣和耐心。

ph.ex: A fence keeps the dogs out.
ph.exzh: 圍籬把狗擋在外面。

ph.ex: Close the door to keep the heat in.
ph.exzh: 把門關上，讓暖氣留在室內。

ph.ex: Her famous recipe was almost an accident.
ph.exzh: 她那道有名的料理幾乎是意外做出來的。

ph.ex: Please step aside and let the old man pass.
ph.exzh: 請讓開，讓老先生過去。

ph.ex: The game was less about skill than about luck.
ph.exzh: 這場比賽與其說是比技術，不如說是比運氣。
ph.m: less the politics than the restraint

ph.ex: Changing old habits can take a generation.
ph.exzh: 改變舊習慣可能要花一個世代的時間。

discuss: Why do you think the fall of the wall happened with so little violence?
Walls and borders still divide people today. When is a border fair, and when is it not?
The wall rose in a night but took years to fall. What does that tell us about freedom?

topic: Chang'e Flies to the Moon
zh: 嫦娥奔月
src: National Geographic · Taiwan News · The New York Times

a.title: Chang'e Flies to the Moon
text: Long ago in China, there were ten suns in the sky. They burned the land, and the people suffered.
A brave archer named Houyi shot down nine of the suns. He left just one, to give light and warmth.
As a reward, Houyi was given a special medicine. If one person drank it, they would live forever.
Houyi's wife was named Chang'e. One day, to keep the medicine safe from a thief, she drank it herself.
At once, Chang'e began to float. She rose up and up, all the way to the moon, where she still lives today.
Every Mid-Autumn Festival, people look at the full moon and remember beautiful, lonely Chang'e.

q.q: What is this story mainly about?
opts: How Houyi shot down nine suns
How Chang'e went to live on the moon
Why a thief wanted the medicine
Why the moon is round at the festival
q.why: 故事主線是嫦娥奔月。

q.q: What did the archer Houyi do?
opts: He shot down all ten of the suns
He built a small house on the moon
He stole the medicine from a god
He shot down nine of the ten suns
q.why: 原文：“A brave archer named Houyi shot down nine of the suns.”

q.q: Why did Chang'e drink the medicine?
opts: Because she wanted to live forever
Because Houyi asked her to
To keep it safe from a thief
Because she was sick
q.why: 原文：“One day, to keep the medicine safe from a thief, she drank it herself.”

q.q: In the story, an “archer” is a person who ___.
opts: shoots a bow and arrow
makes magic medicine
guards the moon at night
tells old stories to children
q.why: archer = 射手。

q.q: Why do people remember Chang'e at the Mid-Autumn Festival?
opts: They see the full moon, where she is said to live
She is said to have invented the first mooncakes
Houyi, her husband, was born on that same day
The extra suns disappeared from the sky that day
q.why: 線索：“Every Mid-Autumn Festival, people look at the full moon and remember beautiful, lonely Chang'e.”

q.q: Your younger cousin asks why people look at the moon at Mid-Autumn. Which answer uses the story best?
opts: “Because the moon comes closest to Earth on that one night.”
“Because long ago Houyi shot an arrow and hit the moon.”
“Chang'e lives on the moon, so we look up and think of family.”
“Because mooncakes are round, just like the full moon.”
q.why: 結合嫦娥住在月亮的傳說與思念之情。

gt.en: Long ago in China, there were ten suns in the sky.
gt.zh: 很久以前在中國，天上有十個太陽。

gt.en: A brave archer named Houyi shot down nine of the suns.
gt.zh: 一位名叫后羿的勇敢射手射下了其中九個太陽。

gt.en: As a reward, Houyi was given a special medicine.
gt.zh: 作為獎賞，后羿得到了一種特別的藥。

gt.en: One day, to keep the medicine safe from a thief, she drank it herself.
gt.zh: 有一天，為了不讓藥被小偷拿走，她自己把它喝了下去。

tz: 很久以前在中國，天上有十個太陽。它們把大地烤焦了，人們非常痛苦。
一位名叫后羿的勇敢射手射下了九個太陽，只留下一個，給大地光和溫暖。
作為獎賞，后羿得到了一種特別的藥。如果一個人喝下它，就能長生不老。
后羿的妻子名叫嫦娥。有一天，為了不讓小偷拿走這藥，她自己把它喝了下去。
嫦娥立刻開始飄起來。她越升越高，一直飄到月亮上，至今仍住在那裡。
每年中秋節，人們望著圓圓的月亮，想起美麗又孤單的嫦娥。

ph.ex: The hunter shot down a bird.
ph.exzh: 獵人射下了一隻鳥。

ph.ex: As a reward, we got an extra day off.
ph.exzh: 作為獎賞，我們多放了一天假。

ph.ex: The balloon went up and up.
ph.exzh: 氣球越飛越高。

ph.ex: We walked all the way to the beach.
ph.exzh: 我們一路走到海邊。

b.title: The Lady in the Moon
text: One of China's best-loved myths explains the shape many people see in the full moon. It begins with a sky scorched by ten suns.
A heroic archer, Houyi, saved the world by shooting down nine of them. For this, the gods rewarded him with an elixir of immortality — enough for one person to live forever.
Houyi loved his wife, Chang'e, and did not want to leave her behind, so he hid the elixir at home. But one day, while he was away, a greedy student tried to steal it.
To stop the thief, Chang'e swallowed the elixir herself. She became weightless and drifted up into the sky, finally coming to rest on the cold, silver moon.
There she has lived ever since, the stories say, with only a jade rabbit for company — forever near the world she loved, yet unable to return to it.
Each Mid-Autumn Festival, families gaze at the round moon and think of Chang'e: a tale of love, sacrifice, and the ache of separation.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Houyi was rewarded with an elixir of immortality for shooting down the suns.
Houyi hid the elixir at home because he did not want to leave his wife.
Long ago, the earth was scorched by ten suns burning in the sky at once.
A myth of love and sacrifice explains how Chang'e came to live on the moon.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: What reward did Houyi receive?
opts: An elixir of immortality
A palace on the moon
A magic bow and arrows
A white jade rabbit
q.why: 原文：“For this, the gods rewarded him with an elixir of immortality — enough for one person to live forever.”

q.q: What happened after Chang'e swallowed the elixir?
opts: She became the queen of the remaining sun
She fell into a long and very deep sleep
She became weightless and drifted to the moon
She became a goddess who ruled over the ten suns
q.why: 原文：“She became weightless and drifted up into the sky, finally coming to rest on the cold, silver moon.”

q.q: In paragraph 2, “immortality” means ___.
opts: having great strength
living forever, never dying
being able to fly
becoming a god of the sky
q.why: immortality = 長生不死。

q.q: What is the main feeling at the heart of the story?
opts: Anger at the ten suns that burned the earth
Love, sacrifice, and the sadness of separation
Joy at the chance to live forever on the moon
Fear of the thief who wanted the elixir
q.why: 線索：“Each Mid-Autumn Festival, families gaze at the round moon and think of Chang'e: a tale of love, sacrifice, and the ache of separation.”

q.q: Why did Houyi hide the elixir instead of drinking it?
opts: He was afraid that living forever would make him lonely in Heaven
He wanted to drink it later with the gods in Heaven
He did not believe the elixir would really work
There was only enough for one, and he would not leave her
q.why: 仙藥只夠一人，他不願拋下妻子。

tr.en: It begins with a sky scorched by ten suns.
tr.zh: 故事從一片被十個太陽烤焦的天空開始。

tr.en: For this, the gods rewarded him with an elixir of immortality — enough for one person to live forever.
tr.zh: 為此，眾神賞給他一瓶長生不老藥——剛好夠一個人永遠活下去。

tr.en: Houyi loved his wife, Chang'e, and did not want to leave her behind, so he hid the elixir at home.
tr.zh: 后羿深愛他的妻子嫦娥，不想丟下她，所以他把仙藥藏在家裡。

tz: 中國最受喜愛的神話之一，解釋了許多人在滿月中看到的形狀。故事從一片被十個太陽烤焦的天空開始。
英勇的射手后羿射下了其中九個太陽，拯救了世界。為此，眾神獎賞他一瓶長生不老藥——足夠讓一個人永遠活下去。
后羿愛他的妻子嫦娥，不想丟下她，所以把仙藥藏在家裡。但有一天，趁他不在時，一個貪心的徒弟想把它偷走。
為了阻止小偷，嫦娥自己吞下了仙藥。她變得輕飄飄的，飄上天空，最後停在寒冷的銀色月亮上。
故事說，從那以後她就一直住在那裡，只有一隻玉兔作伴——永遠靠近她所愛的世界，卻再也回不去。
每年中秋節，家人們凝望著圓圓的月亮，想起嫦娥：一個關於愛、犧牲和分離之痛的故事。

ph.ex: Don't leave your little brother behind.
ph.exzh: 別把弟弟丟下。

ph.ex: While I was away, my cat stayed with a friend.
ph.exzh: 我不在的時候，我的貓待在朋友家。

ph.ex: The smoke drifted up into the sky.
ph.exzh: 煙飄上了天空。

ph.ex: The ball came to rest under a tree.
ph.exzh: 球停在一棵樹下。

ph.ex: We have been friends ever since.
ph.exzh: 從那以後我們一直是朋友。

c.title: What We See in the Moon
text: Every culture that has gazed at the moon has told stories to explain its marks. In China, those marks are Chang'e — a goddess whose legend turns a bright object in the sky into an image of longing.

The tale is deceptively simple. Her husband, the archer Houyi, wins an elixir of immortality; to keep it from a thief, Chang'e drinks it herself and floats, irreversibly, to the moon. What begins as a rescue ends as an exile.

The myth's power lies in its ambivalence. Chang'e gains eternal life but loses everything that made life worth living — her home, her husband, the warm and ordinary world below. Immortality, the story quietly suggests, can be its own kind of prison.

That is perhaps why the legend binds itself so naturally to the Mid-Autumn Festival, a celebration of reunion. Families gathered beneath the full moon are reminded, by the lonely figure within it, of exactly what they have — and how precious togetherness is.
A myth, in the end, is a mirror held up to a people's values. In Chang'e, China sees not only a goddess, but a meditation on sacrifice, distance, and the bittersweet cost of living forever.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: The myth shows that living forever is the greatest reward of all.
The myth is mainly a celebration of Houyi's bravery as an archer.
The myth makes the moon an image of longing and the cost of immortality.
The myth teaches that immortality is a gift worth any sacrifice at all.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In paragraph 2, the writer says the story “ends as an exile,” meaning Chang'e is ___.
opts: rewarded with a palace for her courage
forced to live far away, unable to return
punished by the gods for stealing
happy to live alone, away from people
q.why: exile = 流放。

q.q: What does “immortality…can be its own kind of prison” suggest?
opts: Living forever may cost what made life meaningful
There is a real prison built on the moon's surface
The elixir did not really work as Houyi expected
Houyi was later put in prison for losing the elixir
q.why: 線索：“Chang'e gains eternal life but loses everything that made life worth living — her home, her husband, the warm and ordinary world below.”

q.q: Why does the legend pair so naturally with a festival of reunion?
opts: She is said to return to Earth for one night every year
She returns to her husband on the night of the full moon each year
The festival is mainly a celebration of living forever
Her loneliness reminds families how precious togetherness is
q.why: 文中。

q.q: The final paragraph frames a myth as ___.
opts: a true historical record
a mirror of a people's values
a warning against archery
a guide to the festival's food
q.why: 結尾。

q.q: Which modern situation best reflects the myth's idea that gaining something can mean losing what matters?
opts: Winning a free ticket to see your favourite band play
Saving up your pocket money to buy a new bicycle
Moving with your family to a bigger house nearby
Taking a top job abroad but no longer seeing your family
q.why: 得到某樣東西卻失去最珍貴的（家人）——與嫦娥的故事相同。

tz: 每一個曾經凝望月亮的文化，都說過故事來解釋月亮上的痕跡。在中國，那些痕跡就是嫦娥——一位女神，她的傳說把天空中一個明亮的物體，變成了思念的形象。
這個故事看似簡單。她的丈夫、射手后羿得到了一瓶長生不老藥；為了不讓小偷得手，嫦娥自己喝下了它，然後無法回頭地飄向月亮。一開始是一場救援，最後卻變成了一場放逐。
這則神話的力量在於它的矛盾。嫦娥得到了永恆的生命，卻失去了讓生命值得活下去的一切——她的家、她的丈夫、下方那個溫暖而平凡的世界。故事悄悄地暗示：長生不老本身，也可能是一種監牢。
這或許就是為什麼這個傳說會那麼自然地和中秋節——一個慶祝團圓的節日——連在一起。聚在滿月下的家人們，被月亮裡那個孤單的身影提醒著，自己擁有的究竟是什麼——以及團聚有多麼珍貴。
說到底，神話是一面映照出一個民族價值觀的鏡子。在嫦娥身上，中國人看到的不只是一位女神，更是一段關於犧牲、距離，以及長生不老那份苦樂參半代價的沉思。

ph.ex: The game is deceptively simple.
ph.exzh: 這個遊戲看似簡單，其實不然。

ph.ex: Keep the medicine from small children.
ph.exzh: 把藥放在小孩拿不到的地方。

ph.ex: Friends make life worth living.
ph.exzh: 朋友讓人生值得一過。

ph.ex: Being alone can be its own kind of freedom.
ph.exzh: 獨處也可以是一種自由。

ph.ex: The song binds me to my childhood.
ph.exzh: 這首歌把我和我的童年連在一起。

ph.ex: Hold the photo up to the light.
ph.exzh: 把照片對著光看。

discuss: Would you want to live forever if it meant leaving everyone you love? Why or why not?
Many cultures see shapes or stories in the moon. Why do you think humans do this?
Chang'e's story is tied to a festival about reunion. What makes being together precious to you?

topic: World Food Day
zh: 世界糧食日

a.title: Food for Everyone
text: October 16 is World Food Day. It is a day to think about food and the people who do not have enough of it.
Food gives us energy to live, learn, and play. But not everyone has enough to eat.
Around the world, hundreds of millions of people go to bed hungry. Many of them are children.
