At the same time, a lot of food is wasted. People and shops throw away food that is still good to eat.
We can all help. Take only what you will eat. Save your leftovers. Share food with people in need.
When we grow, share, and respect food, we can build a world where no one is hungry.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How to cook a good meal at home
Why food gives our bodies energy
Food, hunger, and not wasting food
Why World Food Day is held in October
q.why: 全文講食物、飢餓與浪費。

q.q: When is World Food Day?
opts: October 4
October 24
November 16
October 16
q.why: 原文：“October 16 is World Food Day.”

q.q: What does the text say happens to a lot of food?
opts: It is given to hungry people
It is wasted or thrown away
It is sold to other countries
It is kept for next year
q.why: 原文：“People and shops throw away food that is still good to eat.”

q.q: In the text, “leftovers” are ___.
opts: food not eaten that you keep for later
food that is thrown away before it is eaten
food that is grown on local farms
food that is sold cheaply in shops
q.why: leftovers = 剩菜。

q.q: How can YOU help, according to the text?
opts: Eat as much as you can at every meal
Buy more food than you need, just in case
Take only what you will eat, and share
Never eat out at restaurants with friends
q.why: 線索：“Take only what you will eat.”

q.q: At a school buffet, which choice best follows the text's advice?
opts: Fill your plate as high as you possibly can
Take some of everything and leave what you dislike
Skip lunch completely so nothing is wasted
Take a little first, then go back if still hungry
q.why: 只拿吃得完的份量，避免浪費。

gt.en: It is a day to think about food and the people who do not have enough of it.
gt.zh: 這是一個思考食物、以及那些吃不飽的人的日子。

gt.en: Food gives us energy to live, learn, and play.
gt.zh: 食物給我們生活、學習和玩耍的能量。

gt.en: Around the world, hundreds of millions of people go to bed hungry.
gt.zh: 全世界有好幾億人餓著肚子上床睡覺。

gt.en: At the same time, a lot of food is wasted.
gt.zh: 同時，卻有很多食物被浪費掉。

tz: 10 月 16 日是世界糧食日。這是一個想一想食物、以及那些沒有足夠食物的人的日子。
食物給我們生活、學習和玩耍的能量。但不是每個人都有足夠的東西吃。
在全世界，有好幾億人餓著肚子上床睡覺，其中很多是孩子。
同時，有很多食物被浪費了。人們和商店把還可以吃的食物丟掉。
我們每個人都可以幫忙。只拿自己吃得完的份量，把剩菜留起來，和需要的人分享食物。
當我們種植、分享並珍惜食物，就能建立一個沒有人挨餓的世界。

ph.ex: No child should go to bed hungry.
ph.exzh: 沒有孩子應該餓著肚子上床睡覺。

ph.ex: Don't throw away food that is still good.
ph.exzh: 還能吃的食物不要丟掉。

ph.ex: Share your snack with a friend.
ph.exzh: 和朋友分享你的點心。

ph.ex: No one was late today.
ph.exzh: 今天沒有人遲到。

b.title: Enough for All?
text: Every year on 16 October, the United Nations marks World Food Day, led by its Food and Agriculture Organization, or FAO. The date asks an uncomfortable question: why, on a planet that grows plenty, do so many still go hungry?
The numbers are stark. Hundreds of millions of people do not get enough to eat, and hunger has risen in recent years because of conflict, drought, and high prices.
Waste makes the problem worse. Studies suggest that roughly a third of all food produced is lost or thrown away — spoiled on farms, damaged in transport, or scraped off plates in wealthy homes.

The causes are tangled, but solutions exist. Farmers can grow crops that survive a changing climate, shops and families can waste less, and fairer systems can help food reach the people who need it most.
Food is also about health and culture. A good meal is not only fuel; it brings families together and carries the taste of home.
The message of World Food Day is both practical and hopeful: there is enough for everyone, if only we grow, share, and value it wisely.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The world does not grow enough food, so millions of people go hungry.
The FAO, part of the United Nations, leads World Food Day each October.
The world grows plenty, yet many go hungry through waste and unfair access.
The world grows plenty, so hunger has now almost disappeared from most countries.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；第二項與文意相反。

q.q: Which organization leads World Food Day?
opts: The World Health Organization
The FAO, part of the United Nations
UNICEF, which helps the world's children
A large group of farmers from many countries
q.why: 原文：“Every year on 16 October, the United Nations marks World Food Day, led by its Food and Agriculture Organization, or FAO.”

q.q: About how much food is lost or wasted?
opts: Roughly a third
Roughly a tenth
Roughly half
Almost all of it
q.why: 原文：“Studies suggest that roughly a third of all food produced is lost or thrown away — spoiled on farms, damaged in transport, or scraped off plates in wealthy homes.”

q.q: In paragraph 3, “spoiled” means the food ___.
opts: was cooked for far too long
was sold at too low a price
was kept cold so that it stayed fresh
went bad and became unsafe to eat
q.why: spoil = 腐壞。

q.q: What is the main paradox the text points to?
opts: Farmers around the world grow too little food
People today eat their meals far too slowly
There is enough food, yet many are hungry
Food tastes worse now than it used to
q.why: 線索：“The date asks an uncomfortable question: why, on a planet that grows plenty, do so many still go hungry?”

q.q: A supermarket throws away food that is still safe but close to its date. Which action best addresses the problem described in the text?
opts: Throw the food away sooner, before its date arrives
Raise the price so that fewer people waste it
Grow more food on farms to replace what is lost
Give the safe food to food banks before it spoils
q.why: 把安全的食物送到需要的人手上，解決浪費與取得不均。

tr.en: A good meal is not only fuel; it brings families together and carries the taste of home.
tr.zh: 一頓好飯不只是燃料；它讓家人團聚，也承載著家的味道。

tz: 每年 10 月 16 日，聯合國都會舉行世界糧食日，由它的糧食及農業組織（FAO）主導。這個日子提出一個令人不安的問題：在一個能種出充足糧食的星球上，為什麼還有這麼多人挨餓？
數字很嚴峻。好幾億人吃不飽，而且由於戰爭、乾旱和高物價，飢餓問題近年來還在增加。
浪費讓問題更加嚴重。研究顯示，所有生產出來的食物中，大約有三分之一流失或被丟掉——在農場裡腐壞、在運送中損壞，或在富裕的家庭裡從盤子上被刮掉。
原因錯綜複雜，但解決方法是存在的。農民可以種植能適應氣候變遷的作物，商店和家庭可以少浪費一些，而更公平的制度可以幫助食物送到最需要的人手上。
食物也關乎健康和文化。一頓好飯不只是燃料；它讓家人聚在一起，也帶著家的味道。
世界糧食日的訊息既實際又充滿希望：只要我們明智地種植、分享和珍惜，食物足夠讓每個人都吃飽。

ph.ex: The game was cancelled because of the storm.
ph.exzh: 比賽因為暴風雨而取消。

ph.ex: Too much food is thrown away every day.
ph.exzh: 每天都有太多食物被丟掉。

ph.ex: Scrape off the old paint first.
ph.exzh: 先把舊油漆刮掉。

ph.ex: Reading is not only fun; it also helps you think.
ph.exzh: 閱讀不只有趣，也能幫助你思考。

ph.ex: Sports bring people together.
ph.exzh: 運動讓人們聚在一起。

c.title: The Paradox of the Full Plate
text: Each 16 October the United Nations observes World Food Day, an occasion built around a paradox: humanity grows more than enough food to feed itself, and yet hundreds of millions remain hungry.

The contradiction deepens on closer look. Even as some go without, roughly a third of all food produced is never eaten — lost to poor storage in poorer countries, and to sheer waste in richer ones. The world, in effect, starves and squanders at the same time.

Hunger is rarely a simple shortage of food; more often it is a failure of access. War drives families from their fields, drought ruins harvests, and inflation puts the market stall beyond reach. Where food is treated purely as a commodity, those with the least money eat last.

None of this is beyond human repair. Hardier crops, better storage, shorter supply chains, and policies that treat food as a right rather than a privilege could, together, narrow the gap. So could a cultural shift away from waste in kitchens and supermarkets alike.
World Food Day, at its best, refuses an easy despair. It insists that hunger in an age of plenty is not a natural disaster but a human choice — and therefore one that humans can unmake.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Hunger amid plenty is a human choice — and so it can be changed.
Hunger exists mainly because the world cannot grow enough food.
Hunger is a natural disaster that no government is able to stop.
Only farmers, by growing more, can truly solve the problem of hunger.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “squander” means to ___.
opts: grow carefully
sell cheaply
share fairly
waste carelessly
q.why: squander = 浪費。

q.q: “Hunger…is a failure of access” suggests that the main problem is ___.
opts: there is simply not enough food in the world for all
people cannot reach or afford the food that exists
farmers urgently need to grow much more food
many people simply do not like healthy food
q.why: 取得不到，而非不夠。

q.q: The phrase “refuses an easy despair” shows the writer is ___.
opts: completely without hope that hunger can end
unconcerned about how many people go hungry
concerned but hopeful that change is possible
angry at farmers for wasting so much food
q.why: 擔憂但抱持希望。

q.q: What does paragraph 2 (“The contradiction deepens”) mainly do?
opts: Offer a final solution that would end hunger
Show that hunger is caused mainly by bad weather and war
Develop the paradox by setting waste beside hunger
Change the topic from hunger to modern farming
q.why: 第二段。

q.q: A politician says: “We just need to grow more food to end hunger.” How would the writer most likely respond?
opts: Agree completely — more food is the only real answer
Say that hunger can never be ended, however hard we try
Say that only the hunger in rich countries really matters
We already grow enough; cut waste and improve access
q.why: 作者認為飢餓是取得與浪費問題，不是產量問題。

tz: 每年 10 月 16 日，聯合國都會舉行世界糧食日；這個日子圍繞著一個矛盾：人類種出的糧食綽綽有餘，足以養活自己，卻仍有好幾億人在挨餓。
仔細看，這個矛盾更加深刻。就在有些人吃不到東西的同時，所有生產出來的食物大約有三分之一從來沒有被吃掉——在比較貧窮的國家是因為儲存條件差而流失，在比較富裕的國家則純粹是被浪費掉。實際上，這個世界同時在挨餓，也在揮霍。
飢餓很少只是單純的糧食短缺；更常見的是「取得管道」的失敗。戰爭把家庭趕離他們的田地，乾旱毀了收成，通貨膨脹讓市場攤位變得遙不可及。在食物被純粹當成商品的地方，錢最少的人最後才能吃到東西。
這一切都不是人類無法修補的。更耐旱的作物、更好的儲存、更短的供應鏈，以及把食物當作權利而不是特權的政策，合在一起就能縮小這個差距。廚房和超市裡遠離浪費的文化轉變，也能做到。
世界糧食日最好的一面，是它拒絕輕易地陷入絕望。它堅持：在一個富足的時代裡，飢餓不是一場天災，而是人為的選擇——因此，也是人類能夠扭轉的選擇。

ph.ex: The lesson is built around a short story.
ph.exzh: 這堂課以一個短篇故事為中心。

ph.ex: On closer look, the old coin was fake.
ph.exzh: 仔細一看，那枚古幣是假的。

ph.ex: During the storm, we went without power for a day.
ph.exzh: 暴風雨期間，我們停電了一整天。

ph.ex: High prices put new phones beyond reach for many students.
ph.exzh: 高價讓新手機對許多學生來說遙不可及。
ph.m: puts the market stall beyond reach

ph.ex: At its best, social media connects people.
ph.exzh: 在最好的情況下，社群媒體能連結人們。

ph.ex: Hunger is not a natural disaster but a human choice.
ph.exzh: 飢餓不是天災，而是人為的選擇。

discuss: How much food does your family throw away? How could you waste less?
Is having enough food a basic right? Whose job is it to make sure everyone can eat?
Food brings people together. What dish means “home” to you, and why?

topic: Rome: The Eternal City
zh: 羅馬：永恆之城
src: The New York Times · National Geographic · BBC

a.title: Welcome to Rome
text: Rome is the capital city of Italy. People call it the 'Eternal City' because it is so very old.
Almost two thousand years ago, Rome ruled a huge empire. You can still see many things the Romans built.
The Colosseum is a giant stone stadium. Long ago, thousands of people watched games and shows there.
At the Trevi Fountain, visitors throw a coin over their shoulder and make a wish to return one day.
Rome is also famous for its food — pizza, pasta, and creamy gelato ice cream.
Old and new live side by side. You might drink coffee next to a building that is two thousand years old.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: The Colosseum, a giant stone stadium in Rome
Why people throw coins into the Trevi Fountain
Rome, a very old city, and what to see there
How Rome once ruled a huge empire long ago
q.why: 全文介紹羅馬。

q.q: Why is Rome called the 'Eternal City'?
opts: Because it never sleeps
Because it is so very old
Because it was built by gods
Because it is the capital of Italy
q.why: 原文：“People call it the 'Eternal City' because it is so very old.”

q.q: What do visitors do at the Trevi Fountain?
opts: Swim in the cool water on hot days
Drink the water from it for good luck
Take a short boat ride across the pool
Throw a coin and make a wish to return
q.why: 原文：“At the Trevi Fountain, visitors throw a coin over their shoulder and make a wish to return one day.”

q.q: In the text, an “empire” is ___.
opts: many lands ruled by one power
a very old city with many ruins
a huge stone stadium for games
a famous fountain in the city
q.why: empire = 帝國。

q.q: What does “old and new live side by side” mean?
opts: Old people and young people live together
Ancient and modern things exist together
Rome has almost only new buildings now
Old buildings are slowly being replaced
q.why: 文中。

q.q: Which Taiwanese place is MOST like Rome, where old and new live side by side?
opts: A brand-new shopping mall in the middle of a city
A national park with mountains and no buildings
A street where an old temple stands by modern shops
A new science park full of glass office towers
q.why: 古老廟宇與現代商店並存，最像羅馬。

gt.en: Rome is the capital city of Italy.
gt.zh: 羅馬是義大利的首都。

gt.en: Almost two thousand years ago, Rome ruled a huge empire.
gt.zh: 將近兩千年前，羅馬統治著一個龐大的帝國。

gt.en: The Colosseum is a giant stone stadium.
gt.zh: 羅馬競技場是一座巨大的石造競技場。

tz: 羅馬是義大利的首都。人們叫它「永恆之城」，因為它非常非常古老。
將近兩千年前，羅馬統治著一個龐大的帝國。你現在仍然可以看到羅馬人建造的許多東西。
羅馬競技場是一座巨大的石造體育場。很久以前，成千上萬的人在那裡觀看比賽和表演。
在特雷維噴泉，遊客會越過肩膀丟一枚硬幣，許願有一天能再回來。
羅馬也以美食聞名——披薩、義大利麵，還有綿密的義式冰淇淋。
古老和現代在這裡並肩共存。你可能就在一棟兩千年歷史的建築旁邊喝咖啡。

ph.ex: People call it the City of Love.
ph.exzh: 人們把它叫做愛之城。

ph.ex: She threw the coin over her shoulder.
ph.exzh: 她越過肩膀把硬幣丟出去。
ph.m: throw a coin over their shoulder

ph.ex: This town is famous for its pineapple cakes.
ph.exzh: 這個小鎮以鳳梨酥聞名。

ph.ex: The old and new houses stand side by side.
ph.exzh: 新舊房子並排而立。

b.title: The Eternal City
text: Rome, the capital of Italy, has been called the 'Eternal City' for two thousand years — and it wears its age proudly.
At its height, ancient Rome ruled much of Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. The remains of that empire still fill the modern streets.
The Colosseum, a vast arena that once held fifty thousand spectators, remains the city's most famous monument. Nearby lie the ruins of the Forum, the beating heart of the ancient city.
Rome is also layered with art and faith. Within it sits the Vatican, home of the Pope, where visitors line up to see Michelangelo's painted ceiling in the Sistine Chapel.
Yet Rome is no museum. Scooters weave through narrow lanes, markets spill across old squares, and families argue happily over plates of pasta.
To walk through Rome is to walk through time itself — from a Roman temple, to a Renaissance church, to a modern café, often within a single street.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The Colosseum, a giant stadium, once held fifty thousand spectators.
Rome's ancient ruins have been carefully removed so the modern city can grow.
The remains of the Roman Empire still fill many of Rome's streets.
Rome blends an ancient empire with modern life, like walking through time.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: How many spectators could the Colosseum hold?
opts: About five thousand
About fifty thousand
About fifteen thousand
About half a million
q.why: 原文：“The Colosseum, a vast arena that once held fifty thousand spectators, remains the city's most famous monument.”

q.q: What can visitors see at the Vatican?
opts: The Colosseum and its underground tunnels
The Trevi Fountain and its famous coins
Michelangelo's ceiling in the Sistine Chapel
The ruins of the old Roman Forum
q.why: 原文：“Within it sits the Vatican, home of the Pope, where visitors line up to see Michelangelo's painted ceiling in the Sistine Chapel.”

q.q: In paragraph 3, “spectators” are ___.
opts: people who watch an event
people who fight in an event
people who build stadiums
people who sell tickets
q.why: spectators = 觀眾。

q.q: What does “Rome is no museum” suggest?
opts: Rome actually has no museums for visitors to see
Rome keeps its old city closed to protect it from tourists
Most of the museums in Rome are closed to tourists
Rome is full of busy, everyday life, not just the past
q.why: 線索：“Yet Rome is no museum.”

q.q: A travel blogger writes: “Rome is just a city of old ruins.” Which detail from the text best challenges this?
opts: The Colosseum once held fifty thousand people
Busy modern life goes on among the ancient ruins
Rome once ruled over a huge and powerful empire
Visitors throw coins into its famous fountains
q.why: 羅馬不只是古蹟，而是充滿日常生活的城市。

tr.en: Rome, the capital of Italy, has been called the 'Eternal City' for two thousand years — and it wears its age proudly.
tr.zh: 義大利的首都羅馬被稱為「永恆之城」已經兩千年了——而它也驕傲地展現自己的年紀。

tr.en: The remains of that empire still fill the modern streets.
tr.zh: 那個帝國的遺跡至今仍遍布現代的街道。

tr.en: The Colosseum, a vast arena that once held fifty thousand spectators, remains the city's most famous monument.
tr.zh: 曾經能容納五萬名觀眾的巨大競技場——羅馬競技場，至今仍是這座城市最有名的古蹟。

tz: 義大利首都羅馬被稱為「永恆之城」已經兩千年了——而它也以自己的悠久歷史為傲。
在全盛時期，古羅馬統治了歐洲、北非和中東的大部分地區。那個帝國的遺跡，至今仍遍布現代的街道。
羅馬競技場是一座曾經能容納五萬名觀眾的巨大競技場，至今仍是這座城市最有名的古蹟。附近就是古羅馬廣場的遺跡，那是古代城市跳動的心臟。
羅馬也層層疊疊地堆積著藝術和信仰。城裡有梵蒂岡——教宗的所在地，遊客在那裡排隊觀賞米開朗基羅在西斯汀禮拜堂繪製的天花板。
然而，羅馬並不是一座博物館。機車在狹窄的巷弄裡穿梭，市集擠滿了古老的廣場，一家人開心地圍著一盤盤義大利麵爭論。
走過羅馬，就像走過時間本身——從一座羅馬神殿，到一座文藝復興時期的教堂，再到一家現代咖啡館，常常就在同一條街上。

ph.ex: At its height, the empire ruled half the world.
ph.exzh: 在全盛時期，這個帝國統治了半個世界。

ph.ex: We lined up for the new ride.
ph.exzh: 我們排隊玩新的遊樂設施。

ph.zh: 不是一座博物館（不死板）
ph.ex: Our classroom is no museum — please touch and try!
ph.exzh: 我們的教室不是博物館——請動手試試看！

ph.ex: The crowd spilled across the street.
ph.exzh: 人潮擠滿了整條街。

ph.ex: You can find five cafés within a single street.
ph.exzh: 在同一條街上就能找到五家咖啡館。

c.title: A City Built on Itself
text: No city carries its past quite like Rome. Three thousand years of history are not neatly preserved here but piled up, layer upon layer, so that an ancient temple may support a medieval church that now shades a modern bus stop.

The scale of the old city still astonishes. The Colosseum, where crowds once roared at gladiators, and the Pantheon, whose vast dome has stood unbroken for nearly nineteen centuries, remind visitors that the Romans built not merely for their own age but, it seems, for all of them.
Layered atop the empire is another Rome — the spiritual capital of the Catholic world, its skyline crowned by the dome of St Peter's, its galleries holding some of the greatest art ever made.
To live among such grandeur is a daily negotiation. Romans complain, fairly, of crowds, traffic, and the burden of maintaining a city that belongs, in a sense, to the whole world.
And yet the city endures, as it always has — not by freezing its past, but by living inside it, turning ruins into backdrops and history into the ordinary scenery of everyday life.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's central idea?
opts: Rome's ancient buildings matter more than its modern life.
Rome survives by living inside its layered past.
Rome should be turned into a carefully protected open-air museum.
Rome has lost most of its history under modern development.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “astonishes” means ___.
opts: slightly worries or upsets
quickly bores or tires
greatly surprises or amazes
deeply angers or annoys
q.why: astonish = 使驚嘆。

q.q: What does the writer suggest by saying the Romans built “not merely for their own age but, it seems, for all of them”?
opts: They built only to please the emperors of their time
They built quickly and cheaply, so little has survived
They planned the layout of every modern Roman street
Their works were so lasting they still serve today
q.why: 線索：“The scale of the old city still astonishes.”

q.q: What does paragraph 4 add to the picture?
opts: Living among heritage is also a daily burden
Romans generally dislike the tourists who visit
Rome has no real problems with its old buildings
The city's history should simply be forgotten
q.why: 第四段。

q.q: The essay is mainly built around the image of ___.
opts: a ladder climbing up toward the sky
a river flowing through the old city
a locked museum that few can enter
layers — history piled up and lived in
q.why: layers 意象。

q.q: Rome must decide whether to allow a new metro line under ancient ruins. Which consideration reflects the writer's view best?
opts: Stop all new building in Rome to protect its history
Balance modern needs with protecting the past people live in
Ignore the ruins, because modern transport must come first
Move the ruins to a museum so the metro can be built
q.why: 作者認為歷史與日常生活共存，需兼顧。

tz: 沒有一座城市像羅馬這樣承載著它的過去。三千年的歷史在這裡不是被整整齊齊地保存起來，而是一層又一層地堆疊著，所以一座古代神殿可能撐著一座中世紀教堂，而那座教堂如今又為一個現代公車站遮蔭。
古城的規模至今仍令人驚嘆。曾經有群眾對著角鬥士吶喊的羅馬競技場，以及巨大圓頂將近十九個世紀都未曾破損的萬神殿，提醒著遊客：羅馬人建造的東西，似乎不只是為了他們自己的時代，而是為了所有的時代。
在帝國之上，還疊著另一個羅馬——天主教世界的精神首都，它的天際線以聖伯多祿大殿的圓頂為冠，它的藝廊收藏著一些史上最偉大的藝術作品。
生活在這樣的宏偉之中，是一種每天都要進行的協商。羅馬人抱怨人潮、交通，以及維護一座某種意義上屬於全世界的城市所帶來的負擔——這些抱怨很有道理。
然而，這座城市一如既往地延續下去——不是靠凍結它的過去，而是靠住在過去裡面，把廢墟變成背景，把歷史變成日常生活中平凡的風景。

ph.ex: The cake has layer upon layer of cream.
ph.exzh: 這個蛋糕有一層又一層的奶油。

ph.ex: She studies not merely for tests but for herself.
ph.exzh: 她讀書不只為了考試，也是為了自己。
ph.m: not merely for their own age but

ph.ex: Sharing one bathroom is a daily negotiation.
ph.exzh: 共用一間浴室是每天都要協調的事。

ph.ex: This beach belongs to everyone.
ph.exzh: 這片海灘屬於每一個人。

ph.ex: The river flows on, as it always has.
ph.exzh: 河水一如既往地流淌。

ph.ex: They live inside history every day.
ph.exzh: 他們每天都生活在歷史之中。

discuss: Rome mixes 2,000-year-old ruins with daily life. Would you enjoy living somewhere like that? Why?
Protecting old monuments costs a lot. Who should pay to protect world heritage — the city, the country, or the world?
Throwing a coin in the Trevi Fountain is a wish to return. What wish-customs do you know from Taiwan or elsewhere?

topic: Icarus and the Fall
zh: 伊卡洛斯的墜落
src: National Geographic · BBC Culture · The New York Times

a.title: The Boy Who Flew Too High
text: Long ago, in an old Greek story, a clever man named Daedalus and his son Icarus were trapped on an island.
To escape, Daedalus made two big pairs of wings. He joined feathers together with soft wax.
Before they flew, Daedalus warned his son. “Do not fly too low, or the sea will wet your wings. Do not fly too high, or the sun will melt the wax.”
At first, Icarus was careful. But flying felt wonderful, and soon he forgot his father's words.
He flew higher and higher, close to the sun. The wax melted, his wings fell apart, and Icarus dropped into the sea.
People still tell this story today. It teaches us to be brave — but also to listen, and to know our limits.

q.q: What is this story mainly about?
opts: How Daedalus made wings from feathers
A boy who flew too high and fell
Why wax melts in the sun
How a father and son escaped from an island
q.why: 故事主線是伊卡洛斯飛太高墜落。

q.q: How did Daedalus make the wings?
opts: From feathers joined with wax
From wood and cloth
From feathers sewn with thread
From metal and glue
q.why: 原文：“He joined feathers together with soft wax.”

q.q: What did the father warn Icarus NOT to do?
opts: Not to fly high, but flying low was safe
Not to fly at night, when it was dark
Not to fly too high or too low
Not to fly anywhere without his father
q.why: 原文：“Do not fly too high, or the sun will melt the wax.” At first, Icarus was careful.”

q.q: In the story, “melt” means to ___.
opts: break into many small pieces
become hard and very cold
fly away high into the sky
turn soft or liquid from heat
q.why: melt = 融化。

q.q: What lesson does the story teach?
opts: Never try anything new or difficult in life
Be brave, but listen and know your limits
Always fly as high as you possibly can
Fathers are always right about everything
q.why: 線索：“It teaches us to be brave — but also to listen, and to know our limits.”

q.q: Your coach says, “Run fast, but don't sprint the whole race or you'll be too tired.” How is this like the story?
opts: It tells you that you should never run fast in a race
It says that winning the race does not matter at all
It is about making wings from feathers and wax
Stay in a safe middle, like neither too high nor too low
q.why: 保持中庸、不走極端——與代達洛斯的警告相同。

gt.en: To escape, Daedalus made two big pairs of wings.
gt.zh: 為了逃走，代達洛斯做了兩對大翅膀。

gt.en: Before they flew, Daedalus warned his son.
gt.zh: 在他們飛走之前，代達洛斯警告了他的兒子。

gt.en: The wax melted, his wings fell apart, and Icarus dropped into the sea.
gt.zh: 蠟融化了，他的翅膀散開，伊卡洛斯掉進了海裡。

gt.en: He joined feathers together with soft wax.
gt.zh: 他用軟蠟把羽毛黏在一起。

tz: 很久以前，在一個古希臘的故事裡，一位名叫代達洛斯的聰明人和他的兒子伊卡洛斯被困在一座島上。
為了逃走，代達洛斯做了兩對大翅膀。他用軟軟的蠟把羽毛黏在一起。
起飛前，代達洛斯警告兒子：「不要飛得太低，不然海水會把你的翅膀弄濕；也不要飛得太高，不然太陽會把蠟融化。」
一開始，伊卡洛斯很小心。但是飛翔的感覺太美妙了，他很快就忘了父親的話。
他越飛越高，靠近了太陽。蠟融化了，翅膀散開，伊卡洛斯掉進了海裡。
人們至今仍在講這個故事。它教我們要勇敢——但也要懂得傾聽，知道自己的極限。

ph.ex: The hikers were trapped on the mountain.
ph.exzh: 登山客被困在山上。

ph.ex: Join the two pieces together with glue.
ph.exzh: 用膠水把兩片黏在一起。

ph.ex: My old shoes are falling apart.
ph.exzh: 我的舊鞋快壞掉了。

ph.ex: Run hard, but know your limits.
ph.exzh: 努力跑，但要知道自己的極限。

b.title: Between the Sea and the Sun
text: One of the most famous of all Greek myths tells of Daedalus, a brilliant inventor, and his son Icarus, imprisoned on the island of Crete by King Minos.
Daedalus devised a daring escape. From feathers and wax he built two great pairs of wings, so that he and his son might simply fly away.
He gave Icarus one firm warning: fly a middle course. Too low, and the sea's spray would weigh the feathers down; too high, and the sun's heat would melt the wax.
For a while the plan worked, and the two rose into the open sky. But Icarus, thrilled by the sheer power of flight, ignored his father and soared ever upward toward the sun.
The wax softened, the feathers loosened, and the boy plunged into the sea that still bears his name. Daedalus flew on alone, grief-stricken.
For thousands of years the tale has been read as a warning against pride and recklessness — yet some also see in Icarus the beauty of daring to reach for something far greater than yourself.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Daedalus warned his son not to fly too high or too low over the sea.
King Minos imprisoned Daedalus and Icarus on the island of Crete.
Icarus ignored a warning and fell — a story of caution and of daring.
The sun's heat melted the wax, and Icarus fell into the sea.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: Who imprisoned Daedalus and Icarus, and where?
opts: King Minos, in the city of Athens
A sea god, on a small rocky island
Icarus's uncle, in a tall stone tower
King Minos, on the island of Crete
q.why: 原文：“One of the most famous of all Greek myths tells of Daedalus, a brilliant inventor, and his son Icarus, imprisoned on the island of Crete by King Minos.”

q.q: What were the two dangers in the warning?
opts: Too low (sea spray) and too high (the sun's heat)
Flying too fast and flying much too slowly
Large birds and sudden storms over the sea
Too high (the sea spray) and too low (the sun's heat)
q.why: 原文：“Too low, and the sea's spray would weigh the feathers down; too high, and the sun's heat would melt the wax.”

q.q: In paragraph 4, “soared” means ___.
opts: fell very quickly
flew high and freely
flew in circles
landed safely
q.why: soar = 高飛。

q.q: Why does the last paragraph offer two readings of the story?
opts: One reading is true and the other is a common mistake
The myth can mean “don't be reckless” and “dare greatly”
The writer could not remember how the story ended
Daedalus told the story differently from Icarus
q.why: 線索：“For thousands of years the tale has been read as a warning against pride and recklessness — yet some also see in Icarus the beauty of daring to reach for something …”

q.q: A friend wants to try a difficult skateboard trick without practising. Which reading of the myth would warn them, and which would encourage them?
opts: Caution warns against recklessness; daring admires bold effort
Caution admires bold effort; daring warns against being reckless
Both readings tell them to try it without thinking at all
Neither reading has anything to say about real life today
q.why: 文章提供「別魯莽」與「勇於挑戰」兩種讀法。

tr.en: From feathers and wax he built two great pairs of wings, so that he and his son might simply fly away.
tr.zh: 他用羽毛和蠟做了兩對大翅膀，好讓他和兒子可以直接飛走。

tr.en: He gave Icarus one firm warning: fly a middle course.
tr.zh: 他給了伊卡洛斯一個嚴厲的警告：要在中間的高度飛。

tr.en: But Icarus, thrilled by the sheer power of flight, ignored his father and soared ever upward toward the sun.
tr.zh: 但是伊卡洛斯被飛翔的力量沖昏了頭，不理會父親的話，一直往上朝著太陽高飛。

tz: 在所有希臘神話中，最有名的故事之一，講的是傑出的發明家代達洛斯和他的兒子伊卡洛斯，被米諾斯王囚禁在克里特島上。
代達洛斯想出了一個大膽的逃脫計畫。他用羽毛和蠟做了兩對大翅膀，讓他和兒子可以直接飛走。
他給伊卡洛斯一個嚴肅的警告：要飛在中間的高度。太低的話，海浪的水花會讓羽毛變重；太高的話，太陽的熱會融化蠟。
有一段時間計畫很順利，兩人飛上了開闊的天空。但是伊卡洛斯被飛翔的強大力量迷住了，不理會父親的話，一直往上朝太陽飛去。
蠟軟化了，羽毛鬆脫了，男孩墜入了那片至今仍以他命名的海。悲痛欲絕的代達洛斯獨自繼續飛行。
幾千年來，這個故事一直被解讀為對驕傲和魯莽的警告——但也有人在伊卡洛斯身上，看到了勇於追求遠比自己更偉大的事物的美。

ph.ex: The prisoners devised a clever escape.
ph.exzh: 囚犯們想出了一個聰明的逃脫方法。

ph.ex: The bird flew away when I came closer.
ph.exzh: 我一走近，鳥就飛走了。

ph.ex: Wet clothes weighed him down in the water.
ph.exzh: 濕衣服讓他在水裡變得很重。

ph.ex: The children were thrilled by the magic show.
ph.exzh: 孩子們被魔術表演迷住了。

ph.ex: Always reach for your goals.
ph.exzh: 永遠要追求你的目標。

c.title: The Two Lessons of Icarus
text: Few images from mythology have proved as enduring as the fall of Icarus: a boy, feathered wings melting, dropping from a bright sky into an indifferent sea. For nearly three thousand years the Greek tale has been retold, painted, and argued over — chiefly because it refuses to mean only one thing.

The conventional reading is a caution against hubris. Warned by his father Daedalus to keep a middle course, Icarus flew too close to the sun, and his pride — or his carelessness — destroyed him. In this version the moral is restraint: know your limits, and heed those wiser than you.

Yet a second reading has grown louder in modern times. Icarus, after all, did what humankind had only dreamed of — he flew. If his reach exceeded his grasp, perhaps the reaching itself was glorious, and a life spent hugging the safe middle is its own kind of failure.

Tellingly, the myth gives us both a reckless son and a cautious father, and it is the son we remember. Daedalus survives, yet it is Icarus whose name endures — as if the story cannot quite decide whether to mourn his fall or admire his flight.
That unresolved tension is the myth's genius. It hands each listener a mirror and asks a question as old as ambition itself: how high is too high?

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: The myth endures because it clearly teaches that daring is always better.
The myth is mainly about Daedalus's remarkable skill as an inventor.
The myth shows the ancient Greeks believed human flight impossible.
The myth endures by holding two opposing lessons and refusing to choose.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “hubris” means ___.
opts: quiet modesty about your own skills
careful, patient planning
excessive pride or overconfidence
deep and lasting sadness
q.why: hubris = 傲慢自大。

q.q: Why does the writer note that it is Icarus, not Daedalus, whom we remember?
opts: Daedalus died first, so few people remember his name
The story is drawn to the daring son as much as the father
Icarus, not his father, built the wings of wax
Daedalus's careful flight is the real lesson the story wants to teach
q.why: 線索：“Tellingly, the myth gives us both a reckless son and a cautious father, and it is the son we remember.”

q.q: What is the writer's stance on which lesson is correct?
opts: Deliberately leaves the question open
Clearly supports the warning reading
Clearly supports the daring reading
Thinks that both lessons are wrong
q.why: 作者刻意不下定論。

q.q: How is the essay structured?
opts: Two contrasting readings, then their tension
One reading, followed by evidence that proves it
A short biography of Daedalus himself
A comparison of Greek and Roman myths
q.why: 結構如選項。

q.q: Which real-life figure best fits the 'tribute to daring' reading of Icarus?
opts: A student who never tries a new subject at school
A driver who always keeps to the speed limit
An explorer attempting a risky first, knowing the danger
A climber who ignores all warnings and never thinks about danger
q.why: 明知危險仍大膽嘗試——敬佩冒險的解讀。

tz: 很少有神話意象像伊卡洛斯的墜落一樣歷久不衰：一個男孩，羽毛翅膀正在融化，從明亮的天空掉進冷漠的大海。將近三千年來，這個希臘故事一再被重述、被畫成畫、被爭論——主要是因為它拒絕只有一種意思。
傳統的解讀是對傲慢的警告。父親代達洛斯警告他要保持在中間的航道，伊卡洛斯卻飛得太靠近太陽，他的驕傲——或他的粗心——毀了他。在這個版本裡，寓意是節制：知道自己的極限，聽從比你更有智慧的人。
然而，第二種解讀在現代越來越響亮。畢竟，伊卡洛斯做到了人類一直只能夢想的事——他飛了起來。如果他追求的超出了他能掌握的，也許那份追求本身就是光榮的；而一輩子緊緊守在安全的中間，本身也是一種失敗。
值得注意的是，這則神話同時給了我們一個魯莽的兒子和一個謹慎的父親，而我們記住的卻是兒子。代達洛斯活了下來，留名至今的卻是伊卡洛斯——彷彿這個故事始終無法決定，該哀悼他的墜落，還是讚嘆他的飛翔。
這份懸而未決的張力，正是這則神話的天才之處。它遞給每一位聽眾一面鏡子，問了一個和野心本身一樣古老的問題：多高才算太高？

ph.ex: The brothers argued over the last cake.
ph.exzh: 兄弟倆為了最後一塊蛋糕爭吵。

ph.ex: The story is a caution against greed.
ph.exzh: 這個故事是對貪婪的警告。

ph.ex: Exercise hard, but know your limits.
ph.exzh: 努力運動，但要知道自己的極限。

ph.ex: Don't be too hard on him — he is only six, after all.
ph.exzh: 別對他太嚴格，畢竟他才六歲。

ph.ex: Dream big, even if your reach exceeds your grasp.
ph.exzh: 夢想要遠大，即使超出能力所及。

ph.ex: If you always hug the safe middle, you'll never try anything new.
ph.exzh: 如果你總是守著安全的中間，就永遠不會嘗試新東西。

discuss: Which lesson do you take from Icarus — be careful, or be bold? Why?
Have you ever ignored good advice and learned something the hard way?
Is it better to aim very high and risk failing, or to choose a safe, steady path?

topic: La Tomatina: The Great Tomato Fight
zh: 番茄節：西班牙丟番茄大戰

a.title: The Great Tomato Fight
text: In a small town in Spain called Buñol, there is one very messy festival. It is called La Tomatina.
On the last Wednesday of August, thousands of people meet in the town square. They all want to throw tomatoes!
Big trucks bring in piles of soft, ripe tomatoes — more than one hundred tons of them.
When the signal is given, everyone throws tomatoes at each other for one hour. Soon the whole street is red!
The rule is simple: squash each tomato first, so it is soft and does not hurt anyone.
After the fight, fire trucks spray the streets clean. Everyone is covered in tomato, laughing and happy.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How fire trucks clean the streets after a festival
Why tomatoes must be squashed before being thrown
A messy Spanish festival where people throw tomatoes
Big trucks that bring tomatoes to a town square
q.why: 全文介紹番茄節；其他是細節。

q.q: When does La Tomatina happen?
opts: The first Wednesday of August
The last Sunday of August
Every Wednesday in summer
The last Wednesday of August
q.why: 原文：“On the last Wednesday of August, thousands of people meet in the town square.”

q.q: What is the main rule?
opts: Squash each tomato first so it doesn't hurt
Throw tomatoes only at your own friends
Keep throwing for as long as you want
Throw only ripe tomatoes at people's faces
q.why: 原文：“The rule is simple: squash each tomato first, so it is soft and does not hurt anyone.”

q.q: In the text, “ripe” means a tomato that is ___.
opts: still green and very hard
fully grown and soft, ready to eat
red, but frozen solid
picked early, while still green and small
q.why: ripe = 成熟的。

q.q: Why do fire trucks spray the streets afterwards?
opts: To put out fires started by the festival
To cool down the hot crowd in the square
To signal the start of the tomato fight
To wash away the tomato mess
q.why: 線索：“After the fight, fire trucks spray the streets clean.”

q.q: If your school held a small 'water balloon day', which rule from La Tomatina would be MOST useful to copy?
opts: Let the water fight go on for the whole day
Throw the water balloons only at teachers
Make sure what you throw is soft and harmless
Use as many balloons as you can carry
q.why: 番茄節最重要的規則是先壓扁、確保不傷人。

gt.en: In a small town in Spain called Buñol, there is one very messy festival.
gt.zh: 在西班牙一個叫做布尼奧爾的小鎮，有一個非常髒亂的節慶。

gt.en: On the last Wednesday of August, thousands of people meet in the town square.
gt.zh: 在八月的最後一個星期三，成千上萬的人聚集在鎮上的廣場。

gt.en: Big trucks bring in piles of soft, ripe tomatoes — more than one hundred tons of them.
gt.zh: 大卡車運來一堆堆又軟又熟的番茄——總共超過一百噸。

gt.en: When the signal is given, everyone throws tomatoes at each other for one hour.
gt.zh: 信號一響，大家就互相丟番茄，丟整整一個小時。

tz: 在西班牙一個叫布尼奧爾的小鎮，有一個非常髒亂的節慶，叫做番茄節。
在八月的最後一個星期三，成千上萬的人聚集在鎮上的廣場。他們都想丟番茄！
大卡車載來一堆堆又軟又熟的番茄——超過一百噸。
信號一發出，每個人就互相丟番茄，丟一個小時。很快地，整條街都變成紅色的了！
規則很簡單：每顆番茄都要先捏爛，這樣它才會軟軟的，不會傷到任何人。
大戰結束後，消防車會把街道沖乾淨。每個人身上都沾滿了番茄，又笑又開心。

ph.ex: Everyone wants to win.
ph.exzh: 每個人都想贏。

ph.ex: Trucks bring in fresh fish every morning.
ph.exzh: 卡車每天早上運來新鮮的魚。

ph.ex: We played outside for one hour.
ph.exzh: 我們在外面玩了一個小時。

ph.ex: After the game, we were covered in mud.
ph.exzh: 比賽後我們全身都是泥巴。

b.title: A Town Painted Red
text: Once a year, the quiet Spanish town of Buñol, near Valencia, turns bright red. On the last Wednesday of August, it hosts La Tomatina, the world's biggest food fight.
Around twenty thousand people pack the narrow streets — far more than the town's own population. Trucks arrive loaded with over a hundred tons of ripe tomatoes.
At a signal, the battle begins. For one glorious, chaotic hour, strangers hurl tomatoes at anyone within reach, until the streets run with red pulp.
There are a few rules. Tomatoes must be squashed before they are thrown, so they cannot injure anyone, and the fight stops the moment a second signal sounds.
No one is quite sure how it began — perhaps a street scuffle among young people in 1945 — but the tradition stuck, and today it draws visitors from all over the world.
Afterwards, the townspeople hose down the streets, and the tomato juice leaves the old stones unusually clean. The mess, it turns out, washes away easily — and the memories last.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: About twenty thousand people pack Buñol's narrow streets every year.
La Tomatina is the world's biggest food fight, a wild one-hour tradition.
La Tomatina is an ancient religious festival that the town has held for centuries.
The acid in tomato juice leaves the old stones unusually clean.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；其他是細節。

q.q: How many people join, roughly?
opts: About 20,000
About 2,000
About 200,000
Only the town's own population
q.why: 第二段。

q.q: What are two of the rules?
opts: Squash tomatoes first; throw for as long as you like
Wear red; stop when you are tired
Squash tomatoes first; stop at the second signal
Throw only ripe tomatoes; start whenever you arrive
q.why: 原文：“Tomatoes must be squashed before they are thrown, so they cannot injure anyone, and the fight stops the moment a second signal sounds.”

q.q: In paragraph 3, “hurl” means to ___.
opts: throw gently
catch quickly
squash
throw hard
q.why: hurl = 用力投擲。

q.q: What does the text say about how the festival began?
opts: No one is sure, but it may come from a 1945 scuffle
It was carefully planned by the town's leaders in 1945
It started as a harvest celebration for local farmers
It began as an event designed to bring in tourists
q.why: 線索：“No one is quite sure how it began — perhaps a street scuffle among young people in 1945 — but the tradition stuck, and today it draws visitors from all over the world.”

q.q: A travel website says: “La Tomatina was created by Buñol's government to attract tourists.” Based on the text, how accurate is this?
opts: Completely accurate — the town planned it from the start
Accurate, because the festival now attracts many tourists
Not accurate — it was started by the town's tomato farmers
Not accurate — its origin is uncertain, perhaps a scuffle
q.why: 第五段：起源不明，可能源於街頭衝突。

tr.en: On the last Wednesday of August, it hosts La Tomatina, the world's biggest food fight.
tr.zh: 在八月的最後一個星期三，這裡會舉辦番茄節——全世界規模最大的食物大戰。

tr.en: Around twenty thousand people pack the narrow streets — far more than the town's own population.
tr.zh: 大約兩萬人擠滿狹窄的街道——遠遠超過這個小鎮本身的人口。

tr.en: For one glorious, chaotic hour, strangers hurl tomatoes at anyone within reach, until the streets run with red pulp.
tr.zh: 在這精彩又混亂的一小時裡，陌生人把番茄用力丟向身邊的任何人，直到街上流滿紅色的果肉。

tz: 每年一次，西班牙瓦倫西亞附近安靜的小鎮布尼奧爾會變成一片鮮紅。在八月的最後一個星期三，這裡會舉辦番茄節——世界上最大的食物大戰。
大約兩萬人擠滿了狹窄的街道——遠遠超過小鎮本身的人口。卡車載著一百多噸成熟的番茄抵達。
信號一響，戰鬥就開始了。在光榮又混亂的一個小時裡，陌生人把番茄丟向任何搆得到的人，直到街上流滿了紅色的果肉。
這裡有幾條規則。番茄丟出去之前一定要先捏爛，才不會傷到人；第二個信號一響，大戰就要立刻停止。
沒有人確定它是怎麼開始的——也許是 1945 年一群年輕人在街上的扭打——但這個傳統就這樣留了下來，今天吸引著來自世界各地的遊客。
之後，鎮民會用水管沖洗街道，而番茄汁會讓古老的石頭變得格外乾淨。原來這片髒亂很容易就能洗掉——而回憶會一直留下來。

ph.ex: His face turned bright red when he laughed.
ph.exzh: 他一笑臉就變得通紅。

ph.ex: Far more people came than we expected.
ph.exzh: 來的人遠遠比我們預期的多。

ph.ex: Keep your phone within reach.
ph.exzh: 把手機放在伸手可及的地方。

ph.ex: The dog runs to the door the moment it hears the bell.
ph.exzh: 狗一聽到門鈴就跑到門口。

ph.ex: The rain washed away the chalk drawings.
ph.exzh: 雨把粉筆畫沖掉了。

c.title: The Serious Business of Play
text: To an outsider, La Tomatina looks like pure chaos: twenty thousand people, a hundred tons of tomatoes, and one hour of cheerful violence in the streets of a small Spanish town. Yet beneath the mess lies something worth taking seriously — the human need to play.

The festival's origins are humble and uncertain, probably a spontaneous squabble among young people in 1945 that was simply repeated the next year, and the next, until accident hardened into tradition.

What endures is not meaning but release. In everyday life we are told to be careful, clean, and controlled; for one hour, La Tomatina suspends all of that, inviting ordinary adults to be gleefully ridiculous with the full permission of their town.
There is even a quiet logic to the tomato. Soft, cheap, and harmless once squashed, it allows a kind of combat with no real victims — aggression turned entirely into joy.

Every culture builds such safety valves, from carnivals to festivals of colour. La Tomatina is simply one of the loudest: proof that a community sometimes needs, together, to make a glorious and meaningless mess — and then wash it clean.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Beneath the chaos, it meets a real need to play and let go together.
La Tomatina carries a deep, ancient religious meaning for the town.
La Tomatina is meaningless fun that should not be taken seriously.
La Tomatina is, at heart, mainly about wasting good food.
q.why: 主旨：混亂底下有遊戲與釋放的需求。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “spontaneous” means ___.
opts: carefully organised by the town
extremely old and traditional
happening naturally, without planning
repeated on the same day every year
q.why: spontaneous = 自發的。

q.q: Why does the writer say the tomato has “a quiet logic”?
opts: Tomatoes are cheap, so the town can afford to buy many
Once squashed it is harmless, so play-fighting has no victims
Red tomatoes look dramatic in photographs and on TV
Tomatoes are so soft that nobody minds being hit with them whole
q.why: 線索：“Soft, cheap, and harmless once squashed, it allows a kind of combat with no real victims — aggression turned entirely into joy.”

q.q: How does the writer treat this messy festival?
opts: As a serious ritual with no real playfulness left in it
As a dangerous event that should be stopped
As a purely commercial event for the town
As playful on the surface but meaningful beneath
q.why: 認真看待玩樂。

q.q: What idea ties the whole essay together?
opts: Festivals like this should be carefully planned
Food should never be wasted, even in festivals
Societies need 'safety valves' to let go together
Spain has the very best festivals in Europe
q.why: 安全閥概念貫穿全文。

q.q: Which school event BEST works as a 'safety valve' in the writer's sense?
opts: A fun sports day to shout, run and laugh after exams
An extra test on Saturday morning for everyone
A silent reading hour in the school library
A noisy class party held instead of the final exams themselves
q.why: 讓大家一起釋放壓力的活動，就是作者說的安全閥。

tz: 在局外人看來，番茄節就像一場純粹的混亂：兩萬人、一百噸番茄，還有在一座西班牙小鎮的街道上，長達一小時的歡樂暴力。然而，在這片髒亂底下，有某種值得認真看待的東西——人類玩耍的需要。
這個節慶的起源簡單又不確定，很可能是 1945 年一群年輕人之間一場臨時的爭吵，第二年又重演了一次，接著又一次，直到一場意外硬化成了傳統。
延續下來的不是意義，而是釋放。在日常生活中，我們被要求要小心、要乾淨、要自制；在一個小時裡，番茄節暫停了這一切，邀請普通的大人在整個小鎮的完全許可下，開心地胡鬧一番。
番茄甚至有一種安靜的邏輯。它軟軟的、便宜，捏爛後又無害，讓一種沒有真正受害者的戰鬥成為可能——攻擊性完全轉化成了喜悅。
每一個文化都會建立這樣的安全閥，從嘉年華會到色彩節都是。番茄節只是其中最喧鬧的一個：它證明一個社群有時需要一起製造一場光榮而毫無意義的混亂——然後再把它洗乾淨。

ph.ex: Take your health seriously.
ph.exzh: 要認真看待你的健康。

ph.ex: The joke hardened into a school tradition.
ph.exzh: 這個玩笑後來固定成了學校傳統。

ph.ex: They painted the wall with the full permission of the owner.
ph.exzh: 他們在屋主完全同意下彩繪了這面牆。

ph.ex: She turned her fear into courage.
ph.exzh: 她把恐懼化為勇氣。

ph.ex: Sports can be a safety valve for stress.
ph.exzh: 運動可以是紓解壓力的管道。

ph.ex: Wash the vegetables clean before cooking.
ph.exzh: 煮之前把蔬菜洗乾淨。

discuss: Why do you think people enjoy festivals that are messy or a little wild?
La Tomatina lets ordinary adults be 'ridiculous' for an hour. Why might that be healthy?
What festivals in Taiwan or elsewhere act as a 'safety valve' for people to let go?

topic: International Sloth Day
zh: 國際樹懶日：慢慢來的生存高手

a.title: The Slowest Animal in the Trees
text: October 20 is International Sloth Day. It is a day to learn about one of the slowest animals in the world.
Sloths live in the rainforests of Central and South America. They spend almost all their life high up in the trees.
A sloth moves very slowly. It hangs upside down from branches with its long, curved claws.
Sloths eat leaves. Leaves do not give much energy, so sloths save energy by moving slowly and sleeping a lot.
Their fur is often a little green. Tiny plants called algae grow in it! This helps sloths hide in the trees.
Today, many forests are cut down. Sloth Day reminds people to protect the forests where sloths live.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Sloths and why they live slowly
Why green algae grow in sloth fur
How forests are cut down in South America
Why sloths sleep a lot
q.why: 全文介紹樹懶為何慢；其他是細節。

q.q: Where do sloths live?
opts: In the hot rainforests of Central Africa
In the mountains and forests of North America
Near the large rivers of South-East Asia

b.title: Slow and Steady Survives
text: Every October 20, wildlife groups celebrate International Sloth Day, a date created in Colombia in 2010 to raise awareness about one of the rainforest's most unusual animals.
Sloths live in the treetops of Central and South America. There are two main groups, two-toed and three-toed sloths, and both spend nearly their whole lives hanging upside down from branches.

Their famous slowness is not laziness but a clever survival strategy. Sloths live on a diet of leaves, which contain very little energy, so their bodies run at an extremely low speed — they even digest food slowly, sometimes over several days.
Moving slowly also keeps them safe. Eagles and big cats notice movement, and a sloth that barely moves is hard to spot, especially since algae growing in its fur gives it a greenish colour.
Surprisingly, sloths are good swimmers, and they climb down to the ground only about once a week — mainly to go to the toilet.
Their biggest dangers today come from people: forests cleared for farms and roads, electric power lines, and illegal trading of babies as pets.

c.title: The Wisdom of Slowness
text: In a culture that prizes speed, the sloth is an easy joke: the patron saint of laziness, a creature that seems to have opted out of effort altogether. International Sloth Day, held every October 20, invites us to look again.

A sloth's pace is not a flaw but an exquisitely tuned economy. Its diet of tough, low-calorie leaves would starve a more ambitious animal, so the sloth simply spends less — a slow metabolism, little muscle, and a body temperature that drifts with the air around it.
Even its stillness is strategic. Harpy eagles and jaguars hunt by detecting motion; an animal that barely moves, its fur tinted green by algae, all but disappears into the canopy.

Yet the very trait that has served sloths for millions of years leaves them helpless against modern threats. They cannot outrun a bulldozer, and as roads and power lines cut through the forest, an animal designed for patience meets a world that has run out of it.

Perhaps that is the day's quiet lesson. Success need not mean doing more, faster; sometimes it means fitting your life precisely to what your surroundings can give — and asking whether we are leaving room for creatures who live by a different clock.

樹懶的步調不是缺陷，而是一套精密調校的節約系統。牠吃的是堅韌、低熱量的樹葉，這種食物會讓一隻比較有野心的動物餓死，所以樹懶乾脆少花一點——緩慢的新陳代謝、很少的肌肉，還有隨周圍空氣變化的體溫。
就連牠的靜止不動也是一種策略。角鵰和美洲豹靠偵測動作來狩獵；一隻幾乎不動、毛皮被藻類染成綠色的動物，幾乎就消失在樹冠裡了。
然而，正是這個為樹懶服務了數百萬年的特徵，讓牠們在現代的威脅面前束手無策。牠們跑不贏推土機；當道路和電線切穿森林時，一種為耐心而設計的動物，遇上了一個早已失去耐心的世界。
也許這就是這一天安靜的啟示。成功不一定代表做得更多、更快；有時它代表讓你的生活剛好配合周圍環境能給予的東西——也讓我們問問自己：我們是否還為那些按照不同時鐘生活的生物，留下了空間？

a.title: The Man Who Started the Nobel Prize
text: Every year, the world talks about the Nobel Prize. But who was Nobel? His name was Alfred Nobel. He was born in Stockholm, Sweden, on October 21, 1833.
Alfred loved science and languages. When he grew up, he became an inventor.
His most famous invention was dynamite. It was very strong and helped workers build roads, tunnels and railways.
But dynamite was also used in wars. This made Alfred sad. He wanted people to remember him for something good.
So he wrote a special plan: after his death, his money would give prizes to people who help the world.
Today the Nobel Prize goes to great scientists, writers and peacemakers every year.

b.title: From Dynamite to the Nobel Prize
text: Each October the world waits for the Nobel Prize announcements. October 21 is the birthday of the man behind them: Alfred Nobel, born in Stockholm in 1833.
Nobel grew up partly in Russia, spoke several languages and became a gifted chemist. Over his life he collected 355 patents, but one invention made his fortune: dynamite, patented in 1867.

Dynamite made the dangerous liquid nitroglycerin much safer to handle, and it transformed the building of mines, tunnels and railways. Yet it was also used in weapons, and Nobel himself owned factories that made arms.

In 1888, when his brother Ludvig died, a French newspaper reportedly mixed up the brothers and printed Alfred's obituary instead, calling him a 'merchant of death'. Historians are not sure how much this shocked him, but the story is often told.

In 1895, in Paris, Nobel signed a will that left most of his huge fortune to fund prizes for those who had brought 'the greatest benefit to humankind' in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace.
He died in Italy on December 10, 1896. The first prizes were awarded in 1901, and they are still presented on December 10 every year.

諾貝爾有一部分的成長時光在俄國度過，會說好幾種語言，成為一位很有天分的化學家。他一生累積了 355 項專利，但讓他致富的是其中一項發明：1867 年取得專利的炸藥。
炸藥讓危險的液體硝化甘油變得安全許多，也徹底改變了礦坑、隧道和鐵路的建造方式。然而它也被用在武器上，而諾貝爾本人也擁有生產軍火的工廠。
1888 年，他的哥哥路德維格過世時，據說一家法國報紙把兄弟倆搞混了，刊出了阿佛烈的訃聞，還稱他為「死亡商人」。歷史學家不確定這件事讓他受到多大的衝擊，但這個故事常常被人提起。
1895 年，諾貝爾在巴黎簽下一份遺囑，把他龐大財富的大部分留下來設立獎項，頒給在物理、化學、醫學、文學與和平領域為「人類帶來最大利益」的人。
他在 1896 年 12 月 10 日於義大利過世。第一屆獎項在 1901 年頒發，至今每年仍在 12 月 10 日頒獎。

c.title: A Fortune in Search of a Conscience
text: Few names are as firmly attached to virtue as Nobel's — which is a curious fate for a man who made his fortune from explosives. Born in Stockholm on October 21, 1833, Alfred Nobel was a restless polyglot chemist whose 355 patents included the one that defined him: dynamite.

His invention tamed nitroglycerin, a liquid so unstable that it had killed workers, including Nobel's own younger brother in an 1864 factory blast. Packed into a safer form, it blasted open mines, canals and railways across the industrial world — and, inevitably, found its way into war.

Legend holds that in 1888 a French newspaper, mistaking his brother Ludvig's death for his own, branded him 'the merchant of death'. The anecdote is almost too neat, and historians treat it with caution; still, it captures a real tension in a man who wrote poetry, never married, and seemed uneasy with the source of his wealth.

Whatever his motives, his will of 1895 was radical. It bypassed his relatives and directed most of his estate towards prizes, regardless of nationality, for those who had conferred 'the greatest benefit to humankind'.

More than a century later, the prizes are less a monument to Nobel than a standing argument about what benefit means — and a reminder that how a fortune is spent can, in the end, redefine how it was made.

q.q: Which best captures the essay's central idea?
opts: Nobel created the prizes because a newspaper had publicly shamed him.
Nobel's family, not Nobel himself, wanted the prizes to be created.
A man enriched by explosives felt no guilt and wanted only to be remembered as rich.
A man enriched by explosives used his will to tie his name to human benefit.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “unstable” describes nitroglycerin as ___.
opts: likely to explode or change suddenly
very expensive to produce
very heavy and hard to move around
completely safe to use
q.why: unstable = 不穩定的。

q.q: Why does the writer call the 'merchant of death' story “almost too neat”?
opts: It was printed in a well-designed newspaper
It fits so perfectly that it may be simplified
Historians have confirmed every single detail
Nobel himself liked stories to be tidy
q.why: 第三段。

q.q: What is the writer's attitude towards Nobel's motives?
opts: Certain that he acted mainly out of guilt
Sure that guilt alone made him write his will in the end
Open and careful — motives unclear, but the will mattered
Uninterested in what his motives may have been
q.why: Whatever his motives…

q.q: How does the final paragraph relate to the opening?
opts: It lists the most famous winners of the Nobel Prize
It describes Nobel's childhood in Stockholm and Russia
It returns to the irony that spending can redefine a fortune
It introduces his brother Ludvig and the newspaper mistake
q.why: 首尾呼應。

q.q: Which question would the writer MOST want readers to think about?
opts: Can how wealth is spent change how we judge its source?
How many patents can one inventor hold in a lifetime?
Which country has won the most Nobel Prizes so far?
How exactly is dynamite made safer than nitroglycerin?
q.why: 結尾：how a fortune is spent can redefine how it was made。

tz: 很少有名字像諾貝爾這樣和美德緊緊連在一起——對一個靠炸藥致富的人來說，這是一個奇特的命運。阿佛烈・諾貝爾 1833 年 10 月 21 日生於斯德哥爾摩，是一位精通多種語言、靜不下來的化學家；他的 355 項專利中，包括了定義了他一生的那一項：炸藥。
他的發明馴服了硝化甘油——一種極不穩定、曾經害死工人的液體，其中包括 1864 年在一次工廠爆炸中喪生的、諾貝爾自己的弟弟。被包裝成更安全的形式後，它在整個工業世界炸開了礦坑、運河和鐵路——而且無可避免地，也走進了戰爭。
傳說在 1888 年，一家法國報紙把他哥哥路德維格的死誤當成他的死，給他貼上了「死亡商人」的標籤。這則軼事幾乎太過工整，歷史學家對它持保留態度；儘管如此，它捕捉到一個真實的矛盾：這個人會寫詩、終身未婚，而且似乎對自己財富的來源感到不安。
不論他的動機是什麼，他 1895 年的遺囑都是激進的。它繞過了他的親戚，把大部分遺產指定用來設立獎項，不分國籍，頒給那些為「人類帶來最大利益」的人。
一個多世紀後，這些獎項與其說是諾貝爾的紀念碑，不如說是一場關於「什麼是利益」的持續爭論——也提醒我們，一筆財富如何被花掉，最終可以重新定義它是如何被賺來的。

ph.ex: His name is attached to the famous bridge.
ph.exzh: 他的名字和那座著名的橋連在一起。

ph.ex: Plastic has found its way into the ocean.
ph.exzh: 塑膠已經進入了海洋。

ph.ex: Treat online rumours with caution.
ph.exzh: 對網路謠言要謹慎看待。

ph.ex: She was uneasy with the plan.
ph.exzh: 她對這個計畫感到不安。

ph.ex: Everyone can join, regardless of age.
ph.exzh: 不論年齡，人人都可以參加。

ph.ex: The prize is less a reward than a promise.
ph.exzh: 這個獎與其說是獎勵，不如說是一個承諾。
ph.m: less a monument to Nobel than

discuss: Nobel's invention helped build railways but was also used in wars. Can one invention be both good and bad?
If you could create a prize for people who help the world, what would it reward?
Do you think how people spend their money can change how others remember them?

topic: Machu Picchu: The Lost City of the Inca
zh: 馬丘比丘：印加的天空之城
src: UNESCO · National Geographic · The New York Times

a.title: A City in the Clouds
text: High in the mountains of Peru, there is an old stone city. Its name is Machu Picchu.
The Inca people built it more than 500 years ago. It sits on top of a mountain, about 2,400 metres high. Clouds often float around it.
The Inca were great builders. They cut big stones so well that the stones fit together without any cement.
There are houses, temples and long steps on the mountain called terraces. People grew food on them.
Today, many visitors come to see Machu Picchu. Some walk for four days on an old path called the Inca Trail.
Only a certain number of visitors can enter each day. This helps protect the old city.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How the Inca built terraces for food
An old Inca city on a mountain in Peru
The four-day walk called the Inca Trail
How stones fit together without cement
q.why: 全文介紹馬丘比丘；其他是細節。

q.q: How high is Machu Picchu?
opts: About 4,200 metres
About 1,400 metres
About 2,400 metres
About 24,000 metres
q.why: 原文：“It sits on top of a mountain, about 2,400 metres high.”

q.q: What did the Inca grow food on?
opts: Terraces
Roofs of temples
Flat land by the river
Small boats
q.why: 原文：“There are houses, temples and long steps on the mountain called terraces.”

q.q: In the text, “cement” is something used to ___.
opts: cut big stones into neat shapes
grow food on steep mountains
decorate the walls of temples
stick stones or bricks together
q.why: cement = 水泥。

q.q: Why can only a certain number of visitors enter each day?
opts: To protect the old city from damage
Because the Inca Trail is closed in winter
Because there is not enough food for everyone
Because the tickets are far too expensive
q.why: 最後一段。

q.q: You want to visit Machu Picchu. Based on the text, what should you do before you go?
opts: Arrive at any time of day without making any plans
Bring some cement so you can help repair the walls
Book a time in advance, as daily visitors are limited
Plan to camp for a night inside the old stone city
q.why: 每天入場人數有限，需事先安排。

gt.en: It sits on top of a mountain, about 2,400 metres high.
gt.zh: 它位在一座大約兩千四百公尺高的山頂上。

gt.en: They cut big stones so well that the stones fit together without any cement.
gt.zh: 他們把大石頭切得非常好，石頭不用任何水泥就能緊密地拼在一起。

gt.en: There are houses, temples and long steps on the mountain called terraces.
gt.zh: 山上有房子、神廟，還有一層層叫做梯田的長階梯。

gt.en: Today, many visitors come to see Machu Picchu.
gt.zh: 今天，許多遊客來參觀馬丘比丘。

tz: 在秘魯的高山上，有一座古老的石頭城市，它的名字叫馬丘比丘。
印加人在五百多年前建造了它。它坐落在一座大約 2,400 公尺高的山頂上，雲常常飄在它的四周。
印加人是很厲害的建築者。他們把大石頭切得非常精準，石頭之間不用任何水泥就能密合在一起。
那裡有房子、神殿，還有山坡上一層一層叫做梯田的長台階。人們在上面種植食物。
今天，有很多遊客來看馬丘比丘。有些人會走四天，走一條叫做印加古道的老路。
每天只有一定數量的遊客可以進入，這有助於保護這座古城。

b.title: Peru's Citadel Above the Clouds
text: Perched on a narrow ridge in the Andes, about 2,430 metres above sea level, Machu Picchu is one of the most breathtaking places on Earth.
The Inca built it in the mid-1400s, probably as a royal estate for the emperor Pachacuti. Less than a century later the site was abandoned, around the time the Spanish conquered the Inca Empire.

Because the Spanish never found it, Machu Picchu survived largely intact. Local farmers always knew it was there, but it became world-famous after the American explorer Hiram Bingham publicised it in 1911.
Its stonework is remarkable. Builders shaped granite blocks so precisely that they fit together without mortar, and the walls have survived centuries of earthquakes.
In 1983 the site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Today visitors arrive by train and bus from Cusco, or hike the famous Inca Trail, which usually takes four days.
Popularity brings problems, however. To prevent damage, Peru limits daily visitor numbers and sets fixed routes through the ruins.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Hiram Bingham made Machu Picchu famous to the outside world in 1911.
Machu Picchu was lost for centuries until Bingham discovered it for the world in 1911.
Machu Picchu, a well-preserved Inca site, is now a protected world treasure.
The Inca built Machu Picchu in the 1400s for the emperor Pachacuti.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: Why did Machu Picchu survive largely intact?
opts: It was rebuilt after the Spanish left
Bingham protected it from tourists
It was too high for earthquakes
The Spanish never found it
q.why: 原文：“Because the Spanish never found it, Machu Picchu survived largely intact.”

q.q: What do the builders' walls NOT use?
opts: Granite blocks
Mortar
Precisely shaped stones
Stone
q.why: 第四段：without mortar。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “abandoned” means ___.
opts: left empty, no longer used
destroyed during a war
rebuilt again in stone
kept secret from outsiders
q.why: abandoned = 被遺棄。

q.q: What does the writer suggest by saying “Local farmers always knew it was there”?
opts: Bingham made it famous but did not really 'discover' it
Local farmers were the ones who built the stone city
Farmers kept the city a secret from Bingham's team
Nobody at all knew about the site before 1911
q.why: 線索：“Local farmers always knew it was there, but it became world-famous after the American explorer Hiram Bingham publicised it in 1911.”

q.q: A textbook says: “Hiram Bingham discovered Machu Picchu in 1911.” Based on the text, how could this sentence be improved?
opts: “Hiram Bingham and his team built Machu Picchu in 1911.”
“The Spanish conquerors discovered Machu Picchu in 1911.”
“Bingham made it known to outsiders in 1911; locals knew it.”
“Hiram Bingham discovered Machu Picchu for the Inca people in 1911.”
q.why: 當地人一直知道，賓漢是讓外界知道。

tr.en: Less than a century later the site was abandoned, around the time the Spanish conquered the Inca Empire.
tr.zh: 不到一百年後，這個地方就被遺棄了，大約就在西班牙人征服印加帝國的時候。

tr.en: Because the Spanish never found it, Machu Picchu survived largely intact.
tr.zh: 因為西班牙人從來沒有找到它，馬丘比丘大致完整地保存了下來。

tr.en: Builders shaped granite blocks so precisely that they fit together without mortar, and the walls have survived centuries of earthquakes.
tr.zh: 建造者把花崗岩塊切得非常精準，不用灰泥就能拼合，這些牆經歷了好幾個世紀的地震依然屹立。

tz: 馬丘比丘坐落在安地斯山脈一道狹窄的山脊上，海拔大約 2,430 公尺，是地球上最令人屏息的地方之一。
印加人在 1400 年代中期建造了它，很可能是作為帕查庫特克皇帝的王室莊園。不到一個世紀後，這個地方就被遺棄了，大約就在西班牙人征服印加帝國的時候。
因為西班牙人從來沒有找到它，馬丘比丘大致完整地保存了下來。當地農民一直都知道它在那裡，但它是在 1911 年美國探險家海勒姆・賓漢姆大力宣傳之後，才聞名全世界的。
它的石造工藝非常了不起。建造者把花崗岩塊切得極為精準，不用灰漿就能密合在一起，這些牆經歷了好幾個世紀的地震仍然屹立不搖。
1983 年，這個遺址成為聯合國教科文組織的世界遺產。今天，遊客從庫斯科搭火車和巴士前來，或走著名的印加古道，通常要走四天。
然而，名氣也帶來了問題。為了防止損害，秘魯限制每天的遊客人數，並規定在遺址中的固定參觀路線。

c.title: The City That Was Never Lost
text: Machu Picchu is routinely called a 'lost city', a phrase that says more about the outside world than about the place itself. Set on a saddle of rock some 2,430 metres up in the Peruvian Andes, it was never truly lost to the people who farmed the slopes below.

Built in the mid-fifteenth century, most likely as an estate for the Inca ruler Pachacuti, it was occupied for less than a hundred years. When the Spanish conquest shattered the empire, the site simply fell quiet — and, crucially, it escaped the colonisers' attention, sparing it the destruction suffered by so many Inca temples.

What survives is an argument in stone. Granite blocks were shaped to fit so closely that no mortar was needed, and the slightly flexible joints have let the walls ride out earthquakes that toppled later buildings.

Hiram Bingham's 1911 expedition turned the site into an international icon, but it also reflected an era in which foreign 'discovery' erased local knowledge, and artefacts he removed were returned to Peru only in this century.

Today the danger is love rather than neglect. With crowds pressing on fragile terraces, Peru caps daily entries and fixes routes — a reminder that a place can survive centuries of isolation and still be worn away by admiration.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall argument?
opts: It was lost for centuries until Bingham finally discovered it in 1911.
It was never truly 'lost', and its real threat now is too much attention.
Earthquakes in the Andes are the greatest threat the site faces today.
Tourism has had little effect on the condition of Machu Picchu.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “fragile” means ___.
opts: very old
very beautiful
very large
easily damaged
q.why: fragile = 脆弱的。

q.q: Why does the writer say the phrase 'lost city' “says more about the outside world”?
opts: Only outsiders lost track of it; locals always knew
It was hidden so well that even locals forgot it
Visitors often get lost on its winding paths
The city slowly moved over the centuries
q.why: 線索：“Machu Picchu is routinely called a 'lost city', a phrase that says more about the outside world than about the place itself.”

q.q: How does the writer present Bingham's 'discovery'?
opts: As a simple, heroic achievement by a brave explorer
As a complete lie invented to sell newspapers
Critically — it brought fame but erased local knowledge
As a brave discovery of a city that nobody had ever known
q.why: 第四段。

q.q: What contrast frames the final paragraph?
opts: Spanish conquerors versus the Inca builders
Local farmers versus visiting scientists
Centuries of isolation versus harm from admiration
Centuries of damage from visitors versus new protection
q.why: danger is love rather than neglect。

q.q: Which piece of evidence would BEST support the writer's claim that “the danger is love rather than neglect”?
opts: A record of when the Spanish arrived in Peru
The height of the site above sea level in metres
The year the site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site
Data showing terrace wear rising with visitor numbers
q.why: 遊客增加與磨損上升的數據最能支持「被愛磨損」。

tz: 馬丘比丘常被稱為「失落之城」，但這個說法說明的與其說是這個地方本身，不如說是外面的世界。它位於秘魯安地斯山脈海拔約 2,430 公尺的一處岩石鞍部，對於在下方山坡耕作的人們來說，它從來沒有真正失落過。
它建於十五世紀中葉，很可能是印加統治者帕查庫特克的莊園，有人居住的時間不到一百年。西班牙的征服粉碎了帝國之後，這個地方就這樣沉寂下來——而關鍵在於，它逃過了殖民者的注意，因此免於許多印加神殿所遭受的破壞。
留存下來的，是一段用石頭寫成的論證。花崗岩塊被切得如此密合，根本不需要灰漿；而這些略帶彈性的接縫，讓牆壁撐過了那些震倒了後來建築的地震。
海勒姆・賓漢姆 1911 年的探險讓這個遺址成為國際地標，但它也反映了一個時代：外國人的「發現」抹去了當地人的知識，而他帶走的文物，直到本世紀才歸還給秘魯。
今天，危險來自喜愛，而不是忽視。由於人潮擠壓著脆弱的梯田，秘魯限制每天的入場人數並固定參觀路線——這提醒我們，一個地方可以熬過好幾個世紀的與世隔絕，卻仍然可能被讚嘆一點一點磨損。

discuss: Why do you think the Inca built a city on top of a mountain?
Is it fair to say an explorer 'discovered' a place that local people already knew? Why or why not?
Famous places can be damaged by too many visitors. What rules would you make to protect a site like this?

topic: Mole Day: Counting the Tiny
zh: 莫耳日：怎麼數數不清的原子？

a.title: A Day for a Very Big Number
text: October 23 is Mole Day. It is not about the little animal! It is a day for chemistry.
Everything is made of atoms. Atoms are so small that we cannot see them, even with a normal microscope.
Because atoms are tiny, scientists count them in big groups. One group is called a mole.
One mole is about 602,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 things. People write it as 6.02 × 10²³.
That is why Mole Day is on 10/23, from 6:02 in the morning to 6:02 in the evening.
On Mole Day, students do fun experiments, bake cakes and make puns about moles.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Why atoms are far too small to see
How students bake cakes on Mole Day
Why 6:02 is a special time of day
Mole Day, a day about counting atoms
q.why: 全文介紹莫耳日。

q.q: Why do scientists count atoms in big groups?
opts: Atoms are too heavy to count one by one
Atoms move much too fast to be counted
Atoms are tiny, so there are far too many
Atoms can only exist in big groups
q.why: 原文：“Because atoms are tiny, scientists count them in big groups.”

q.q: When does Mole Day start?
opts: At 6:02 in the morning on October 23
At 6:02 in the evening on October 23
At 10:23 in the morning on June 2
At exactly midnight on October 23
q.why: 原文：“October 23 is Mole Day.”

q.q: In the text, “tiny” means ___.
opts: very heavy
very small
very fast
very important
q.why: tiny = 極小的。

q.q: Why is Mole Day on 10/23?
opts: The date matches the number 6.02 × 10²³
It is the birthday of a famous scientist
It is the first day of the school chemistry year
It is the day atoms were discovered
q.why: 日期對應 6.02 × 10²³。

q.q: Which everyday example works most like a 'mole'?
opts: Measuring your height in centimetres
Telling the time with a clock on the wall
Reading a long book page by page
Buying eggs by the dozen, not one by one
q.why: 莫耳和「一打」一樣，是成組計數的單位。

gt.en: It is a day for chemistry.
gt.zh: 這是一個屬於化學的日子。

gt.en: Everything is made of atoms.
gt.zh: 所有的東西都是由原子組成的。

gt.en: Because atoms are tiny, scientists count them in big groups.
gt.zh: 因為原子非常微小，科學家就把它們一大群一大群地計算。

gt.en: On Mole Day, students do fun experiments, bake cakes and make puns about moles.
gt.zh: 在莫耳日，學生們做有趣的實驗、烤蛋糕，還會說關於莫耳（鼴鼠）的雙關笑話。

tz: 10 月 23 日是莫耳日。它跟那種小動物（鼴鼠，英文也叫 mole）無關！這是一個屬於化學的日子。
所有的東西都是由原子組成的。原子小到我們看不見，就算用一般的顯微鏡也看不到。
因為原子很小，科學家會把它們分成一大群一大群來計算。一群就叫做一莫耳。
這就是為什麼莫耳日在 10 月 23 日，從早上 6:02 到晚上 6:02。
在莫耳日，學生們會做有趣的實驗、烤蛋糕，還會用「mole」這個字玩雙關語。

b.title: Why Chemists Celebrate at 6:02
text: Every year on October 23, chemistry classrooms celebrate Mole Day. The party runs from 6:02 a.m. to 6:02 p.m., and the timing is a clue to what it honours.
In chemistry, a mole is not an animal but a unit for counting particles. Just as a 'dozen' means twelve, a mole means about 6.02 × 10²³ — a six followed by twenty-three digits.
This value is known as Avogadro's number, named after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro, whose ideas in the early 1800s helped explain how gases behave.
Why such an enormous number? Atoms are unimaginably small. A single sip of water — about 18 grams — contains roughly one mole of water molecules.
Using moles lets chemists connect the invisible world of atoms to amounts they can actually weigh on a scale, which is essential for medicine, cooking chemistry and industry.
Mole Day began in American schools in the 1980s, and today teachers mark it with experiments, mole-shaped cakes and plenty of terrible puns.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Mole Day celebrates the mole, which links tiny atoms to weighable amounts.
Avogadro's number is named after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro.
A single sip of water contains roughly one mole of water molecules.
Mole Day began in American chemistry classrooms in the 1980s.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: Who is Avogadro's number named after?
opts: An American chemistry teacher in the 1980s
A French scientist who studied gases
The founder of the National Mole Day group
An Italian scientist, Amedeo Avogadro
q.why: 原文：“This value is known as Avogadro's number, named after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro, whose ideas in the early 1800s helped explain how gases behave.”

q.q: About how much water contains one mole of water molecules?
opts: About 18 litres
About 18 grams, a single sip
About 180 grams, a full glass
About 1.8 grams, a single drop
q.why: 原文：“A single sip of water — about 18 grams — contains roughly one mole of water molecules.”

q.q: In paragraph 2, a “unit” is ___.
opts: a tiny kind of particle inside an atom
a single atom counted on its own, one by one
a standard amount used to measure or count
a scientific experiment done in a lab
q.why: unit = 單位。

q.q: Why does the writer compare a mole to a 'dozen'?
opts: A mole is exactly equal to twelve things
Both are ways of counting things in groups
Both are used mainly in cooking recipes
To show that moles are easy to see
q.why: 線索：“In chemistry, a mole is not an animal but a unit for counting particles.”

q.q: Why is the mole especially useful for chemists who make medicines?
opts: It tells them exactly how big each single atom is in size
It lets chemists see atoms with their own eyes
It removes the need for any careful measuring
It links invisible atoms to amounts they can weigh
q.why: 第五段：連接看不見的原子與可秤量的份量。

tr.en: Every year on October 23, chemistry classrooms celebrate Mole Day.
tr.zh: 每年十月二十三日，化學教室都會慶祝莫耳日。

tr.en: In chemistry, a mole is not an animal but a unit for counting particles.
tr.zh: 在化學裡，莫耳不是一種動物，而是計算粒子的單位。

tr.en: A single sip of water — about 18 grams — contains roughly one mole of water molecules.
tr.zh: 一小口水——大約十八公克——就含有大約一莫耳的水分子。

tz: 每年 10 月 23 日，化學課的教室都會慶祝莫耳日。派對從早上 6:02 一直到晚上 6:02，而這個時間正是它所紀念的東西的線索。
在化學裡，莫耳不是一種動物，而是一個計算粒子數量的單位。就像「一打」代表十二個，一莫耳大約代表 6.02 × 10²³ 個——也就是 6 後面跟著二十三位數字。
這個數值叫做亞佛加厥數，是以義大利科學家阿莫迪歐・亞佛加厥命名的；他在 1800 年代初期提出的想法，幫助解釋了氣體的行為。
為什麼是這麼巨大的數字？因為原子小得難以想像。一小口水——大約 18 公克——裡面就有大約一莫耳的水分子。
使用莫耳，讓化學家能把看不見的原子世界，和他們真的能放在秤上秤的份量連結起來，這對醫藥、烹飪化學和工業都非常重要。
莫耳日在 1980 年代從美國的學校開始，今天老師們會用實驗、鼴鼠造型的蛋糕，還有一大堆很冷的雙關語來慶祝它。

c.title: A Bridge Between Two Worlds
text: On October 23, from 6:02 in the morning until 6:02 at night, chemistry teachers indulge in a ritual of cakes, costumes and shameless puns. Mole Day is silly by design, but the number it celebrates is one of the quiet pillars of modern science.

A mole is simply a counting unit — like a dozen, only vastly larger. It stands for roughly 6.02 × 10²³ particles, a quantity named in honour of Amedeo Avogadro, the Italian scientist who proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of gas hold equal numbers of molecules.

Avogadro's idea was largely ignored in his lifetime. Only decades after his death did chemists recognise how neatly it untangled the confusion over atomic weights, and the constant bearing his name was measured with real precision only much later.

The mole's genius lies in translation. Atoms are far too small to count or weigh individually, yet a mole of any substance has a mass in grams that matches its atomic or molecular weight. A sip of water, about eighteen grams, contains a mole of water molecules — a number larger than the grains of sand on many beaches combined.
Mole Day, then, celebrates a bridge: between the invisible and the measurable, and between an overlooked idea and its eventual vindication.

q.q: Which best captures the essay's main idea?
opts: Avogadro was widely celebrated for his ideas during his own lifetime.
Mole Day is mostly pointless fun with little to do with real chemistry.
Behind a playful holiday lies the mole, linking atoms to the measurable.
The size of the mole was measured precisely by Avogadro in 1811.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In the last paragraph, “vindication” means ___.
opts: proof that an idea was right after all
proof that an idea was wrong from the start
a mistake that is later corrected
a measurement made very precisely
q.why: vindication = 被證明正確。

q.q: What does paragraph 3 suggest about how science sometimes works?
opts: Famous scientists' ideas are accepted quickly
A correct idea can be ignored for years
Scientists never really change their minds
Only experiments, not ideas, really matter
q.why: 線索：“Avogadro's idea was largely ignored in his lifetime.”

q.q: How does the writer view the silliness of Mole Day?
opts: As embarrassing for serious chemistry teachers
Serious on the surface, but really just a joke for students
As a purely serious event with no humour at all
Playful on the surface, celebrating something important
q.why: silly by design, but …

q.q: What image ties the essay together?
opts: A cake baked in the shape of a mole
A map of Italy in Avogadro's time
The mole as a 'bridge' to the measurable
A list of gases that Avogadro studied
q.why: bridge 意象。

q.q: Which modern situation is MOST like Avogadro's experience?
opts: An unusual idea ignored for years, later widely accepted
A popular idea that everyone accepts immediately
A scientist who wins a big prize in their first year
A famous scientist's idea accepted at once, then forgotten later
q.why: 想法被忽視多年後才獲承認。

tz: 10 月 23 日，從早上 6:02 到晚上 6:02，化學老師們沉浸在一場有蛋糕、扮裝和毫不害臊的雙關語的儀式裡。莫耳日是刻意弄得很傻氣的，但它所慶祝的那個數字，是現代科學中一根安靜的支柱。
莫耳只是一個計數單位——就像「一打」，只是大得多。它代表大約 6.02 × 10²³ 個粒子，這個數量是為了紀念阿莫迪歐・亞佛加厥而命名的；這位義大利科學家在 1811 年提出，相同體積的氣體含有相同數目的分子。
亞佛加厥的想法在他有生之年大多被忽視。直到他死後幾十年，化學家才發現它如何俐落地解開了原子量的混亂；而以他命名的常數，更是很久以後才被真正精確地測量出來。
莫耳的天才之處在於「翻譯」。原子太小了，無法一個一個地數或秤，但任何物質一莫耳的質量（以公克計），都正好等於它的原子量或分子量。一小口大約十八公克的水，就含有一莫耳的水分子——這個數字比許多海灘上的沙粒加起來還多。
所以，莫耳日慶祝的是一座橋：在看不見與可測量之間，也在一個被忽視的想法和它最終被證明為正確之間。

discuss: Why do you think scientists need special units like the mole to talk about atoms?
Avogadro's idea was ignored for years. Can you think of other ideas that were laughed at before people accepted them?
Should school subjects have 'fun days' like Mole Day? Which subject would you choose, and how would you celebrate?

topic: World Polio Day
zh: 世界小兒麻痺日：只差最後一步

a.title: Almost Gone for Good
text: October 24 is World Polio Day. Polio is a disease caused by a virus. It mostly makes young children sick.
Polio can hurt the body's nerves. Some children cannot walk again after they get it.
In the past, polio was common all over the world. Parents were very afraid of it.
Then scientists made vaccines. One was a shot, and later one was a few drops in the mouth. The drops are cheap and easy to give.
Since then, millions of children have got the vaccine. Polio is now almost gone. Taiwan has been free of polio for many years.
But the virus is still found in a few places. World Polio Day reminds us to finish the job.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Why polio hurts the nerves in the body
Polio, a disease vaccines have almost ended
How the vaccine drops for polio are made
Why polio still exists in a few places
q.why: 全文講小兒麻痺與疫苗。

q.q: Who does polio mostly make sick?
opts: Old people
Doctors and nurses
Teenagers
Young children
q.why: 原文：“It mostly makes young children sick.”

q.q: Why are the vaccine drops useful?
opts: They work after only one drop for life
They cure children who already have polio
They are cheap and easy to give
They taste sweet
q.why: 原文：“The drops are cheap and easy to give.”

q.q: In the text, “common” means ___.
opts: seen very often
very dangerous
easy to cure
very rare indeed
q.why: common = 常見的。

q.q: What does “finish the job” mean in the last sentence?
opts: Stop giving vaccines because polio is gone
Build more hospitals
Find a new disease to fight
Make sure polio disappears everywhere
q.why: 讓小兒麻痺在全世界消失。

q.q: Taiwan has been free of polio for many years. Should Taiwanese children still get the vaccine? Which answer fits the text?
opts: Yes — the virus still exists elsewhere and could return
No — Taiwan has had no polio for many years now
No — vaccines are no longer useful against polio
No — the virus can only survive in very hot countries
q.why: 病毒仍存在少數地方，可能再傳入。

gt.en: Polio is a disease caused by a virus.
gt.zh: 小兒麻痺是一種由病毒引起的疾病。

gt.en: Polio can hurt the body's nerves.
gt.zh: 小兒麻痺會傷害身體的神經。

gt.en: In the past, polio was common all over the world.
gt.zh: 過去，小兒麻痺在世界各地都很常見。

gt.en: But the virus is still found in a few places.
gt.zh: 但是在少數幾個地方，仍然可以找到這種病毒。

tz: 10 月 24 日是世界小兒麻痺日。小兒麻痺是一種由病毒引起的疾病，大多讓幼兒生病。
小兒麻痺會傷害身體的神經。有些孩子得了以後，就再也不能走路了。
以前，小兒麻痺在全世界都很常見，父母們非常害怕它。
後來，科學家做出了疫苗。一種是打針，後來還有一種是在嘴裡滴幾滴。滴劑便宜又容易使用。
從那以後，數百萬名孩子接種了疫苗。小兒麻痺現在幾乎消失了，台灣也已經很多年沒有小兒麻痺了。
但是這種病毒在少數幾個地方仍然存在。世界小兒麻痺日提醒我們要把這件事做完。

b.title: The Last Mile Against Polio
text: Every October 24, health workers mark World Polio Day, an awareness day started by Rotary International to honour the fight against one of history's most feared childhood diseases.
Polio is caused by a virus that spreads mainly through contaminated water and hands. In a small number of cases it attacks the nerves and can cause lifelong paralysis.

In the early 1950s, epidemics left thousands of children unable to walk each year. In 1955 a vaccine developed by a team led by Jonas Salk was declared safe and effective, and a few years later Albert Sabin's oral vaccine — given as drops — made mass vaccination cheap and simple.

In 1988 the World Health Organization and its partners launched a global campaign to end polio. Back then, the disease paralysed an estimated 350,000 children a year. Since then, cases have fallen by more than 99 percent.
Wild poliovirus now survives in only two countries, Pakistan and Afghanistan, where conflict and distrust make it hard to reach every child.
Taiwan was certified polio-free as part of its region in 2000. Experts warn, though, that as long as the virus exists anywhere, every country must keep vaccinating.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Wild poliovirus now survives only in Pakistan and Afghanistan.
Polio cases have fallen by more than 99 percent since 1988.
Vaccines have now completely wiped out polio, so vaccination can stop everywhere.
Vaccines have nearly wiped out polio, but the last cases need lasting work.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: How much have polio cases fallen since 1988?
opts: By more than 99 percent
By about 90 percent
By just under 90 percent
By about 9 percent
q.why: 原文：“Since then, cases have fallen by more than 99 percent.”

q.q: Where does wild poliovirus still survive?
opts: India and Pakistan
Pakistan and Afghanistan
Afghanistan and Nigeria
Taiwan and Japan
q.why: 原文：“Wild poliovirus now survives in only two countries, Pakistan and Afghanistan, where conflict and distrust make it hard to reach every child.”

q.q: In paragraph 2, “contaminated” water is water that is ___.
opts: clean but very cold and hard
salty from the sea
dirty or carrying germs
boiled until safe
q.why: contaminated = 受汙染的。

q.q: Why must polio-free countries keep vaccinating?
opts: Polio is still common in most countries of the world
The vaccines stop working after just one year
The virus could travel back from where it still exists
The law on vaccinating children has no end date
