q.why: 線索：“Experts warn, though, that as long as the virus exists anywhere, every country must keep vaccinating.”

q.q: Which reason from the text best explains why the last polio cases are so hard to end?
opts: The polio vaccine no longer works against the virus
Doctors in most countries have stopped trying
Most families in those places have never heard of polio
Conflict and distrust make it hard to reach every child
q.why: 第五段：衝突與不信任使難以接觸每個孩子。

tr.en: Polio is caused by a virus that spreads mainly through contaminated water and hands.
tr.zh: 小兒麻痺是由一種病毒引起的，主要透過受汙染的水和手傳播。

tr.en: In the early 1950s, epidemics left thousands of children unable to walk each year.
tr.zh: 在 1950 年代初期，每年的疫情都讓好幾千名孩子無法走路。

tr.en: In 1988 the World Health Organization and its partners launched a global campaign to end polio.
tr.zh: 1988 年，世界衛生組織和它的夥伴發起了一場終結小兒麻痺的全球行動。

tz: 每年 10 月 24 日，醫療工作者都會紀念世界小兒麻痺日；這個宣導日由國際扶輪發起，向對抗史上最令人畏懼的兒童疾病之一的努力致敬。
小兒麻痺是由一種病毒引起的，主要透過受污染的水和手傳播。在少數情況下，它會攻擊神經，造成終身癱瘓。
在 1950 年代初期，每年的流行讓數千名孩子無法走路。1955 年，由喬納斯・沙克帶領的團隊研發的疫苗被宣布安全有效；幾年後，阿爾伯特・沙賓的口服疫苗——以滴劑的方式服用——讓大規模接種變得便宜又簡單。
1988 年，世界衛生組織和它的夥伴發起了一場終結小兒麻痺的全球行動。當時，這種疾病每年估計讓 35 萬名孩子癱瘓。從那以後，病例已經減少了超過 99%。
野生小兒麻痺病毒如今只存在於兩個國家：巴基斯坦和阿富汗；在那裡，戰爭和不信任讓人很難接觸到每一個孩子。
台灣在 2000 年隨所在區域一起被認證為無小兒麻痺地區。不過專家警告，只要這種病毒還存在於任何地方，每個國家都必須持續接種疫苗。

c.title: Why the Last One Percent Is the Hardest
text: There are few public-health stories as triumphant, or as unfinished, as polio's. World Polio Day, marked each October 24, celebrates a disease driven to the brink of extinction — and admits how stubbornly it clings on.

In the first half of the twentieth century, summer polio epidemics emptied swimming pools and terrified parents; the virus, usually silent, occasionally invaded the nervous system and left children paralysed. The 1955 announcement that Jonas Salk's injected vaccine worked was greeted almost like the end of a war, and Albert Sabin's oral drops later made immunisation affordable on a mass scale.

When the Global Polio Eradication Initiative began in 1988, polio paralysed an estimated 350,000 children a year in more than 125 countries. Cases have since fallen by over 99 percent, and wild virus persists in just two, Pakistan and Afghanistan.

Yet the final fraction is the most expensive and the most fragile. The remaining cases sit where conflict blocks vaccinators, where rumours breed suspicion, and where a single missed child can seed a new outbreak.

Eradication, after all, is unforgiving arithmetic: ninety-nine percent is not a near-success but an unfinished task. Only smallpox has ever been fully defeated in humans; polio's last mile will test whether the world can sustain attention long after a crisis stops feeling urgent.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Polio is almost gone, but the last fraction demands lasting effort.
Polio cases have fallen by over 99 percent, so the work is done.
Polio remains a major threat to children in most countries.
Smallpox and polio were defeated together at the same time.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In the final paragraph, “eradication” means ___.
opts: a slight reduction in cases
a newly developed vaccine
complete removal of something
a worldwide health campaign
q.why: eradication = 根除。

q.q: Why does the writer call eradication “unforgiving arithmetic”?
opts: The last few cases are the cheapest and easiest to stop
Anything short of 100 percent leaves the job unfinished
The case numbers are very hard to calculate accurately
Reaching 99 percent is close enough to call it a success
q.why: 99% 不算成功。

q.q: How would you describe the writer's tone?
opts: Purely celebratory
Hopeless and gloomy
Gloomy, but quietly hopeful
Celebratory but cautious
q.why: 讚揚中帶警惕。

q.q: How is the essay structured?
opts: A short biography of Jonas Salk and his life's work
A list of polio's symptoms and how to treat them
Vaccines → progress → why the end is the easiest part
Past fear → vaccines → progress → why the end is hardest
q.why: 結構如選項。

q.q: Which other situation best shows the writer's idea that the last 1 percent is the hardest?
opts: Starting a new project, the hardest part
Picking up the last bits of litter on a beach
Buying a new bike after saving for months
Starting to pick up litter on a very dirty beach
q.why: 最後一小部分最費力——與根除疾病的道理相同。

tz: 很少有公共衛生的故事像小兒麻痺這樣既光輝又尚未完結。每年 10 月 24 日的世界小兒麻痺日，慶祝一種被逼到滅絕邊緣的疾病——也承認它有多麼頑強地苟延殘喘。
在二十世紀上半葉，夏天的小兒麻痺流行讓游泳池空無一人，讓父母們驚恐萬分；這種病毒通常無聲無息，偶爾卻會入侵神經系統，讓孩子癱瘓。1955 年，喬納斯・沙克的注射疫苗被宣布有效，人們迎接這個消息的心情幾乎就像戰爭結束；後來阿爾伯特・沙賓的口服滴劑，更讓大規模接種變得負擔得起。
全球根除小兒麻痺行動在 1988 年開始時，小兒麻痺每年估計讓一百二十五個以上國家的 35 萬名孩子癱瘓。此後病例減少了超過 99%，野生病毒只殘存在兩個國家：巴基斯坦和阿富汗。
然而，最後那一小部分是最昂貴、也最脆弱的。剩下的病例，出現在戰爭阻擋了疫苗接種人員的地方、謠言滋生猜疑的地方，以及只要漏掉一個孩子，就可能引發一波新疫情的地方。
說到底，根除是一道毫不留情的算術：百分之九十九不是「差一點就成功」，而是「還沒完成的任務」。人類至今只徹底戰勝過天花；小兒麻痺的最後一哩路，將考驗世界能否在危機不再讓人覺得緊迫之後，仍然持續關注。

discuss: Why do you think the last few cases of a disease are often the hardest to stop?
Polio vaccines changed millions of lives. What other inventions have protected children's health?
If a disease is almost gone, should people keep getting vaccinated? Explain your view.

topic: United Nations Day
zh: 聯合國日
src: The New York Times · The Economist · United Nations

a.title: One Day for the World
text: October 24 is United Nations Day. It celebrates the day the United Nations, or UN, began in 1945.
The UN started after the Second World War. Countries were tired of fighting and wanted to keep peace.
Today, almost every country in the world is a member. They meet and talk instead of fighting.
The UN does many things. It helps people after disasters, sends food and medicine, and protects children's rights.
It also works on big problems that no country can solve alone, like disease, war, and climate change.
United Nations Day reminds us of one simple idea: when countries work together, the world is safer for everyone.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: The United Nations and why countries work together
How the UN helps people after big disasters
Why almost every country is a member of the UN
How the Second World War finally came to an end
q.why: 全文介紹聯合國。

q.q: When is United Nations Day?
opts: October 31
October 14
October 24
November 24
q.why: 原文：“October 24 is United Nations Day.”

q.q: Why did the UN start?
opts: During the Second World War, to win it
After the Second World War, to keep peace
After the First World War, to punish countries
To build one world government
q.why: 原文：“The UN started after the Second World War.”

q.q: In the text, a “member” is ___.
opts: the leader of one of the countries
a person who works for the UN
a meeting held in New York
a country that belongs to the group
q.why: member = 成員。

q.q: What is the main lesson of the day?
opts: Big countries should make decisions for everyone
The UN has already ended all wars in the world
When countries work together, the world is safer
Countries should stop talking to one another
q.why: 線索：“United Nations Day reminds us of one simple idea: when countries work together, the world is safer for everyone.”

q.q: Two classes keep arguing about the playground. Which idea is MOST like how the UN works?
opts: Hold a meeting where both classes agree on fair rules
Let the bigger class decide what everyone must do
Close the playground forever so nobody can use it
Let the two classes keep arguing until one gives up
q.why: 聯合國提供各國對話協商的場所。

gt.en: It celebrates the day the United Nations, or UN, began in 1945.
gt.zh: 它慶祝的是聯合國在 1945 年成立的那一天。

gt.en: Countries were tired of fighting and wanted to keep peace.
gt.zh: 各國厭倦了戰爭，想要維持和平。

gt.en: Today, almost every country in the world is a member.
gt.zh: 今天，世界上幾乎每個國家都是會員。

gt.en: It helps people after disasters, sends food and medicine, and protects children's rights.
gt.zh: 它在災難後幫助人們、送去食物和藥品，並保護兒童的權利。

tz: 10 月 24 日是聯合國日。它慶祝的是聯合國在 1945 年成立的那一天。
聯合國是在第二次世界大戰後成立的。各國厭倦了打仗，想要維護和平。
今天，世界上幾乎每個國家都是會員。它們開會、對話，而不是打仗。
聯合國做很多事。它在災難後幫助人們、送去食物和藥品，也保護兒童的權利。
它也處理那些沒有一個國家能獨自解決的大問題，像是疾病、戰爭和氣候變遷。
聯合國日提醒我們一個簡單的想法：當各國一起合作，世界對每個人都會更安全。

b.title: When Nations Talk
text: Each year on 24 October, the world marks United Nations Day, the anniversary of the day in 1945 when the UN officially came into being.
The organisation was born from the ruins of the Second World War. Its founders, having seen two world wars in thirty years, hoped that a place where countries could talk might stop a third.
Today the UN has 193 member states — nearly every nation on Earth. They gather in New York to debate, to vote, and, when they can, to agree.
The UN's work reaches far beyond politics. Its agencies feed refugees, fight diseases, care for children, protect human rights, and coordinate action on climate change.
It is far from perfect. Powerful countries can block decisions, and the UN often cannot force anyone to obey. Critics say it is too slow and too weak.
Yet its defenders point to a simple fact: since 1945 there has been no third world war. Imperfect as it is, a place where enemies must at least talk may be worth keeping.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The UN has grown to include 193 member states since its founding.
The UN, though imperfect, gives nations a place to talk instead of fight.
The UN, though imperfect, now makes all big decisions for its member nations.
The UN has managed to end all wars between nations since 1945.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；第四項錯誤。

q.q: How many member states does the UN have, according to the text?
q.why: 原文：“Today the UN has 193 member states — nearly every nation on Earth.”

q.q: Which is part of the UN's work beyond politics?
opts: Running national elections in each country
Building and training national armies
Collecting taxes from its member countries
Feeding refugees and fighting diseases
q.why: 原文：“Its agencies feed refugees, fight diseases, care for children, protect human rights, and coordinate action on climate change.”

q.q: In paragraph 4, a “refugee” is a person who ___.
opts: works for the UN in another country
travels abroad for a long holiday
has been forced to flee their home
moves to a new city for a better job
q.why: refugee = 難民。

q.q: What is the defenders' main argument in the last paragraph?
opts: No third world war since 1945, so a place to talk is worth it
The UN has successfully stopped every war since it was founded
The UN is a perfect organisation that needs no reform at all
The UN should be given its own powerful army to keep peace
q.why: 線索：“Yet its defenders point to a simple fact: since 1945 there has been no third world war.”

q.q: Critics say the UN is slow and often blocked. Which response best reflects the defenders' view in the text?
opts: The critics are completely wrong about the UN's problems
It is imperfect, but a place to talk beats having none
The UN should be closed and replaced with something new
Countries should simply act alone without the UN
q.why: 不完美，但對話的場所仍值得保留。

tr.en: Its founders, having seen two world wars in thirty years, hoped that a place where countries could talk might stop a third.
tr.zh: 它的創立者在三十年內見證了兩次世界大戰，希望一個讓各國可以對話的地方，能阻止第三次世界大戰。

tr.en: They gather in New York to debate, to vote, and, when they can, to agree.
tr.zh: 他們聚集在紐約辯論、投票，並在可能的時候達成共識。

tr.en: Its agencies feed refugees, fight diseases, care for children, protect human rights, and coordinate action on climate change.
tr.zh: 它的各個機構提供難民食物、對抗疾病、照顧兒童、保護人權，並協調對抗氣候變遷的行動。

tz: 每年 10 月 24 日，全世界都會紀念聯合國日，這是 1945 年聯合國正式成立那一天的週年紀念。
這個組織誕生於第二次世界大戰的廢墟之中。它的創立者在三十年內經歷了兩次世界大戰，希望有一個讓各國可以對話的地方，也許就能阻止第三次。
今天，聯合國有 193 個會員國——幾乎是地球上所有的國家。它們聚集在紐約辯論、投票，並在可能的時候達成共識。
聯合國的工作遠遠不只是政治。它的各個機構為難民提供食物、對抗疾病、照顧兒童、保護人權，並協調對抗氣候變遷的行動。
它離完美還很遠。強大的國家可以阻擋決議，而聯合國常常無法強迫任何人服從。批評者說它太慢、太無力。
然而，支持者指出一個簡單的事實：自 1945 年以來，沒有發生第三次世界大戰。儘管不完美，一個讓敵人至少必須對話的地方，或許值得保留。

c.title: An Imperfect Necessity
text: On 24 October the world observes United Nations Day, commemorating the moment in 1945 when a charter signed in San Francisco brought the organisation formally to life.

The UN was an act of exhausted hope. Its architects, surveying a planet twice shattered by world war within a single generation, built not a world government but something humbler: a permanent table around which states, however hostile, would be obliged to sit.

Judged against its loftiest ideals, the UN disappoints. Its Security Council can be paralysed by a single veto; its resolutions are often ignored; its peacekeepers arrive late, or not at all. To its critics it is a mere talking shop, long on words and short on power.

Judged more modestly, the record looks different. UN agencies vaccinate children, shelter refugees, monitor elections, and feed tens of millions; its very existence has made war between great powers, if not impossible, at least harder to begin. Absence, not presence, is often the truer measure of such an institution.
That may be the paradox worth marking each October: an organisation too weak to command and too useful to abandon — an imperfect necessity in a world that has, so far, invented nothing better.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: The UN is flawed but remains a useful, hard-to-replace institution.
The UN should be replaced by a new body with real powers.
The UN already controls much of world politics behind the scenes.
The UN has failed completely in its mission to keep peace.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “however hostile” describes states that are ___.
opts: very small and recently formed
friendly and working closely together
unfriendly or opposed to each other
newly independent from empires
q.why: hostile = 敵對的。

q.q: What does “Absence, not presence, is often the truer measure” suggest?
opts: It is most useful when countries stay away
Members are often absent from its meetings
It should hold its meetings less often
To see its value, imagine a world without it
q.why: 想像沒有聯合國的世界。

q.q: How would you describe the writer's attitude toward the UN?
opts: Completely admiring of everything it does
Critical of its weaknesses, yet valuing it
Completely hostile to the whole institution
Indifferent to whether it succeeds or fails
q.why: 批評中仍肯定。

q.q: How are paragraphs 3 and 4 organised?
opts: A list of the UN's agencies and what they do
The UN's history, told in time order
A harsh judgement, then a more modest defence
A comparison of two wars since 1945
q.why: 對比批評與辯護。

q.q: Which method from the writer would help you judge the value of any organisation?
opts: Imagine what would happen if it did not exist
Count how many offices and buildings it has
Look only at the times when it has failed
Ask only its leaders how well it is doing
q.why: 作者用「若它不存在」來衡量價值。

tz: 10 月 24 日，全世界紀念聯合國日，紀念 1945 年在舊金山簽署的一份憲章，正式讓這個組織誕生的那一刻。
聯合國是一份精疲力竭的希望。它的設計者看著一個在短短一個世代內被世界大戰粉碎了兩次的星球，打造的不是一個世界政府，而是某種更謙卑的東西：一張永久的桌子，讓各國——不管彼此多麼敵對——都必須坐下來。
若用它最崇高的理想來衡量，聯合國令人失望。它的安全理事會可能因為一張否決票而癱瘓；它的決議常常被無視；它的維和部隊總是晚到，甚至根本沒來。在批評者眼中，它只是一個空談俱樂部，話很多、權力很少。
若用比較謙虛的標準來衡量，紀錄就不一樣了。聯合國各機構為兒童接種疫苗、收容難民、監督選舉，餵飽了數千萬人；它的存在本身，讓大國之間的戰爭就算不是不可能，至少也更難開打。對這樣的機構來說，衡量它更真實的方式，往往是想像它「不存在」，而不是看它「存在」時做了什麼。
這或許就是每年十月值得紀念的矛盾：一個太弱而無法發號施令、又太有用而無法拋棄的組織——在一個至今還沒發明出更好東西的世界裡，一個不完美的必需品。

discuss: Should countries always try to solve problems by talking first? When is that hard to do?
The UN is strong in some ways and weak in others. Should it be given more power? Why or why not?
Name one global problem you think only countries working together can solve. How might they start?

topic: Pablo Picasso: Seeing the World in Pieces
zh: 畢卡索：把世界拆開來畫的人
src: Museo Picasso · The Guardian · The New York Times

a.title: The Painter Who Broke the Rules
text: Pablo Picasso was born on October 25, 1881, in Málaga, Spain. He became one of the most famous artists in the world.
Picasso could draw very well when he was a child. His father was an art teacher.
When Picasso was young, he felt sad, and he painted many pictures in blue. People call this his Blue Period.
Later, he and his friend Georges Braque tried a new way of painting. They showed faces and objects from many sides at the same time. This style is called Cubism.
Picasso made thousands of paintings, drawings and sculptures. He kept working until he was 91 years old.
His art shows us that there is more than one way to see the world.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Why Picasso painted so many pictures in blue
How Picasso's father taught him to draw and paint
The artist Picasso and his new ways of painting
How Cubism shows things from many sides at once
q.why: 全文介紹畢卡索。

q.q: What was Picasso's father's job?
opts: A famous painter
A sculptor
A museum guard
An art teacher
q.why: 原文：“His father was an art teacher.”

q.q: What is Cubism?
opts: Showing faces and objects from many sides at once
Painting only in cold shades of blue
Painting faces exactly as they look in real life
Making large sculptures out of wooden cubes
q.why: 原文：“They showed faces and objects from many sides at the same time.”

q.q: In the text, a “style” is ___.
opts: a kind of paint used by artists
a special way of doing something
a period of time in history
a famous painting in a museum
q.why: style = 風格。

q.q: Why do people call some of his paintings the Blue Period?
opts: He had only blue paint because he was poor
He lived in a small house near the blue sea
He felt sad and painted many pictures in blue
Blue had been his favourite colour as a child
q.why: 線索：“When Picasso was young, he felt sad, and he painted many pictures in blue.”

q.q: You want to draw your cat the way a Cubist would. What should you do?
opts: Draw the cat exactly as it looks in real life
Paint the whole cat in sad shades of blue
Take a photo of the cat instead of drawing it
Show the cat from the front and the side at once
q.why: 立體派同時呈現多個面向。

gt.en: He became one of the most famous artists in the world.
gt.zh: 他成為了全世界最有名的藝術家之一。

gt.en: When Picasso was young, he felt sad, and he painted many pictures in blue.
gt.zh: 畢卡索年輕的時候很難過，他用藍色畫了許多畫。

gt.en: They showed faces and objects from many sides at the same time.
gt.zh: 他們同時從許多不同的面向來呈現臉孔和物體。

gt.en: Picasso made thousands of paintings, drawings and sculptures.
gt.zh: 畢卡索創作了好幾千件畫作、素描和雕塑。

tz: 巴勃羅・畢卡索 1881 年 10 月 25 日出生於西班牙的馬拉加。他成為世界上最有名的藝術家之一。
畢卡索小時候就畫得非常好。他的父親是一位美術老師。
畢卡索年輕時心情很難過，畫了很多藍色的畫。大家把這段時期叫做他的「藍色時期」。
後來，他和朋友喬治・布拉克嘗試了一種新的畫法。他們同時從好幾個角度畫出臉和物體。這種風格叫做立體主義。
畢卡索創作了好幾千件畫作、素描和雕塑。他一直工作到 91 歲。
他的藝術告訴我們，看世界的方法不只一種。

b.title: The Artist Who Kept Reinventing Himself
text: Born in Málaga, Spain, on October 25, 1881, Pablo Picasso is often called the most influential artist of the twentieth century.
Trained by his father, an art teacher, he showed remarkable skill as a teenager. But he soon grew bored with simply copying what he saw.

In his early twenties he moved between Barcelona and Paris. After the death of a close friend, he painted poor and lonely people in cold shades of blue — the Blue Period — and later turned to warmer pinks and circus performers in his Rose Period.

Around 1907 he painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, a shocking picture of sharp, broken shapes. With his friend Georges Braque he then developed Cubism, a style that shows an object from several viewpoints at once.
In 1937, after German and Italian planes bombed the Spanish town of Guernica during the Spanish Civil War, Picasso painted Guernica, a huge black-and-white protest against the horror of war.
He kept experimenting with painting, sculpture and pottery until his death in 1973, leaving behind tens of thousands of works.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Picasso painted Guernica in 1937 as a protest against the horror of war.
Picasso painted in one style all his life and became the century's best-known artist.
Picasso painted circus performers in warm pinks during his Rose Period.
Picasso kept changing his style and became his century's most influential artist.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: What did Picasso paint during his Rose Period?
opts: Poor and lonely people in blue
Warmer pinks and circus performers
Faces seen from many sides at once
Black-and-white scenes of war
q.why: 原文：“After the death of a close friend, he painted poor and lonely people in cold shades of blue — the Blue Period — and later turned to warmer pinks and circus …”

q.q: What was the painting Guernica about?
opts: A happy town festival in the south of Spain
Picasso's childhood home in Málaga
The horror of war after a town was bombed
A circus performance he saw in Paris
q.why: 原文：“In 1937, after German and Italian planes bombed the Spanish town of Guernica during the Spanish Civil War, Picasso painted Guernica, a huge black-and-white protest …”

q.q: In paragraph 1, “influential” means ___.
opts: having a strong effect on others
having a lot of money and fame
very famous around the world
very creative and original
q.why: influential = 有影響力的。

q.q: What does the title “Kept Reinventing Himself” suggest?
opts: He invented new kinds of paint for other artists
He kept the same style but painted in many new cities
He kept changing his style and trying new ways of art
He moved to new cities often to find new friends
q.why: 不斷改變風格。

q.q: Which statement best explains why Guernica is still shown in discussions about war today?
opts: Art can make people feel the human cost of a real event
It is the most colourful painting that Picasso ever made
It was painted by a soldier who fought in the war
It shows a hopeful, happy ending to a terrible war
q.why: 格爾尼卡讓人感受戰爭的恐怖。

tr.en: Born in Málaga, Spain, on October 25, 1881, Pablo Picasso is often called the most influential artist of the twentieth century.
tr.zh: 1881 年 10 月 25 日出生於西班牙馬拉加的巴勃羅・畢卡索，常被稱為二十世紀最有影響力的藝術家。

tr.en: Trained by his father, an art teacher, he showed remarkable skill as a teenager.
tr.zh: 在當美術老師的父親指導下，他十幾歲時就展現出非凡的才華。

tr.en: With his friend Georges Braque he then developed Cubism, a style that shows an object from several viewpoints at once.
tr.zh: 接著，他和朋友喬治・布拉克發展出立體派，一種同時從好幾個角度呈現物體的風格。

tz: 1881 年 10 月 25 日生於西班牙馬拉加的巴勃羅・畢卡索，常被稱為二十世紀最具影響力的藝術家。
他由身為美術老師的父親訓練，十幾歲時就展現出驚人的技巧。但他很快就厭倦了只是照著看到的東西畫。
二十出頭時，他往返於巴塞隆納和巴黎之間。在一位好友過世後，他用冰冷的藍色畫貧窮和孤單的人——這就是「藍色時期」；後來他在「玫瑰時期」轉向較溫暖的粉紅色，畫馬戲團的表演者。
大約 1907 年，他畫了《亞維農的少女》，一幅由尖銳、破碎形狀組成、令人震驚的畫。接著他和朋友喬治・布拉克發展出立體主義，一種同時從好幾個角度呈現一個物體的風格。
1937 年，西班牙內戰期間，德國和義大利的飛機轟炸了西班牙小鎮格爾尼卡，畢卡索隨後畫了《格爾尼卡》，一幅巨大的黑白畫作，抗議戰爭的恐怖。
他在繪畫、雕塑和陶藝上不斷實驗，直到 1973 年過世，留下了數以萬計的作品。

c.title: Why Picasso Painted Faces from Two Sides
text: It is a familiar complaint in galleries: 'My child could paint that.' Pablo Picasso, born in Málaga on October 25, 1881, would hardly have been offended; by his teens he could already draw with academic polish, and he spent the rest of his long life deliberately unlearning it.

His early work was melancholy and lyrical — the cold blues of beggars and outcasts, then the softer roses of acrobats. But around 1907, with Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, he broke with the idea that a painting must imitate a single, fixed view of the world.

Cubism, which he developed alongside Georges Braque, fractured objects into planes and showed them from several angles at once. A face might appear in profile and from the front simultaneously, not because Picasso could not see, but because he wanted to paint what we know about an object, not merely how it looks from one spot.

That restlessness became a method. He moved from painting to collage, sculpture and ceramics, and in Guernica (1937) he turned the bombing of a Basque town into an enduring image of civilian suffering.

Picasso's legacy is complicated, including how he treated the people closest to him. Yet his central provocation endures: that seeing is not a passive act, and that an artist's job may be to show us the world in pieces so that we look at it again.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's main point?
opts: Picasso painted strangely because he never learned to draw realistically.
Cubism was invented largely by accident while Picasso was experimenting.
Picasso broke with realism to show how we see, challenging viewers to look again.
Picasso broke with realism because realistic painting was too hard for him to master.
q.why: 主旨。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “simultaneously” means ___.
opts: one after another
at the same time
very slowly
in secret
q.why: simultaneously = 同時。

q.q: Why does the writer say Picasso “would hardly have been offended” by 'My child could paint that'?
opts: Children's paintings were the inspiration for Cubism
He agreed that his paintings were really quite simple
He never heard such complaints during his lifetime
He mastered realism early and chose to unlearn it
q.why: 線索：“It is a familiar complaint in galleries: 'My child could paint that.' Pablo Picasso, born in Málaga on October 25, 1881, would hardly have been offended; by his …”

q.q: How does the writer treat Picasso's life and legacy?
opts: Admiring his art, while calling it 'complicated'
As flawless in both his art and his life
As completely negative about his influence
Criticising his art, while praising his private life
q.why: 最後一段。

q.q: How does the essay use the opening complaint?
opts: It raises a misunderstanding the essay then answers
It introduces a story about a talented child artist
It lists the famous galleries that show his work
It is never mentioned again after the first line
q.why: 以常見質疑開場。

q.q: Should we still admire an artist's work if they behaved badly in private? Which answer best matches the writer's approach?
opts: Ignore the artist's behaviour completely when judging
Destroy or hide the work of artists who behaved badly
Treat their behaviour as proof that the art is bad
Value the art while honestly admitting their faults
q.why: 作者肯定藝術，也承認爭議。

tz: 在美術館裡常聽到一句抱怨：「我的小孩也畫得出來。」1881 年 10 月 25 日生於馬拉加的巴勃羅・畢卡索，大概一點也不會被冒犯；他十幾歲時就已經能畫出學院派的精緻程度，而他漫長的餘生，都在刻意地把這些拋開。
他早期的作品憂鬱而抒情——先是乞丐和被社會遺棄者的冰冷藍色，接著是雜技演員的柔和玫瑰色。但大約在 1907 年，他以《亞維農的少女》打破了「一幅畫必須模仿單一、固定視角的世界」的觀念。
他和喬治・布拉克一起發展的立體主義，把物體拆解成一個個平面，同時從好幾個角度呈現。一張臉可能同時以側面和正面出現，不是因為畢卡索看不清楚，而是因為他想畫出我們對一個物體的「了解」，而不只是它從某一個位置看起來的樣子。
那份不安於現狀變成了一種方法。他從繪畫轉向拼貼、雕塑和陶藝；在《格爾尼卡》（1937）中，他把一座巴斯克小鎮遭到的轟炸，變成了一幅關於平民苦難、歷久不衰的影像。
畢卡索的歷史定位很複雜，包括他如何對待身邊最親近的人。然而，他最核心的挑釁至今仍然存在：觀看不是一種被動的行為，而藝術家的工作，也許就是把世界拆成碎片呈現給我們，讓我們重新去看它。

discuss: Picasso painted faces from several sides at once. Why might an artist choose not to paint things exactly as they look?
Guernica is a painting against war. Can art change how people feel about a real event?
Should we still admire an artist's work if the artist behaved badly in private life? Explain your view.

topic: The Day Football Got Its Rules
zh: 足球規則誕生的那一天
src: The FA · BBC Sport · The Guardian

a.title: One Game, One Set of Rules
text: Football is the most popular sport in the world. But long ago, there was a big problem: every school played it in a different way.
At some schools, players could carry the ball in their hands. At others, they could kick other players' legs!
On October 26, 1863, a group of men met in London. They started the Football Association, or the FA.
They wrote one set of rules for everyone. Players could not carry the ball, and they could not kick other players.
Some people liked carrying the ball, so they left. Their game later became rugby.
Today, people in almost every country play football with the same rules. It all started at one meeting in London.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How rugby became a different game
How football got one set of rules
Why football is the most popular sport
Why some schools let players carry the ball
q.why: 全文講 1863 年統一足球規則；其他是細節。

q.q: When was the Football Association started?
opts: On October 26, 1963
In December 1863
On November 26, 1863
On October 26, 1863
q.why: 第三段：On October 26, 1863。

q.q: Which rule did the FA make?
opts: Players could carry the ball but not kick legs
Players could kick other players' legs
Players could not carry the ball
Each school could keep its own rules
q.why: 第四段：Players could not carry the ball, and they could not kick other players。

q.q: In the text, “popular” means ___.
opts: liked by many people
very old
played by rules
played only in schools
q.why: popular = 受歡迎的。

q.q: Why was having one set of rules important?
opts: So football games would be much shorter and safer
So schools could finally stop playing football at all
So that rugby could become more popular than football
So teams from different places could play together
q.why: 統一規則後，不同地方的人才能一起比賽。

q.q: Two classes want to play a game together, but each class plays it differently. What does the text suggest they should do first?
opts: Let the stronger class decide during the game
Play twice, once with each class's rules, without talking
Agree on one set of rules before they play
Stop playing because they are different
q.why: FA 的做法：先開會訂出一套共同規則。

gt.en: Football is the most popular sport in the world.
gt.zh: 足球是全世界最受歡迎的運動。

gt.en: At some schools, players could carry the ball in their hands.
gt.zh: 在一些學校，球員可以用手拿著球。

gt.en: They started the Football Association, or the FA.
gt.zh: 他們成立了足球協會，也就是 FA。

gt.en: They wrote one set of rules for everyone.
gt.zh: 他們為所有人寫了一套規則。

tz: 足球是世界上最受歡迎的運動。但很久以前有一個大問題：每所學校踢足球的方式都不一樣。
有些學校的球員可以用手拿著球跑；有些學校甚至可以踢其他球員的腿！
1863 年 10 月 26 日，一群人在倫敦開會，成立了足球總會（FA）。
他們為所有人寫了一套規則：球員不能用手拿球，也不能踢其他球員。
有些人喜歡拿著球跑，所以他們離開了。他們的比賽後來變成了橄欖球。
今天，幾乎每個國家的人都用同一套規則踢足球。這一切都從倫敦的一場會議開始。

b.title: How a Pub Meeting Shaped the World's Game
text: On the evening of October 26, 1863, a group of men met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London. They represented a dozen clubs and schools, and they had one goal: to agree on a single set of rules for football.
At the time, the game was chaotic. Each English school had its own version. Some allowed players to pick up the ball and run; some allowed 'hacking' — deliberately kicking an opponent's shins.
Led by Ebenezer Morley, a solicitor who had founded his own club, the group formed the Football Association. Over several more meetings they debated what the game should look like.
The biggest arguments were about handling and hacking. When the FA banned both, a few clubs walked out, and their style of play later developed into rugby.
The first Laws of the Game were published in December 1863. Many details have changed since, but the core idea — a kicking game with shared rules — spread around the world.
Even the word 'soccer' comes from the FA: it is a playful short form of 'association football'.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: A few clubs walked out of the FA, and their game later became rugby.
An 1863 London meeting created shared rules that later spread worldwide.
The word 'soccer' comes from a short form of 'association football'.
Ebenezer Morley, a lawyer, had founded his own football club in London.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；其他是細節。

q.q: What was 'hacking'?
opts: Picking up the ball and running with it
Pushing other players off the field
Deliberately kicking an opponent's shins
Arguing loudly with the referee
q.why: 原文：“Some allowed players to pick up the ball and run; some allowed 'hacking' — deliberately kicking an opponent's shins.”

q.q: What happened when the FA banned handling and hacking?
opts: A few clubs walked out, and their game became rugby
All of the clubs agreed to the new rules immediately
The FA cancelled the ban after a few weeks
Schools across England stopped playing football
q.why: 原文：“When the FA banned both, a few clubs walked out, and their style of play later developed into rugby.”

q.q: In paragraph 2, “version” means ___.
opts: an official book of rules
the first official rule book of a sport
a single football match
a different form of the same thing
q.why: version = 版本。

q.q: Where does the word 'soccer' come from?
opts: A small town in England called Soccer
The name of Ebenezer Morley's own club
A short form of 'association football'
An American word meaning 'to kick'
q.why: 線索：“Even the word 'soccer' comes from the FA: it is a playful short form of 'association football'.”

q.q: Some clubs left the FA because they disagreed. Which statement best describes the result, based on the text?
opts: Two different sports developed — football and rugby
Football became much less popular in England
Rugby replaced football in most of the English schools
The clubs that left stopped playing completely
q.why: 退出的俱樂部發展出橄欖球，形成兩種不同運動。

tr.en: They represented a dozen clubs and schools, and they had one goal: to agree on a single set of rules for football.
tr.zh: 他們代表十幾個俱樂部和學校，而且只有一個目標：為足球訂出一套共同的規則。

tr.en: Some allowed players to pick up the ball and run; some allowed 'hacking' — deliberately kicking an opponent's shins.
tr.zh: 有些學校允許球員撿起球就跑；有些則允許「踢脛」——故意踢對手的小腿。

tr.en: Over several more meetings they debated what the game should look like.
tr.zh: 在接下來的幾次會議中，他們辯論這項運動應該是什麼樣子。

tz: 1863 年 10 月 26 日晚上，一群人在倫敦的共濟會酒館開會。他們代表十幾個俱樂部和學校，目標只有一個：為足球訂出一套統一的規則。
當時這項運動一團混亂。每一所英國學校都有自己的版本。有些允許球員撿起球就跑；有些允許「踢脛」——故意踢對手的小腿。
在自己創辦了一家俱樂部的律師埃比尼澤・莫利帶領下，這群人成立了足球總會。接下來又開了幾次會，討論這項運動應該是什麼樣子。
最大的爭論在於用手持球和踢脛。當足球總會把兩者都禁止時，有幾個俱樂部退出了，他們的踢法後來發展成橄欖球。
第一版《足球競賽規則》在 1863 年 12 月公布。之後許多細節都改變了，但核心概念——一種用腳踢、而且大家共用同一套規則的運動——傳遍了全世界。
就連「soccer」這個字也來自足球總會：它是「association football（協會足球）」一個俏皮的簡稱。

c.title: The Invention of a Common Language
text: It is easy to forget that the world's most popular sport was once barely a single sport at all. Before October 26, 1863, 'football' in England was a family of local customs, each school jealously guarding its own peculiar version.

That evening, representatives of a dozen clubs gathered at the Freemasons' Tavern in London and founded the Football Association. Their ambition was modest and practical: a shared code so that teams from different places could actually play one another.

The negotiations exposed a deeper divide. Some clubs prized handling the ball and 'hacking', the bruising practice of kicking an opponent's shins, as tests of manliness; others saw them as obstacles to skill. When the FA outlawed both, the dissenters withdrew, and their tradition hardened into rugby.

The Laws of the Game published that December were brief and, by modern standards, strange. Yet they established something more durable than any single rule: the principle that a game could belong to everyone only if everyone agreed to play it the same way.

From that principle grew leagues, international fixtures and eventually FIFA. A pub meeting about kicking and shins turned out to be an early experiment in global cooperation — a common language spoken with the feet.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: It mattered most because it banned hacking and handling for good.
The first Laws of the Game are still used, unchanged, today.
Football became a global game mainly because of FIFA alone.
It mattered less for any rule than for the idea of shared rules.
q.why: 主旨：重點在「共同規則」的原則。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “dissenters” are people who ___.
opts: write the rules
organise the meetings
disagree with a decision
play for the national team
q.why: dissenters = 持異議者。

q.q: Why does the writer call the FA's ambition “modest and practical”?
opts: They planned from the start to spread football worldwide
They simply wanted different teams to play each other
They hoped to make money by selling tickets to matches
They mainly wanted to ban the game of rugby
q.why: 第二段：目標務實。

q.q: How does the writer describe the first Laws of the Game?
opts: Brief and strange now, yet vital for their principle
As perfect rules that have never needed changing
As a failure that most clubs simply ignored
Long and detailed, much like the rules still used today
q.why: 第四段。

q.q: What image does the final sentence use to sum up the essay?
opts: A common language spoken with the feet
A long battle between rival schools
A ladder climbing to world success
A map of England's football clubs
q.why: 結尾比喻。

q.q: Which modern example BEST shows the writer's idea that shared rules make global cooperation possible?
opts: A school deciding to change its uniform colours
A football team choosing its new captain
Each country keeping its own type of phone charger
Countries agreeing on one standard for phone chargers
q.why: 共同標準讓各國能互通——和共同規則讓足球全球化相同。

tz: 我們很容易忘記，這個世界上最受歡迎的運動，曾經幾乎算不上是一項運動。在 1863 年 10 月 26 日以前，英國的「足球」是一群地方習俗的總稱，每一所學校都小心翼翼地守著自己那一套特殊的版本。
那天晚上，十幾個俱樂部的代表聚集在倫敦的共濟會酒館，成立了足球總會。他們的抱負既謙虛又實際：一套共用的規則，讓來自不同地方的隊伍真的能夠互相比賽。
協商過程暴露出一道更深的分歧。有些俱樂部把用手持球和「踢脛」——踢對手小腿的粗暴做法——視為男子氣概的考驗；另一些俱樂部則認為這些阻礙了技巧的發揮。當足球總會把兩者都定為違規時，持反對意見的人就退出了，他們的傳統後來固定成了橄欖球。
那年十二月公布的《足球競賽規則》很簡短，以現代的標準來看也很奇怪。然而，它確立了一個比任何單一規則都更長久的東西：一項運動只有在每個人都同意用同樣的方式來玩時，才能屬於每一個人。
從這個原則裡，長出了聯賽、國際比賽，最後還有國際足總（FIFA）。一場在酒館裡討論踢球和踢小腿的會議，原來是一場早期的全球合作實驗——一種用腳說的共同語言。

discuss: Why do games and sports need everyone to follow the same rules?
Some clubs left the FA and created rugby. Is it better to agree on one set of rules, or to let different versions exist?
Can you think of other things (not sports) that need shared rules so people around the world can work together?

topic: Gods of the North
zh: 北歐諸神
src: National Geographic · BBC Culture · The Economist

a.title: Gods of the North
text: Long ago, the Vikings of northern Europe told stories about powerful gods who lived in a world called Asgard.
The king of the gods was Odin. He was wise and old, and he gave up one eye to gain great knowledge.
The strongest god was Thor. He carried a magic hammer, and he made thunder when he swung it.
The most clever — and most tricky — was Loki. He could change his shape, and he loved to cause trouble.
A giant tree called Yggdrasil joined nine worlds together, from the gods above to the dead below.
The Vikings believed the world would one day end in a great battle called Ragnarok — and then begin again.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How Odin gave up one of his eyes for wisdom
Why Thor made thunder with his great hammer
The gods and world of Norse (Viking) myth
How the world ended in one great final battle
q.why: 全文介紹北歐神話；其他是細節。

q.q: What did Odin give up to gain knowledge?
opts: His hammer
One eye
His throne
One hand
q.why: 原文：“He was wise and old, and he gave up one eye to gain great knowledge.”

q.q: What happened when Thor swung his hammer?
opts: It made thunder
It made rain
It opened the nine worlds
It started Ragnarok
q.why: 原文：“He carried a magic hammer, and he made thunder when he swung it.”

q.q: In the text, “knowledge” means ___.
opts: a story told by the old gods
a magic weapon of the gods
a kind of battle or fight
things you know and understand
q.why: knowledge = 知識。

q.q: What was Ragnarok?
opts: A final battle, after which the world begins again
A battle that ended the whole world forever
A final battle that the gods won, so the world lasted
The name of the huge tree Odin hung from
q.why: 末段：大戰之後世界重新開始。

q.q: Odin gave up something precious to gain wisdom. Which real-life choice is MOST similar?
opts: Giving up your homework time to play games with friends
Sleeping late on a school day to feel rested
Giving up game time to study for an important goal
Asking a friend to do your homework for you
q.why: 犧牲珍貴的東西換取知識——如放棄遊戲時間去學習。

gt.en: The king of the gods was Odin.
gt.zh: 眾神之王是奧丁。

gt.en: The strongest god was Thor.
gt.zh: 最強壯的神是索爾。

gt.en: The most clever — and most tricky — was Loki.
gt.zh: 最聰明、也最愛耍詐的，是洛基。

gt.en: A giant tree called Yggdrasil joined nine worlds together, from the gods above to the dead below.
gt.zh: 一棵名叫世界樹的巨樹把九個世界連在一起，從上面的眾神一直到下面的亡者。

tz: 很久以前，北歐的維京人會講述一些住在一個叫阿斯嘉的世界裡、法力強大的神的故事。
眾神之王是奧丁。他睿智又年長，為了得到偉大的知識，他放棄了一隻眼睛。
最強壯的神是索爾。他拿著一把神奇的鎚子，一揮動鎚子就會打雷。
最聰明——也最狡猾——的是洛基。他會變身，而且很喜歡惹麻煩。
一棵叫做尤克特拉希爾的巨樹，把九個世界連在一起，從上面的眾神一直到下面的亡者。
維京人相信，世界有一天會在一場叫做「諸神黃昏」的大戰中結束——然後再重新開始。

b.title: The World Tree and Its Gods
text: More than a thousand years ago, the Norse peoples of Scandinavia told rich myths about gods, giants, and the fate of the world. The Vikings carried these stories across the seas.
At the centre stood Yggdrasil, an immense tree whose roots and branches linked nine worlds — the home of the gods, the land of humans, the realm of the dead, and more.

The gods themselves were powerful but far from perfect. Odin, the one-eyed king, hungered for wisdom and traded an eye to drink from a well of knowledge. Thor defended the gods with his thunderous hammer, Mjölnir.
And then there was Loki, a shape-shifting trickster, sometimes helpful and often dangerous, whose schemes drove many of the tales.
Unlike many mythologies, the Norse one had a clear ending in mind: Ragnarok, a final battle in which gods and monsters would destroy one another and the world would sink beneath the sea.
Yet even this end was not truly final. From the ruins, the myths promised, a green new world would rise, and life would begin again.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Odin traded one of his eyes for a drink from the well of wisdom.
Loki was a clever shape-shifting trickster who caused the gods trouble.
Thor, with his hammer, was the strongest of all the Norse gods.
Norse myth has flawed gods, a world-tree, and an end that brings renewal.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: What was Yggdrasil?
opts: An immense tree linking nine worlds
The deep well of knowledge and wisdom
Odin's great hall high in the sky
The final battle at the end of time
q.why: 原文：“At the centre stood Yggdrasil, an immense tree whose roots and branches linked nine worlds — the home of the gods, the land of humans, the realm of the dead, and more.”

q.q: What did Odin trade for wisdom?
opts: His hammer
A ship
An eye
His crown
q.why: 原文：“Odin, the one-eyed king, hungered for wisdom and traded an eye to drink from a well of knowledge.”

q.q: In paragraph 4, a “trickster” is someone who ___.
opts: fights bravely in every battle
uses tricks, often to cause trouble
rules the other gods with wisdom and care
protects the great world-tree
q.why: trickster = 搗蛋鬼。

q.q: Why is the Norse view of the end unusual?
opts: The gods always win the final battle against the giants
After the battle, a new world rises and life begins again
There is no final battle at all in the Norse myths
The world ends completely and nothing comes after it
q.why: 線索：“From the ruins, the myths promised, a green new world would rise, and life would begin again.”

q.q: A student says Norse gods are just like perfect superheroes. Which detail from the text best shows this is not true?
opts: Thor is the strongest god and protects the world
Odin is the wise king who rules the other gods
The gods have flaws and can even die at Ragnarok
The gods live in a great hall up in the sky
q.why: 北歐諸神不完美，也會在諸神黃昏中死去。

tr.en: Odin, the one-eyed king, hungered for wisdom and traded an eye to drink from a well of knowledge.
tr.zh: 獨眼之王奧丁渴望智慧，用一隻眼睛換來喝一口智慧之泉的水。

tr.en: And then there was Loki, a shape-shifting trickster, sometimes helpful and often dangerous, whose schemes drove many of the tales.
tr.zh: 還有洛基，一個會變身的搗蛋鬼，有時幫得上忙，卻常常很危險，許多故事都是由他的詭計引起的。

tr.en: From the ruins, the myths promised, a green new world would rise, and life would begin again.
tr.zh: 神話說，一個綠意盎然的新世界會從廢墟中升起，生命會重新開始。

tz: 一千多年前，斯堪地那維亞的北歐民族流傳著許多關於神、巨人和世界命運的豐富神話。維京人把這些故事帶過了大海。
故事的中心是尤克特拉希爾，一棵巨大的樹，它的根和枝幹連接著九個世界——眾神的家、人類的土地、亡者的國度，還有更多。
眾神本身力量強大，卻遠遠不完美。獨眼的國王奧丁渴望智慧，用一隻眼睛換來喝一口智慧之泉的機會。索爾則用他雷聲隆隆的鎚子「妙爾尼爾」保衛眾神。
還有洛基，一個會變身的搗蛋鬼，有時候幫得上忙，卻常常很危險；他的詭計推動了許多故事。
和許多神話不同，北歐神話心中有一個明確的結局：諸神黃昏——一場最後的大戰，眾神和怪物會互相毀滅，世界會沉入海底。
然而，就連這個結局也不是真正的終點。神話承諾，從廢墟之中，會升起一個嶄新的綠色世界，生命會重新開始。

c.title: A Mythology That Expected the End
text: Most mythologies tell how the world began; the Norse myths are unusual in dwelling, with grim relish, on how it will end. For the peoples of early Scandinavia, even the gods were mortal, and doom was written into the structure of things.

Their cosmos hung upon Yggdrasil, a vast world-tree binding nine realms. Among its branches moved gods who were strikingly human — Odin, who sacrificed an eye and hung himself upon the tree for wisdom; Thor, strong and short-tempered; Loki, whose cunning was both the gods' tool and their undoing.

What distinguishes these stories is their honesty about loss. The gods know that Ragnarok is coming — that they will fall, that Loki's children will break free, that the sun will be swallowed — and they fight on regardless.

There is a bleak courage in this. To act well while knowing you cannot win is, in the Norse imagination, close to the very definition of heroism; glory lies not in victory but in how one meets the end.
And yet the myths refuse final despair. After the fire and flood, a new earth rises, green and clean. Even a mythology braced for the end could not quite give up on beginning again.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Heroism is acting well when defeat is certain, yet hope remains.
In Norse myth, true heroes are those who always win their battles.
Norse myth teaches that the end of the world can still be avoided.
Norse myth is, above all, a celebration of the power of Thor.
q.why: 主旨：明知必敗仍行善，並期待重生。

q.q: In paragraph 1, “even the gods were mortal” means the gods ___.
opts: were very powerful
lived among humans
could die, like humans
were afraid of humans
q.why: mortal = 終將一死。

q.q: Why do the gods keep fighting at Ragnarok?
opts: They still believe that they can win in the end
They are certain that they will win the battle at the end
Odin forces all of them to keep on fighting
Meeting the end well is heroic, even without victory
q.why: 線索：“To act well while knowing you cannot win is, in the Norse imagination, close to the very definition of heroism; glory lies not in victory but in how one meets the end.”

q.q: How would you describe the mood of these myths?
opts: Cheerful and light from start to finish
Bleak yet courageous, and finally hopeful
Hopeless from beginning to end
Angry and violent, and nothing more
q.why: 淒涼帶勇氣，終有希望。

q.q: How is the essay mainly developed?
opts: Thor's many adventures → Loki's clever tricks
A simple list of the gods and their powers
The Norse world → a happy ending with no real doom
The Norse world → its honesty about doom → renewal
q.why: 結構如選項。

q.q: A team knows it will probably lose the final but plays fairly and with full effort. How would the Norse myths view this?
opts: As foolish — the team should simply give up
As heroic — meeting likely defeat with courage
As cheating, since the result was already known
As unimportant, because only winning counts
q.why: 北歐觀念：如何面對終局才是英雄。

tz: 大多數神話講的是世界如何開始；北歐神話特別的地方，在於它帶著一種陰沉的興味，細細描述世界將如何結束。對早期斯堪地那維亞的民族來說，就連神也會死，而毀滅早已寫進萬物的結構之中。
他們的宇宙掛在尤克特拉希爾上——一棵連結九個國度的巨大世界之樹。在它的枝幹之間活動的神，有著驚人的人性——為了智慧犧牲一隻眼睛、把自己吊在樹上的奧丁；強壯又脾氣暴躁的索爾；還有洛基，他的狡詐既是眾神的工具，也是眾神覆滅的原因。
讓這些故事與眾不同的，是它們面對失去時的坦誠。眾神知道諸神黃昏就要來臨——知道他們會倒下、洛基的孩子會掙脫束縛、太陽會被吞噬——而他們依然繼續奮戰。
這裡面有一種陰鬱的勇氣。在北歐人的想像中，明知不會贏卻仍然好好地行動，幾乎就是英雄氣概的定義；榮耀不在於勝利，而在於一個人如何迎接終點。
然而，這些神話拒絕最終的絕望。在大火和洪水之後，一片新的大地升起，綠意盎然、潔淨如新。就連一套準備好迎接末日的神話，也終究沒辦法放棄重新開始。

discuss: The Norse gods fight even knowing they will lose. Is that brave or foolish? Why?
What might a culture's idea of 'the end of the world' tell us about its people?
The Norse gods are flawed and mortal. Do flawed heroes feel more real to you than perfect ones?

topic: Why Your Mother Language Matters
zh: 母語的力量：國際母語日

a.title: The Day We Celebrate Our First Language
text: Every year on February 21, the world celebrates International Mother Language Day.
Your mother language is the first language you learn at home, from your family.
There are thousands of languages on Earth. Each one carries a culture, stories, and a way of seeing the world.
UNESCO, part of the United Nations, says children learn best when they can first study in their own language.
Around the world, teachers make books and lessons in local languages. In some places, they also teach in sign language so more children can join in.
Learning English is wonderful — and so is keeping the language your grandparents speak. Every language is worth protecting.

q.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: Why there are thousands of languages on Earth
How teachers make books in local languages
A day that asks every child to learn English first
A day that celebrates the first language we learn
q.why: 全文介紹國際母語日。

q.q: When is International Mother Language Day?
opts: February 12
December 21
February 21
September 21
q.why: 國際母語日是 2 月 21 日。

q.q: According to UNESCO, children learn best when they ___.
opts: can first study in their own language
study only in English from the start
learn many languages at the same time
study without any books at all
q.why: UNESCO：先用自己的語言學習。

q.q: In the text, “protect” means ___.
opts: to teach something new
to keep something safe
to change something
to forget something
q.why: protect = 保護。

q.q: What is the main message?
opts: Only the most popular languages are worth learning
Every language, including yours, is worth keeping
You should forget your mother tongue to learn English
All of the world's languages are really the same
q.why: 每種語言都值得保存。

q.q: A new student from another country speaks little Chinese. Based on the text, what would help most at first?
opts: Telling the student never to use their own language
Giving the student only Chinese tests from day one
Ignoring the student until they learn more Chinese
Letting them use their own language while learning
q.why: 文章：先用熟悉的語言學習效果最好。

gt.en: Every year on February 21, the world celebrates International Mother Language Day.
gt.zh: 每年的二月二十一日，全世界都會慶祝國際母語日。

gt.en: Your mother language is the first language you learn at home, from your family.
gt.zh: 你的母語是你在家裡、從家人身上學會的第一種語言。

gt.en: There are thousands of languages on Earth.
gt.zh: 地球上有好幾千種語言。

gt.en: Around the world, teachers make books and lessons in local languages.
gt.zh: 世界各地的老師都用當地的語言製作書本和課程。

tz: 每年 2 月 21 日，全世界都會慶祝國際母語日。
你的母語，是你在家裡從家人那裡學會的第一種語言。
地球上有好幾千種語言。每一種語言都承載著一種文化、許多故事，以及一種看世界的方式。
聯合國的一部分——聯合國教科文組織——說，孩子先用自己的語言學習時，學得最好。
在世界各地，老師們用當地的語言製作書本和課程。在有些地方，他們也用手語教學，讓更多孩子能一起學習。
學英文很棒——保留爺爺奶奶說的語言也一樣棒。每一種語言都值得保護。

b.title: Mother Tongues, Open Doors
text: On 21 February each year, UNESCO marks International Mother Language Day. In 2026, it focused on the role of young people in multilingual education.
A 'mother tongue' is the language you grow up speaking at home. For many children, though, school begins in a different language they barely understand.
Research shows that children learn to read and think more easily when they start in their own language. A familiar language is a bridge, not a barrier.

Across the world, projects are building that bridge. In Indonesia, young people are trained to teach in Indigenous languages. In Thailand, award-winning digital tools include features in sign language.
One organisation, active in 29 countries, publishes storybooks in local languages and makes versions in braille and sign language, so no child is left out.
Speaking more than one language is a gift. Learning a global language like English opens the world — while keeping your mother tongue keeps you connected to who you are.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: An organisation now publishes storybooks in local languages in 29 countries.
Children learn better starting in their mother tongue, and support is growing.
In 2026 the day focused on young people's voices in multilingual education.
Every child should start school in English to succeed in the modern world.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文；第四項相反。

q.q: Why can starting school in an unfamiliar language be a problem?
opts: Teachers do not like teaching in other languages
Books in other languages are far too expensive
Children forget their mother tongue straight away
Children may barely understand it and fall behind
q.why: 用聽不懂的語言上學，孩子可能跟不上。

q.q: What does the organisation active in 29 countries do?
opts: Trains new English teachers for village schools
Translates English storybooks for schools in big cities
Publishes storybooks in local languages, even braille
Makes language-learning apps for phones
q.why: 出版當地語言故事書。

q.q: A language is called a “bridge, not a barrier.” Here a bridge means ___.
opts: something that helps you cross or connect
something that blocks your way forward
a long and difficult road to travel
a special kind of language school
q.why: bridge 比喻連結。

q.q: What is the writer's view of learning English?
opts: It should replace your mother tongue entirely
It is not really useful for young children
It is valuable, alongside your mother tongue
It should wait until students reach university
q.why: 學英語有價值，同時保留母語。

q.q: A school plans to forbid students from speaking their home languages so they learn English faster. Which argument from the text challenges this plan?
opts: Children starting in a familiar language do better later
English is spoken in many countries around the world
There are thousands of different languages on Earth
Children who learn English first always do better later on
q.why: 研究顯示先用熟悉語言學習效果更好。

tr.en: In 2026, it focused on the role of young people in multilingual education.
tr.zh: 2026 年，這個節日的重點是年輕人在多語教育中的角色。

tr.en: For many children, though, school begins in a different language they barely understand.
tr.zh: 然而，對許多孩子來說，上學卻是從一種他們幾乎聽不懂的語言開始。

tr.en: A familiar language is a bridge, not a barrier.
tr.zh: 熟悉的語言是一座橋樑，而不是一道障礙。

tz: 每年 2 月 21 日，聯合國教科文組織都會舉行國際母語日。2026 年的主題聚焦在年輕人在多語教育中扮演的角色。
「母語」是你從小在家裡說的語言。然而，對許多孩子來說，學校卻是用一種他們幾乎聽不懂的語言開始上課的。
研究顯示，孩子先用自己的語言開始學習時，學閱讀和思考會比較容易。一種熟悉的語言是一座橋，而不是一道障礙。
世界各地都有計畫在搭建這座橋。在印尼，年輕人接受訓練，用原住民語言教學；在泰國，得獎的數位工具加入了手語功能。
一個在 29 個國家活動的組織，用當地語言出版故事書，還製作點字版和手語版，讓沒有一個孩子被排除在外。
會說不只一種語言是一份禮物。學會英文這樣的國際語言能打開世界——而保留你的母語，能讓你和自己是誰保持連結。

c.title: The Case for Mother Tongues
text: Each 21 February, UNESCO's International Mother Language Day celebrates the world's linguistic diversity. The 2026 edition spotlighted young people as leaders in multilingual education.

A mother tongue is more than a tool for communication; it is woven into identity, memory, and belonging. Yet millions of children begin school in a language they scarcely speak, and many fall behind before they have truly begun.
Decades of research point the same way: pupils who first learn to read in a familiar language understand more, stay in school longer, and later pick up additional languages more easily.

Around the globe, educators are putting this into practice. In Indonesia, local youth are trained to teach in Indigenous tongues; in Thailand, award-winning digital tools weave in sign language; and in India, thousands of sign-language videos now span more than twenty official languages.
A charity working across twenty-nine countries prints storybooks in local languages and adapts them into braille and sign language, so that disability and poverty need not mean exclusion.

None of this competes with learning powerful world languages such as English. The goal is addition, not subtraction: to open global doors while keeping alive the languages that carry a community's history.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: How India has made thousands of sign-language videos for its pupils
Why mother-tongue learning helps children, and how the world supports it
Why English has become the most important language for every child
Why children should switch to an international language as early as possible
q.why: 全文講母語學習的好處與全球推動。

q.q: What does decades of research repeatedly show?
opts: Pupils learn faster when they start in a foreign language
The language of teaching makes no real difference
Only gifted pupils benefit from their mother tongue
Pupils first reading a familiar language learn more
q.why: 研究一再顯示的結果。

q.q: Which real example is mentioned in the text?
opts: In Taiwan, all schools now teach in English only
In India, all pupils now learn in one shared official language
India's sign-language videos span over twenty languages
In Africa, nearly everyone speaks just one language
q.why: 印度的手語影片。

q.q: In the last paragraph, “addition, not subtraction” suggests the goal is to ___.
opts: add new languages while keeping your own
replace your mother tongue with English
learn fewer languages, but learn them well
study only maths and science instead
q.why: 保留母語，再學新語言。

q.q: Why does the writer value mother tongues?
opts: They are much easier to spell than English
They carry a community's identity and history
They are spoken by more people than English
Schools are required by law to teach them
q.why: 母語承載身分與歷史。

q.q: Which school policy best reflects the writer's idea of “addition, not subtraction”?
opts: Teaching only in English from the very first day
Removing English classes from the school entirely
Letting each student study in no language at all
Local language first, with English classes as well
q.why: 先用母語、再加學英語＝加法。

tz: 每年 2 月 21 日，聯合國教科文組織的國際母語日都在慶祝世界語言的多樣性。2026 年這一屆把焦點放在年輕人，作為多語教育的領導者。
母語不只是溝通的工具；它和身分認同、記憶與歸屬感交織在一起。然而，數百萬名孩子開始上學時所用的語言，是他們幾乎不會說的，很多人在真正開始之前就已經落後了。
數十年的研究都指向同一個方向：先用熟悉的語言學閱讀的學生，理解得更多、在學校待得更久，之後學習其他語言也更容易。
在全球各地，教育工作者正把這一點付諸實行。在印尼，當地青年接受訓練，用原住民語言教學；在泰國，得獎的數位工具融入了手語；在印度，數千支手語影片如今涵蓋了二十多種官方語言。
一個在二十九個國家工作的慈善組織，用當地語言印製故事書，並改編成點字版和手語版，讓身心障礙和貧窮不必等於被排除在外。
這一切都不是在和學習英文等強勢國際語言競爭。目標是「加法」，而不是「減法」：打開通往世界的大門，同時讓承載一個社群歷史的語言繼續活下去。

discuss: What is your mother tongue, and what can you express in it that is hard to say in English?
Should every child be taught first in their home language, even if very few people speak it? What would that take?
You are learning English now. How can you grow a new language without losing your first one?

topic: "LO": The First Message on the Internet
zh: 「LO」：網路史上第一則訊息

a.title: Two Letters That Changed the World
text: Today we send messages every day. But do you know the first message on the internet? It had only two letters: LO.
On October 29, 1969, a student in Los Angeles sat at a big computer. He wanted to send the word LOGIN to another computer far away.
He typed L, and it arrived. He typed O, and it arrived. Then he typed G — and the system crashed!
So the first message was just LO, like the start of 'hello'. About an hour later, the full word worked.
That small network was called ARPANET. Over many years, it grew into the internet we use today.
Now billions of people go online. It all began with two little letters.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: The first message ever sent on the internet
Why the computer system suddenly crashed
How many people around the world go online
How the word LOGIN was first invented
q.why: 全文講網路上第一則訊息。

q.q: What word did the student want to send?
opts: LO
HELLO
LOGIN
ARPANET
q.why: 第二段：LOGIN。LO 只是實際送出的部分。

q.q: What happened when he typed G?
opts: The full word arrived
The system crashed
The message went to the wrong computer
Another student replied
q.why: 原文：“Then he typed G — and the system crashed!”

q.q: In the text, “crashed” means the computer ___.
opts: became much faster
fell off the table
sent a very long message
stopped working suddenly
q.why: crashed = 當機。

q.q: What does the writer mean by “It all began with two little letters”?
opts: The internet is still only two letters long today
Today's huge internet began with a tiny first step
The first message was a mistake that was never fixed
Only two people used the internet back in 1969
q.why: 龐大的網路起點只是兩個字母。

q.q: Your first try at a new game app crashes. Based on the story, what is the best attitude?
opts: Give up, because a crash means the idea is bad
Delete the app forever and never try it again
Wait for someone else to fix it, since crashes are never your job
Fix it and try again — the first message crashed too
q.why: 第一則訊息也當機，修好後一小時就成功了。

gt.en: Today we send messages every day.
gt.zh: 今天我們每天都會傳訊息。

gt.en: He typed L, and it arrived.
gt.zh: 他打了 L，它傳過去了。

gt.en: That small network was called ARPANET. Over many years, it grew into the internet we use today.
gt.zh: 那個小小的網路叫做 ARPANET。經過許多年，它成長為我們今天使用的網際網路。

gt.en: Now billions of people go online.
gt.zh: 現在有幾十億人上網。

tz: 今天，我們每天都在傳訊息。但你知道網路上的第一則訊息是什麼嗎？它只有兩個字母：LO。
1969 年 10 月 29 日，洛杉磯的一個學生坐在一台大電腦前。他想把「LOGIN（登入）」這個字傳給遠方的另一台電腦。
他打了 L，傳過去了；他打了 O，也傳過去了。接著他打了 G——系統就當機了！
所以第一則訊息只有 LO，就像「hello」的開頭。大約一個小時後，完整的字才成功傳送。
那個小小的網路叫做 ARPANET。經過許多年，它成長為我們今天使用的網際網路。
現在有數十億人上網。這一切，都從兩個小小的字母開始。

b.title: The Night the Internet Said Its First Word
text: At about 10:30 p.m. on October 29, 1969, a student programmer named Charley Kline sat at a terminal at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA).
His team, led by computer scientist Leonard Kleinrock, was testing ARPANET, a new network funded by the US government to connect research computers in different places.
Kline's goal was simple: log in to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute, about 560 kilometres away. He began typing the word LOGIN while talking to a colleague at the other end by telephone.
'Did you get the L?' 'Yes.' 'Did you get the O?' 'Yes.' Then, as he typed the G, the Stanford system crashed. The first message ever sent across the network was therefore 'LO'.
After a quick fix, the full login worked about an hour later. By the end of 1969, four computers were connected.
ARPANET kept growing and introduced ideas, such as breaking messages into small packets, that still power the internet today.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: A 1969 test sent the first network message, 'LO', leading to today's internet.
ARPANET was a computer network funded by the United States government.
The Stanford computer crashed as soon as Kline typed the letter G.
A 1969 test sent a complete LOGIN message, proving the network worked perfectly.
q.why: 第一項涵蓋全文。

q.q: Who funded ARPANET?
opts: Stanford University
UCLA
The US government
A telephone company
q.why: 原文：“His team, led by computer scientist Leonard Kleinrock, was testing ARPANET, a new network funded by the US government to connect research computers in different places.”

q.q: How did Kline check whether the letters arrived?
opts: By looking at a screen at Stanford himself
By talking on the telephone with a colleague
By sending a short email to Stanford
By waiting for a printed reply to arrive
q.why: 原文：“He began typing the word LOGIN while talking to a colleague at the other end by telephone. 'Did you get the L?' 'Yes.' 'Did you get the O?' 'Yes.' Then, as he typed …”

q.q: In paragraph 3, a “colleague” is ___.
opts: a computer program
a university teacher
a government official
a person you work with
q.why: colleague = 同事。

q.q: Why does the writer mention 'packets' at the end?
opts: To show ARPANET sent each message in one large piece
To show ARPANET's ideas still power today's internet
To explain exactly why the first system crashed
To describe how letters were once sent by mail
q.why: 封包概念至今仍在使用。

q.q: Which piece of evidence BEST supports the claim that ARPANET led to today's internet?
opts: Its idea of packets still powers the internet today
It sent the two letters L and O as its first message
It had connected four computers by the end of 1969
Its first test took place late in the evening
q.why: 最後一段：封包概念延續到今天的網路。

tr.en: He began typing the word LOGIN while talking to a colleague at the other end by telephone.
tr.zh: 他一邊開始打 LOGIN 這個字，一邊用電話和另一端的同事說話。

tr.en: By the end of 1969, four computers were connected.
tr.zh: 到了 1969 年底，已經有四台電腦連在一起。

tr.en: ARPANET kept growing and introduced ideas, such as breaking messages into small packets, that still power the internet today.
tr.zh: ARPANET 持續成長，並提出了一些點子，例如把訊息切成小封包，這些點子到今天仍在推動網際網路運作。

tz: 1969 年 10 月 29 日晚上大約 10 點半，一位名叫查理・克萊恩的學生程式設計師，坐在加州大學洛杉磯分校（UCLA）的一台終端機前。
他的團隊由電腦科學家倫納德・克萊因羅克帶領，正在測試 ARPANET——一個由美國政府資助、用來連接不同地方研究電腦的新網路。
克萊恩的目標很簡單：登入大約 560 公里外、史丹佛研究所的一台電腦。他一邊打「LOGIN」這個字，一邊用電話和另一端的同事通話。
「收到 L 了嗎？」「收到了。」「收到 O 了嗎？」「收到了。」接著，就在他打 G 的時候，史丹佛的系統當機了。所以，第一則在這個網路上傳送的訊息就是「LO」。
快速修好之後，大約一個小時後，完整的登入成功了。到了 1969 年底，已經有四台電腦連上了網路。
ARPANET 持續成長，並引進了一些至今仍驅動著網際網路的概念，例如把訊息拆成一個個小小的「封包」。

c.title: An Accidental Hello
text: History rarely announces itself, and on the night of October 29, 1969, it arrived as a crash. At a terminal in a UCLA laboratory, the student programmer Charley Kline set out to log in to a computer at the Stanford Research Institute, some 560 kilometres north, over a fledgling network called ARPANET.

The procedure was almost comically low-tech. Kline typed while a colleague in Stanford confirmed each character over the telephone. The L arrived; so did the O. On the G, the remote system collapsed, and the first message transmitted across what would become the internet was an unintended 'LO'.
Leonard Kleinrock, who led the UCLA team, later relished the accident: no one could have scripted a more fitting first word than an abrupt 'lo', as in 'lo and behold'.

Funded by the US Defense Department to link scattered research computers, ARPANET was built on packet switching, which chops data into small, independently routed pieces. The design was meant for resilience and efficient sharing, not for billions of users.

That gap between intention and outcome is the real lesson of the night. The engineers were solving a narrow technical problem; they could not foresee social media, online classrooms or misinformation. Small experiments, it turns out, can grow far beyond the imagination of the people who run them.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's main point?
opts: The engineers designed ARPANET from the start to connect billions of people.
The first message came by accident, and the system outgrew its makers' aims.
ARPANET was essentially a failure, as the crash in its first test showed.
Kleinrock deliberately chose 'lo' as a fitting first word for the network.
q.why: 主旨：意外的開端，遠超設計者的想像。

q.q: In paragraph 1, “fledgling” describes the network as ___.
opts: large and fully finished
secret and military
fast and reliable
new and still developing
q.why: fledgling = 初生的。

q.q: Why does the writer call the procedure “almost comically low-tech”?
opts: A groundbreaking test was checked by telephone
The computers were built mostly out of wood
The engineers typed on an old typewriter
The test happened late at night in a lab
q.why: 突破性測試竟靠電話確認。

q.q: How does the writer view the crash?
opts: With embarrassment on the engineers' behalf
With anger at the engineers' carelessness
With amusement and a sense of its symbolism
As a serious failure that nearly ended the project
q.why: lo and behold 的巧合。

q.q: What does the final paragraph add to the story?
opts: A technical explanation of how packets work
A short biography of Leonard Kleinrock
A warning about modern internet security
A wider lesson about intention versus result
q.why: 延伸到意圖與結果的落差。

q.q: Which modern example best fits the writer's lesson about intention and outcome?
opts: A product that does exactly what it was designed to do
A school rule that has stayed the same for fifty years
A tool made for a small purpose later changes millions of lives
A tool built to connect billions that ends up used by only a few
q.why: 小目的的發明產生巨大、意想不到的影響。

tz: 歷史很少會預先宣告自己的到來；而在 1969 年 10 月 29 日晚上，它是以一次當機的方式出現的。在 UCLA 一間實驗室的終端機前，學生程式設計師查理・克萊恩準備透過一個剛起步、名叫 ARPANET 的網路，登入大約 560 公里以北、史丹佛研究所的一台電腦。
整個程序簡陋得近乎好笑。克萊恩一邊打字，史丹佛的一位同事一邊透過電話確認每一個字元。L 到了；O 也到了。打到 G 的時候，遠端的系統崩潰了，於是在後來成為網際網路的這個網路上，傳送的第一則訊息，是一個意外的「LO」。
帶領 UCLA 團隊的倫納德・克萊因羅克，後來很享受這場意外：沒有人能寫出比一聲突兀的「lo」更貼切的第一個字了——就像「lo and behold（瞧啊）」裡的那個「lo」。
ARPANET 由美國國防部資助，用來連結分散各地的研究電腦，建立在「封包交換」的技術上：把資料切成一個個小塊，各自找路傳送。這個設計是為了穩定可靠和有效率地分享資源，而不是為了數十億名使用者。
「原本的意圖」和「最後的結果」之間的落差，才是那一晚真正的啟示。工程師們在解決一個範圍很窄的技術問題；他們無法預見社群媒體、線上教室或假訊息。原來，小小的實驗，可以成長到遠遠超出主持它的人的想像。

discuss: The first internet message was an accident. Can you think of other inventions that started with a mistake?
The engineers could not imagine social media or online classes. What inventions today might change the world in ways we can't predict?
If you could send one message to the whole world, what two words would you choose?

topic: The War of the Worlds: Did Radio Really Cause a Panic?
zh: 《世界大戰》廣播：真的造成全美恐慌嗎？
src: Smithsonian Magazine · NPR · The Washington Post

a.title: Martians on the Radio
text: On October 30, 1938, the night before Halloween, many Americans were listening to the radio.
A radio show told a famous story called The War of the Worlds. In the story, Martians land in New Jersey and attack!
The show sounded like real news. There were 'reporters', loud noises and scared voices.
The next day, newspapers said that thousands of people were very frightened. They said people ran into the streets.
But later, historians studied it again. They found that not many people were really scared. The newspapers made the story bigger.
This story teaches us something important: always check if news is true.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How Martians landed in a small town in New Jersey
Why newspapers in America write about radio shows
A radio story about Martians, and whether it scared people
A radio story about Martians that made the whole country panic
q.why: 全文談火星人廣播劇與恐慌真假。

q.q: Where did the Martians land in the story?
opts: In New Jersey
In New York
On the Moon
In Washington
q.why: 原文：“In the story, Martians land in New Jersey and attack!”

q.q: What did historians find later?
opts: Thousands of people ran into the streets
Not many people were really scared
The show was never broadcast
People thought it was a joke from the start
q.why: 原文：“They found that not many people were really scared.”

q.q: In the text, “frightened” means ___.
opts: surprised
excited
confused
scared
q.why: frightened = 害怕的。

q.q: What lesson does the writer want us to learn?
opts: Never listen to the radio
Always check if news is true
Radio shows are always fake
Martian stories are dangerous
q.why: 線索：“This story teaches us something important: always check if news is true.”

q.q: You see a post: “Aliens have landed in Taipei!” What should you do first, based on the text?
opts: Share it with all your friends straight away
Share it first, then check later whether it was true
Check reliable news sources to see if it is true
Believe it, because it sounds so exciting
q.why: 文章結論：一定要查證新聞是否為真。

gt.en: In the story, Martians land in New Jersey and attack!
gt.zh: 在故事裡，火星人降落在紐澤西州並發動攻擊！

gt.en: There were 'reporters', loud noises and scared voices.
gt.zh: 節目裡有「記者」、很大的聲響，還有害怕的聲音。

gt.en: The next day, newspapers said that thousands of people were very frightened.
gt.zh: 第二天，報紙說有好幾千人非常害怕。

gt.en: But later, historians studied it again.
gt.zh: 但是後來，歷史學家重新研究了這件事。

tz: 1938 年 10 月 30 日，萬聖節的前一晚，很多美國人正在聽收音機。
一個廣播節目講了一個有名的故事，叫做《世界大戰》。故事裡，火星人降落在紐澤西州，發動攻擊！
這個節目聽起來就像真的新聞。有「記者」、很大的聲響，還有驚恐的聲音。
第二天，報紙說成千上萬的人非常害怕，還說人們都跑到了街上。
但是後來，歷史學家重新研究了這件事。他們發現，其實沒有很多人真的被嚇到。是報紙把這個故事誇大了。
這個故事教我們一件重要的事：永遠要查證新聞是不是真的。

b.title: The Panic That Wasn't Quite a Panic
text: On the evening of October 30, 1938, CBS radio broadcast a drama by Orson Welles and his Mercury Theatre: an adaptation of H. G. Wells's novel The War of the Worlds.

Instead of telling the story in the usual way, the show was written like a series of breaking news reports. Music was interrupted by 'bulletins' describing explosions on Mars and a strange object landing at Grover's Mill, New Jersey.
The next morning, newspapers across America reported that the broadcast had caused mass hysteria, with listeners fleeing their homes in terror.

The legend has lasted for decades. But many historians now argue that the panic was greatly exaggerated. Ratings suggest relatively few people were even listening, and most of those knew it was a play.
Why would newspapers exaggerate? Radio was a fast-growing rival for advertising money, and a story showing radio as dangerous and irresponsible served their interests.
So the real lesson of The War of the Worlds may be less about gullible listeners and more about how a dramatic story can spread — even when the facts are thin.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The famous 1938 panic was probably much smaller than newspapers claimed.
The show was cleverly written to sound like a series of breaking news reports.
Orson Welles adapted the story from a novel by the writer H. G. Wells.
Radio and newspapers were competing with each other for advertising money.
q.why: 第一項是核心；其他是細節。

q.q: Why did the show sound so real?
opts: It used interviews with real scientists
It was broadcast on every radio station
It was written like breaking news reports
It went on for the whole of the night
q.why: 原文：“Instead of telling the story in the usual way, the show was written like a series of breaking news reports.”

q.q: According to the text, why might newspapers have exaggerated the panic?
opts: Orson Welles had asked them to report a big panic
They truly believed that Martians had landed
They wanted to protect listeners from future shows
Radio was competing with them for advertising money
q.why: 原文：“Radio was a fast-growing rival for advertising money, and a story showing radio as dangerous and irresponsible served their interests.”

q.q: In paragraph 4, “exaggerated” means ___.
opts: reported fairly and accurately
made to seem bigger than it was
completely invented from nothing
quickly forgotten by everyone
q.why: exaggerated = 誇大。

q.q: What does the writer suggest the 'real lesson' is?
opts: Listeners in 1938 believed everything they heard on the radio
Radio is a more dangerous medium than newspapers are
Dramatic stories can spread even when facts are thin
Famous novels should never be adapted for the radio
q.why: 線索：“So the real lesson of The War of the Worlds may be less about gullible listeners and more about how a dramatic story can spread — even when the facts are thin.”

q.q: A website earns money when more people click its stories. Based on the text, why should readers be careful with its dramatic headlines?
opts: Websites that earn money from clicks never make mistakes
Like 1938 papers, it may gain from making stories bigger
Dramatic headlines on any website are always false
Only radio shows, not websites, can exaggerate stories
q.why: 報紙因利益誇大恐慌——有利可圖的媒體也可能誇大。

tr.en: Music was interrupted by 'bulletins' describing explosions on Mars and a strange object landing at Grover's Mill, New Jersey.
tr.zh: 音樂被「新聞快報」打斷，快報描述火星上的爆炸，以及一個奇怪的物體降落在紐澤西州的格羅弗磨坊。

tr.en: The next morning, newspapers across America reported that the broadcast had caused mass hysteria, with listeners fleeing their homes in terror.
tr.zh: 隔天早上，全美各地的報紙報導說，這個廣播造成了集體恐慌，聽眾驚恐地逃離家園。

tr.en: But many historians now argue that the panic was greatly exaggerated.
tr.zh: 但是現在許多歷史學家認為，那場恐慌被大大地誇大了。

tz: 1938 年 10 月 30 日晚上，哥倫比亞廣播公司（CBS）播出了奧森・威爾斯和他的水星劇團的一齣廣播劇：改編自 H・G・威爾斯的小說《世界大戰》。
這個節目沒有用一般的方式說故事，而是寫成一連串的新聞快報。音樂被一則則「快報」打斷，描述火星上的爆炸，以及一個奇怪的物體降落在紐澤西州的格羅弗斯米爾。
第二天早上，全美國的報紙都報導這次廣播造成了大規模的恐慌，聽眾嚇得逃離家園。
這個傳說流傳了幾十年。但現在許多歷史學家認為，當時的恐慌被大大誇大了。收聽率顯示，當時在聽的人其實相對很少，而大部分在聽的人都知道那是一齣戲。
報紙為什麼要誇大呢？因為廣播是一個快速成長、和報紙搶廣告收入的對手，而一個把廣播描繪成危險又不負責任的故事，對報紙有利。
所以，《世界大戰》真正的教訓，也許不在於聽眾有多容易受騙，而在於一個戲劇性的故事可以傳播得多廣——即使背後的事實很薄弱。

c.title: A Hoax About a Hoax
text: Few media legends are as durable as the night America supposedly believed it was being invaded by Mars. On October 30, 1938, Orson Welles's Mercury Theatre adapted H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds for CBS radio, cleverly disguising the story as a sequence of urgent news bulletins.

By the next morning, front pages were thick with accounts of terrified listeners crowding roads and churches. The episode became a textbook example of mass credulity — proof, it seemed, of the hypnotic power of the new medium.

Later scholarship has been far more sceptical. Audience ratings indicate that only a small share of radio owners were tuned in, and contemporary reports of chaos rest largely on anecdote. Some listeners were certainly alarmed, but the nationwide hysteria appears to have been largely a newspaper creation.
The motive is not hard to find. Print journalism was losing advertisers to radio, and a tale of irresponsible broadcasting flattered newspapers as the sober guardians of truth.

The irony is delicious: the enduring story about people being fooled by fake news was itself, in large part, fake news. In an age of viral rumours, the episode is worth remembering less as a warning about credulous audiences than as a reminder to ask who benefits when a sensational story is told.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: The panic was largely a newspaper invention — a lesson in doubting sensation.
The broadcast proves that radio listeners in 1938 were very easily fooled.
Orson Welles carefully intended to fool the American public that night.
Radio was far more trusted than newspapers by Americans in 1938.
q.why: 主旨：恐慌多半是報紙製造的。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “sceptical” means ___.
opts: certain and confident
easily fooled by what you hear
doubtful; not easily convinced
interested and excited
q.why: sceptical = 懷疑的。

q.q: Why does the writer call it ironic that the story was “itself, in large part, fake news”?
opts: Orson Welles pretended that the broadcast was real news
Two different radio stations broadcast fake shows that night
The novel the show was based on was a fake as well
The claim that people were fooled was itself largely false
q.why: 「被假新聞騙」的說法本身大半也是假新聞。

q.q: What tone does the writer use in “The irony is delicious”?
opts: Angry and bitter
Amused and pointed
Sad and regretful
Neutral and dry
q.why: 玩味、一針見血。

q.q: How is the essay organised?
opts: Legend → newspaper version → evidence → motive → lesson
The broadcast → the novel → Orson Welles's later career
A list of the most famous fake news stories in history
A comparison between early radio and early television
q.why: 結構如選項。

q.q: Which question is MOST useful to ask, following the writer's advice, when you read a shocking story?
opts: How many people have shared it so far?
Has a famous newspaper already reported it?
Is it longer than most other stories?
Who benefits if people believe this story?
q.why: 結尾：ask who benefits when a sensational story is told。

tz: 很少有媒體傳說像「美國以為自己被火星入侵的那一晚」那樣經久不衰。1938 年 10 月 30 日，奧森・威爾斯的水星劇團為 CBS 廣播改編了 H・G・威爾斯的《世界大戰》，巧妙地把故事偽裝成一連串緊急的新聞快報。
到了第二天早上，各報頭版充斥著驚恐聽眾擠滿道路和教堂的報導。這件事成了「群眾輕信」的教科書範例——似乎證明了這種新媒體催眠般的力量。
後來的研究則抱持懷疑得多的態度。收聽率顯示，只有一小部分擁有收音機的人收聽了這個節目，而當時關於混亂的報導，大多只是依據一些軼聞。確實有些聽眾受到驚嚇，但全國性的歇斯底里，看起來大多是報紙製造出來的。
動機並不難找。平面媒體正把廣告主流失給廣播，而一個關於廣播不負責任的故事，正好把報紙捧成了冷靜可靠的真相守護者。
諷刺得令人玩味：這個流傳不衰、關於人們被假新聞欺騙的故事，本身在很大程度上就是假新聞。在一個謠言瘋傳的時代，這件事值得被記住的原因，與其說是對輕信觀眾的警告，不如說是在提醒我們：當一個聳動的故事被講出來時，要問一問——誰能從中得到好處？

discuss: Why do you think a story about people panicking became so famous, even if it was exaggerated?
When you see shocking news online today, how can you check whether it is true?
The writer says to ask 'who benefits' when a sensational story is told. Can you give an example?

topic: Halloween
zh: 萬聖節

a.title: Trick or Treat!
text: October 31 is Halloween. It is a fun and spooky night, loved by children in many countries.
People wear costumes. They dress up as ghosts, witches, superheroes, or even cats!
Children go from house to house and say, “Trick or treat!” Neighbours give them candy.
Families carve pumpkins. They cut a scary face into a pumpkin and put a light inside. This is called a jack-o'-lantern.
Homes are covered in spider webs, bats, and paper skeletons. Everything looks a little scary — but it is all just for fun.
Halloween is a night of games, sweets, and imagination. What costume would you like to wear?

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How to carve a face into a pumpkin
Why so many children love Halloween candy
Halloween and how people celebrate it
Spider webs, bats and paper skeletons
q.why: 全文介紹萬聖節；其他是細節。

q.q: When is Halloween?
opts: November 1
October 31
October 13
December 31
q.why: 原文：“October 31 is Halloween.”

q.q: What do children say to get candy?
opts: “Happy Halloween!”
“Give me candy!”
“Thank you!”
“Trick or treat!”
q.why: 原文：“Children go from house to house and say, “Trick or treat!” Neighbours give them candy.”

q.q: To “carve” a pumpkin means to ___.
opts: cut a shape or face into it
paint it bright orange
fill it with candy and sweets
grow it in the garden
q.why: carve = 雕刻。

q.q: How does the writer say the scary decorations feel?
opts: Truly frightening for most people
Sad, lonely and a little strange
Scary-looking, but just for fun
Boring, old and not very exciting
q.why: 線索：“Everything looks a little scary — but it is all just for fun.”

q.q: Your class is planning a Halloween party for young children. Which idea matches the spirit described in the text?
opts: Very scary masks that might make children cry
Fun costumes and a little spooky decoration
No costumes or decorations of any kind at all
A quiet spelling test instead of a party
q.why: 文中萬聖節「看起來有點嚇人，但都是為了好玩」。

gt.en: It is a fun and spooky night, loved by children in many countries.
gt.zh: 這是一個好玩又有點嚇人的夜晚，深受許多國家的孩子喜愛。

gt.en: They dress up as ghosts, witches, superheroes, or even cats!
gt.zh: 他們打扮成鬼、女巫、超級英雄，甚至是貓！
